div.head: }.7,r4.,1 McDOUGALL's pent SELF-RAISING FLOUR unrivalled The Examiner. Saturday, July 31, 1909,
div.p: }.7,r4.,1 McDOUGALL's pent SELF-RAISING FLOUR unrivalled The Examiner. Saturday, July 31, 1909,
iPRACTICAL POULTRY FARMING.
[By Redcap.]
CONTRASTS BETWEEN OLD AND NEW BIRDS
OF POULTRY.

The rapid growth of exhibition poultry farming is indirectly affecting a similar growth in utility stock. Most of the grand old breeds have had to give placel to maily' modernised and made breeds. Many novices have the impression that unless you obtain the latest fashion you cannot succeed. 'lbis is an erroneous idea and I shall endeavour to explain why. When aiming at perfection in show points, inbreeding has to be resorted to. This is detrimental from a utility standpoint, or why -should crossbreds be so often _recommended. A short review therefore will soon show how very much altered are the breeds to-day, compared with those of a few years past. Take, for instance, the Langshan. Since its importation into this country in 1872 it has been sub- jected to very much alteration in tye and also quality. The originals were called Croad Langshans, taking their name from' Major Croad who first imported them to England. The modern Langshan is different altogether in type, and I must say that the result of such modernising has been detrimental to its utility qualities. Length of -limb and slim bless of feather in the modern Langshan has been aimed at to make it more distinct from the broad. Now the broad Lano•shan is a cobby bird, low on leg, and with an abundance of feather; two essentials in an all-round utility bird. Without-the least doubt the broad-is one ! of the very best breeds of poultry we possess. A good layer of rich brown eggs and a very acceptable table bird. It seemed at one time to have lost a-great deal of its original popularity owing to the modernising process of the eXhihition men, who are often mere faddists. Now lam glad to say it is more extensively bred, and in a few- years time we shall have the broad Lan,gshan once more placed in its right position as a good all-round utility fowl. , Let me just note by the way, that it is about the very best pure breed of poultry we possess for town runs, being dark in plumage and docile in habit, and easy to rear. Not so with the modern Langshan. infusion of other blood has robbed it of many qualities. It is far more difficult to rear than the broad, principally owing to great length of leg. And as a result leg weakress is prevalent among young stock. So if your mind is made up for Lan,,shans, and utility purposes your object, select the broad.

THE MEDITERRANEAN BREEDS have undergone a great change during the last twenty years or more. The minorca of to-day is a far different fowl than the minorca of a few years ago. Length of limb again, as, in the Langshan, has proved detrimental, together with the desire for excess in. comb and wattles. Large combs and wattles are not only unnecessary but very burden- some not to sr. eak of the danger of frost in winter. It is a common occurrence to see the combs of the light breeds badly frost-bitten in winter time. It must therefore be a great drawback and is often found a necessity to take off the comb by dub- bing, so as to enable the fowl to exist at all. Surely this unessential craze could be very much modified by the exhibition men. And if so it would add to the popularity of the Minorca and it would also mean a more extensive breeding of this most useful egg pro- -ducer. The same remarks apply equally to the Andalusian Ancona, and the whole of the Leghorn tribe. There is not so much heard to-day of the marvellous egg producing feats of the black Leghorn as was the case in say the years 1901-02. I do not intend to infer that there are not good laying strains to-day. I know that there are ; but, generally speaking the exhibition specimen has been so much the victim of craze for show- points at the cost of utility points that very much progress cannot be recorded. The Andalusian already mentioned is not so largely bred as it used to be. For what reason Ido not know. It is a most useful fowl ; and I am inclined to think that when the craving for new breeds is waning the Andalusian will again find many admirers. I could not close my remarks on the Mediterranean breeds without saying a word in praise of the old black Spanish fowl. Where are they to-cry? I have to confess. that perhaps I might have urged their claims sooner. But, however, "never too late to mend," and I hope some one, as a result, will adopt this grand old breed. They are layers of the largest white-shelled eggs of any breed of poultry, and 'plenty of them. handsome in appearance and very much more hardy, than is claimed for them by many back-yards! this is the fowl for you ! Eggs ! Why the eggs from a black Spanish is as big as three -of those from some of the new-fangled breeds, It is counnonly understood that Spanish are weakly and difficult to rear. Given proper natural conditions this is not so. It is rather because the methods of forcing so commonly adopted by exhibition men make Jowls weakly. The Spanish fowl with its great amount of white-lobed face is more a victim to such methods of forcing than all other breeds put together. Thus, you have the cause of their weakness in a nut- shell. Any fowl which is kept in a very warm, confined and dark room is bound to be more or less weakly in constitution. Great diffi- culty is now experienced in obtaining a good strain of Spanish : but when possible to do as I would strongly recommend my readers to go in for them. And in the course of a few seasons you would be able to create a good sound strain for yourself. The fine qualities of the Spanish would soon create their own demand. Ready sales for surplus stock would not be a difficult matter- at all. It is only when the practical knowledge is gained of the best that is in some of the old breeds that their return in the poultry world -will be assured, What I want to try and show in this article is this. Utility poultry and exhibition poultry are entirely separate sections in poultrydom. The two have through lack of knowledge by novices and others, became mixed. People who have decided lo go in for utility stock have purchased fowls bred from exhibition specimens, thinking of course. that by so doing they would obtain the best. Their mistake has been in • not taking into consideration the fact that all exhibition specimens have been so unbred as to be practically useless for utility purposes. The old pure breeds of poultry have been used in he making up of the more fashionable new breeds. "Many have been neglected until now one scarcely sees the farm-yard head by, for instance, the grand old Dorking or Black Spanish Cockerel. I did not want it to be understood that exhibition poultry is a drawback to the progress of poultry culture. What I would like to sees this. That the foremost points of excellence in fancy poultry should be from a commercial point of view. Show your fowls, win your cups and special prizes ; but at -the same time try and reduce the national egg bill. This cannot be done by.. inking the broad-langshan " walk on stilts "any mOre than a modern Minorca is kept so busy carrying an abnormally iZed comb that it hasn't time to lay an egg. Again, might I remind some of our fanciers that a Black Spanish was never intended to be reared in a greenhouse, but rather on a green field. Take any other line of live. stock and notice how carefully and distinctly the two factors are watched.
UTILITY AND EXHIBITION,

What we want to-day in poultry culture is, that points which assist utility properties should be aimed at. And not points which are so difficult to obtain that much injurious inbreeding has to be adopted. For a fixed type you must inbreed, which means a high percentage of wasters. For utility pui poses you must have the infusion of new and unrelated blood, which means in turn constitutionally sound stock and good returns. In conclusion let me make an appeal for the hod old breeds. It is difficult in the booming of the new ones to make one's self heard. But as time goes on, and when one realizes that such booming has been chiefly forielfish interests that the old breeds will have another chance. We have got sufficient in numbers of variety already. What we want is the careful improving and retaining of the best qualities of those we now have. But if we continue to go on adding each year to an already congested list, we shall scarcely lave a pure-bred variety left. There will be so many new breeds and all" pure-breeds " that they will be all cross-bred. And the fOreigner will con- tinue to dump his eggs on the British Market. Next week" Diseases of Poultry and their Cure."

Amongst stories dEaling with the science of box'ng 'there are few finer examples than "Rodney Stone" and "The Croxley Master," by Sir A. Conon Doyle, who is -a recognised authority on the subject. Readers of the "Strand Magazine,' in which these stories first appeared, will be interested to know that the August number will contain a splendid complete story by Sir &Conan Doyle entitled " The Lord of Falcon-bridge." In thl;--.3tory will be found not only a super descrip- tion of 'L. fight, but also one of the most dramatic situations has leen put before the public of recent years.

div.head: [ALL RIGHTS RESERVED.] WHOSE HAND?
div.p: [ALL RIGHTS RESERVED.] WHOSE HAND?
Dr ANNIE 0. TIBBITS.
Author of "The Love that Won," " Hunied Down," "Hidden Hands," "The Finger of Fate," "Robes of Shame," eze.

SYNOPSIS OF PRECEDING CHAPTERS: As a vessel is going down Olga Murray tells Dr. Dacre that, six years since, she /murdered Stephen Henderson,. of Greatbridge 'Hall, for which crime suspicion fell on Richard Sterry. If possible, the statement which she signs is to be kept from her lover, Sir Geoffrey Verriker. A bottle containing the document is flung- into the sea Sir Geoffrey, who rescues Olga from 'the wreck, insists on taking her to his mother at fiemscote Hall, of whidh he has just come into possession by the death of his uncle. Mrs. Dunston was to have married the uncle, and she plots with her daughter Julia to make the latter Lady Verriker by a Marriage with Geoffrey. or Geoffrey's cousin Edward. Dick Sterry owns the neighbouring estate to tile Verrikers, and is in love with Geoffrey's sister. As Geoffrey and Olga are nearing home Dick gets into the railway carriage. He lives near Greatbridge. Ho does not recognise Olga, but when Ethel Verriker introduces him next day Olga fainta. VIII.
CHAPTER.

When - Olga had opened her eyes she had found herself in a darkened room, with only Geoffrey beside her. She sprang up with a start. • " Geoffrey," she said, wilely. "I thought-" "Thought what. darling? A lot of non- sense, of course. But never mind it now. Le back, and shut your eyes again. That beas:ty sea business has upset you more even than I thought, and we shall have to take care of you, Olga, I .can .see."
She slrugglecl_ for hien th.

"But I---ut I am all right," she stam- mered. "There is nothing th matter " "Then what made you faint?" Geoffrey asked, smiling at her. "It looks as if the was nothing the matter when you faint tar nothing, doesn't it, eh? " • Olga shuddered, and lay back. She shut her eyes, and again she seemed to hear Ethel'a voice announcing Richard Sterry; and again Olga seemed to see him standing there, a fo!in dim to her eyes, with the sunshine streami;t: from behind him, leaving his face in th shadow. " I—l must have seemed very silly," si:e said, suddenly, opening her eyes again and looking closely at Geoffrey. " Didn't they think me very silly?" "They? Ethel and Dick Sterry, do you mean?" he asked. "Well, I don't know. We were too much alarmed to stop and think whether you looked silly or not, darling. I dare Say you did, my goose. But tall me, how do you feel now? "All right--quite all right." she said, hastily. "Only "—she passed her -hand across her face—" only—what made me faint like that?" she added, unsteadily. "That's what I want to . know," sall Geoffrey. "That's what we all want to kno.v. But the fact is, you haven't got right again since our dip in the sea. Your nerves are un- strung or something, and I've sent for a doctor to come in and see you this afternoon. Sterry says there's a man at Greatbridge who is a specialist, and we've sent for him." "A doctor? Oh, no, no " Olga started un again. "Geoffrey, there is nothing the matter—nothing—nothing. the matter. won't see any doctor, Geoffrey. And—and did you say a doctor from Greatbridge? " Her eyes were fixed wildly on his. Ti breath came in quick gasps from between I .er white _lips.

" Why- not, darling? " Geoffrey asked. "It is only a matter of ten miles or o, and I wanted the best man we could get. You are bound to be, shaken a bit by our adventure, and I can't have you ill, darling. I must have you right." „ . . _ . _

"Bit Gre-atbridge ! " She lay back again, staring with wild, bright eyes across the room. She saw nothing of it—nothing of the quaint old Queen Anne furniture, nothing the heavy tapestries or the carved panelling —nothing but a picture that was beginning to haunt her afresh—a picture of herself stand- ing on the thresh Old of a darkened room, pausing to hear a man draw his last breath. "It is—it is such a long way," she said, unsteadily, after a -minute. think you mad ! Who is it you have sent for?"

",Collins, I think Sterry said his name was —Sir John Collins, a nerve specialist." Olga passed her hand Across her face, and kept it over her eyes. And—and Mr. Sterry—didn't he think— didn't he think I was silly?" she asked, slowly, with great effort. " Well, he didn't say so, and he didn't be- have as though he did," Geoffrey said. ,"lie helped to carry you here, and he tore about for brandy and water; so it doesn't look as though he thought you were doing it on purpose, goose !" Olga lay still again for a moment. Richard Starry ! How his name rang in her ears ! How it drowned every other sound for her ! "Did he—did he say anything about me?" she said. "I —I was speaking to him, wasn't I, when I fainted?"

"No, ;darling. He was standing in the doorway. I don't think you halt] seen him. But, anyhow, you w 'll have an opportunity of making it up. He'll be in again this afternoon. You heard Ethel say he lived only next door." Olga nodded. _

"Has he always lived there?" she asked. "I don't know," said Geoffrey. "You see, we ourselves have only just come. Mother and Ethel have not been here for many months, and they have only known him since they_ came."

"-And he—he—didn't say anything about me?" Olga repeated, and Geoffrey turned almost sharply to look down at her. Why was she so anxious about Richard Sterry:' Her face was hidden .from him by her laud, and he put his own upon it. "Why, what -foolish idea have you got into your head nor, darling?" he asked. • "02 course he didn't. What could he say? He had never seen you before, and there was no time to say anything. Oh ! I believe he did say 'lt's the heat,' or something like that; but I couldn't bother about that. You WE'..??, all I thought about—von, darling, lying like 3 dead thing in Ethel's arms, my nyeetinart, and I felt almost as I did when 'I saw you in the sea, with the salt water splashing your face, an:l your head down on my shoulder. Oh, darling ! I've had a bad. ten minutes." She put down her hands, and looked up. "You love me so much ! Ah, Geoffrey, you love me too much ! I—l—feel sometime, that I can't bear it. You are too good for me."
In an instant lie was on his knees beside the, couch.

"Olga, you are not to say that again. When a man asks a woman to be his wife be can never love her too much. Olga darling, I shall never say that you love me too much." She started up out of his arms. " But it is different," she cried. " You and I are different. I---- "
_ She bioke o _ ff. The door had opened, and Ethel was coming in with smelling salts 111 her hands.

"Oh. thank goodness you are Fettor," she cried, running across the room. "Why, you quite frightened us. I don't believe I ever saw anybody faint before in my life. But Mr. Sterry says that dreadful time in the water must have upset you." "Did he say that ? " Olga asked, sharply. Her wide' eyes were fixed on .Ethel's pale face, and Geoffrey looked at her half uneasily. It occurred to him again that she had harped rather strangely on what Lichard Sterry, and thought. Did he say that that accountal for—for my faint ? " Ethel nodded.
"And it was quite enough to upset one," she said. "Why, that hour before the boat went down must have bum awful."

Olgaftshut her eyes sharply. --How horribly it came back to her—that dreadful lmur when, she had made her confesSion to Dr. Daere, when she had signed it,. and seen I,lza force it into the neck of the soda water bottle. Where was it now, that confession? :.Where, and when, would it come back?

She lay back, and tried to think. Ethel shook her head at Geoffrey. "She isn't a bit well, she whispered. "We must take care of her." Olga scarcely heard. Her thoughts were travelling round and round. If the confes- sion came back, what then? But suppose it didn't? And why should it? The chances against a soda water bottle being washed ashore were ten to one. And John Dacre was dead. He lay deep under the green wave. His hard, bright eyes would never force a secret from her again. His strew: face, that had given her such reluctant ail miration, would never look into hers agail. He was dead. He must be dead, and if he was dead what had she to fear? Only a soda water bottle far away, sailing in mid- ocean. It would take weeks, for it to drift to shore, and in those weeks -a thousand things might happen. It might be broken—it might be picked up ! Her thoughts stopped their racing, awl stood still.

If it was picked up? She sat upright sudder. ly. • The room swami round her. Ethel's ft,oe faded—was blotted out. Then Geoffrey was looking at her, and as he looked it seemed to her that his fa-le was changed int 6 the face of a dead man. She gave a cry, and thrust him from her. " Oh, if I could only forget ! " she cried. "If I could only forget. ! " Ethel looked into Geoffrey's eyes. " He was right," she whispered. "113 r nerves are upset, and we shall have to take care of her. We had better let her lie hee quietly for a bit. She shall have her lunch here, and afterwards We'll carry her out into the rose garden. She can sit there in the shade, and we'll all go out and have tea there this afternoon." She arranged everything as she wish 341. Olgh lay in the darkened room for an hour or two, and then Geoffrey carried her ut into the rose garden. He established her in a deep chair under the hedge, and it was there that Mrs. Dunston and Julia found her. GeoffreY had just put his mother opposite her and had seated himself on the arm of Olga's chair when they arrived. "Now, we'll just be lazy," he was saying, " and I for one will think of nothing but the pattern of mother's new cap. What will you think about, Ethel?" "I'll think of the smudge on your nose,'' Ethel said, "and wonder if it will be there to-morrow morning," She threw back her head laughing its Geoffrey rubbed at it, and Mrs. V erriker looked up, smiling. "There wasn't one there," she said. " Then I owe you two for that, my lady," said Geoffrey, "and if I didn't hear the butler Coming with the tea I'd pay you now. I'll wait till he has laid the cloth.' But the man had no cloth, and he was fol- lowed by Mrs. Dunston and Julia. Eth2l and Geoffrey sprang up, and Mrs. Verriker looked round in her chair. her face flushing
' That I don't know," said Mrs. Dunston. and Olga fell back again against her clishions.

Her face looked very white, and Geoffrey looked clown at her almost anxiously. "We won't talk about the wreck any more," he said. Then he turned to Mrs. Dunston : "Miss Murray isn't well," he added, in a low voice, "and we think it dis- turbs her."

Mrs. Dunston smiled back at him, though just then-she would have liked to fling her glove across his handsome face. He wn.s, there in her shoes—he ang -that girl, that no body, who looked so pale, and slight, and ill. Her eyes sharpened a little, and her red lips grew tight over her teeth. Well, let them wait—let them wait ! They hadn't finisher! with her yet. She turned, and picked up her gloves from the table as the butler appeared again to lay, apon it a white cloth.
"Mr. Sterry is here, sir," he said. "He told me to ask if he should come out to you." _

"Yes, yes, by all means," cried Geoffrey. He rose to walk across the grass to meet him; and as he went Mrs. Dunston noticed that Olga was sitting up sharply in her chair, with strained eyes on the corner of the hedge round which Dick Sterry would appear. She watched her nervously, and as. Olga's face grew more set and strained a tiily faint smile appeared at the corner of Mrs. Dunston's _ _

-She did not move her eyes. Ethel got • Ill) with a . flush deepening in her cheeks, and began hastily arranging the tea things on the table. She began talking, too, a little at random, and JUlia replied absently, rnd all th 3 time Olga sat, a sfrange image, rigid and set, her hands clutching at the arms of her chair, her eyes fixed sharply on the corner round which Geoffrey and Dick would come.
"Mr. Sterry must have been very useful to you before Sir Geoffrey came,", Mrs. Dunston said, still watching Olga; " and don't you think he is a nice-looking man, Miss Murray?"

The' sudden question startled Olga curi- ously. She caught her breath. "You can scarcely say you have met yet, can you? " laughed Ethel. " But you shall be introduced properly this time. Here they are."

Mrs. Dunston, watching, .saw Olga's hands tighten, saw her face grow paler, and then flush suddenly, as the two men rounded the corner and came up to them. Mrs. Dunston noticed that Olga stared curiously at Dick Sterry's face, and though her voice was very low Mrs. Dunston heard it. "."I.z.Q you are Mr. Sterry? " Olga said. "It was horrid of me to faint just as you came this morning. But you forgive me? "Yes, now that I see you looking so much better," said Dick. Afterwards, as they went back,* Mrs. Dun- ton looked into Julia's face.
cs -
cez,"
ear of the Greatbrldge murder ?'_,;
"I'm not so sure," Mrs. Dunston said.
*".l'here is some mystery about that girl,* sho said, sharply. Julia turned, a little startled.
"A mystery?" she cried. "I wish we could find one. . I wish we. -could find some- thing that would—that would send .her about her business." Mrs. Dunston twisted her sunshade.

"We may," she cried. "Have patience, Julia. We may. Did you notice this after- noon how frighten:A she looked once or twice? The first time was when I mentioned that another person had been saved from the ship, and the other was when " Dick Sterry came. Why should she Ete afraid of Dick Sterry before she saw him, Julia? After- wards she looked relieved, as if she had been afraid of recognising him—or of his recognis- ing her. And why ,was she afraid of soml- one else being saved from the wreck?" " Oh ! but she couldn't ,be afraid of that," Julia cried.

Olga and Geoffrey and Ethel and Dick lingerad on the lawn. Mrs. Verriker had gone in after Julia and Mrs. Dunston had left, and they all four lay back idly in their chairs. The sun was sinking, but it was still hot. No breeze crept up over the smooth grass. The roses in their beds hung still and heavy on their branches.

Ethel drew a deep breath. "Oh ! how lovely everything is," she said. "You are back and safe, Geoff, and every- thing is as lovely as can be. It is almost too good to last." Her idle glance fell on Olga, and a queer feeling swept over her. She had told Richard Sterry only that morning that there was something strange about Olga Murray—that she, looked haunted. Now the 'truth of her words se nned to come to her with startling reality. Olga did look haunted. It was exactly the word which expressed the stranrie terror that was in her face now as she stared at Dick Sterry. Haunted ! Ethel sat upright in hr seat, with upon her a queer, breathless feeling of excitement. What was the meaning of the strange -look in Olga's eyes? Why was she watching Dick Sterry like that? _ _ . - - _
--Sh3 clasped her hands foOther, and looked '-om one to the other, and then, as if realis- ing that Ole -,vas watching Olga strangely, she fell back in her chair, and lowered her eyes. _ _

Geoffrey and Dick we 3 busy .talking. Ethel sat and listened, and Olga, with her head drooping, with the shadow of the hedge be- ginning to creep over . her face, listen 3d too. "have you lived here all your life ?" • Geoffrey was asking. Dick Sterry hesitated. Then, in a qUear, abrupt way, No," he said, "it is • only about , a year since I took the Laurels—my house yonder. and heaven knows what possessed me to do it, I don't. I have every r3aBon •to hate the neighbourhood. I swOre I would never come back to it. until—"
lie broke off, and for an instant there was silence. Then Geoffrey turned. "Then you have lived here before?" he asked.

Olga, with her eyes, suddenly light and glittering, fixed on Dick's face, fancied that it had grown deathly white. "Not here exactly," he said, with an effort, "not here, but at Greatbridge. I lived at Greatbridge six yzars,ago, and when I left I never dreamt that I should ever come within a hundred miles of it again. But— here I am."
He laughed a little! uneasily, and his 13p^ searched Ethel's face. There was a sudden hungry look in them. In the growing shaaw there was .a strange look of suffering in his ac 3.
Olga got up suddenly. The shadows wen getting longer. She shivered a little, and Geoffrey, catching her hand in his, found that it was icy cold.

"I'll go in," she said, • little huskily; " you come later." corn,3 now," Geoffrey said; "at any rate, I'll take you to the house. Ethel and Mr. Sterry can follow if they like." He put his arm through hers, and then turned to look back.
"I say, Sterry, you won't go, will you? be cried. " Stay and dine with us. Ethel you persuade him." .
For a few minutes after they had gone Ethel and Dick sat in silence. Then sud- denly he leant forward. His face was grey in, the. fading light ;..his. hands trembled.

"Miss V—zrriler," he said, "would you— would you care to hear why I left Great. bridge six years ago? I ought to tell you. I am sailing under false pretences as long as I don't. Miss Verriker, I must tell you. It not fair; I ought never to have Coma hero without telling you." " Without telling us what? " said Ethel. . . .

He hesitated. -Then suddenly got up, . ano stood besid3 her. She looked wonderfully pretty in, the growing dusk. Her fair, pale face was upturned to his, and her eyes werl shining. She was trying to- reckon up th.. time in which she had known him, and some. how it seemed as if she had known him all her life, and yet now she was becoming sud- denly aware that there, was .something in his life which she had not thought of—sonic secret which she had not dr3amt cf.
She turned, and faced him with a sudden feeling of cold. Perhaps the • night wa growing chilly, yet no wind had risen. Till roses hung in the same leaden, languorout way, and no air stirred.
She drew a deep breath. "I don't understand," she said.
He faced her for a moment in silence. Hit lips were tight set, his hand clenched on thi back of his chair.
"Mims Verriker,. did you ever hear of tht Greatbridge murder?" he asked, abruptly. She lifted her head sharply. "A murder? A, Greatbridge murder?" sbe nsked No, I don't think I did."
"I think you must have done," he said, slowly, almost mechanically. "It—it created a st•nsation at the time. not more than six years ago. But you were young, perhaps, at school at the time."

She .nodded, with her eyes on his face. "Well? " she asked in a whisper. "Well, six years ago a man named Stephen Henderson was murdered at. Greatbridge Hall. He was a young fellow—twenty-five or so, but he had lived through a perfect whirl- wind before he inherited the Greatbridge es- tate. He was a bad lot—bad to th 3 eor - You may have heard his. name; you would have done if you had been to Greatbridge, for his grandfather was a great man there. Old Stephen Henderson made a fortune, built a great hall, fouuded his family as he

- thoitght, and at twenty-four his grandson in- herited it, and in a' few years had thrown everything to the winds. Wh3n—when he was murdered he had five shillings at the bank, and a sea of debts." He brok3 off.

" Yes?" said Ethel, quietly. . "Stephen Henderson was once my worst enemy," Dick added after a minute. Ethel gave a start, and looked up. "I had ev3ry reason to hate him," Dick went on. "He robbed me, not only of money, but of my sister too."
His 'voice NI. and Ethel, looking up at his face, saw that it was desperately drawn, as he paced up and down across the shadowy grass...

Suddenly h? catne to a standstill again. "My sister. and I," he went on, abruptly, "lived on the other side of Grea t- briclg 3 then, not fir ft.( Greatbridge Hail, and. old H•qtd-rson took a fancy to Ruth. EvPn before Stephen and she met, it was his hope that they would marry. But Stephen then was roaming the world. His grand- father thought he ought to sea life, and he was seeing it— seeing the worst side of it. lie was recalled by his grandfather's .death, which came very suddenly. He was th3n twenty-four, and he inherited the estate un- ttonlrolled, and at once plunged into excesses ev3ry description. The money ran through his fingers like water through a sieve, and it was almost at his wildest time, just six years ago, when he was about twenty-five, that lie began r: .king love to my sister Ruth." His voice Btopp34 again, and Ethel sud- denly getting up put her hands on his arm, and looked into his grey face. "Would you rather not speak of this ? " she asked, softly. "It is painful to you. Would you rather not tell me —" "I must !". he broke in. "I must tell you. I—l want you to know evarYthing about me— everything. He looked into -her eyes, and a queer thrill ran through her. She, did not take her hand from his arm for a moment.

"Then go on," she said, in a whisper. "113 began making love to Ruth," he said, slowly. "Ruth • was a girl, innocent, unsus- pecting. She knew nothing of the world, and Stephen was a handsome . liar—handsome enough to turn any girl's head, and un- scrupulous enough to swindle even his own mother, if she had been alive. He did _ not hesitate with regard to Ruth. What his life in London was when he was living there heaven knows, but about a week before he was to have married Ruth I h3ard enough to make me threaten to shoot him lik3 a dog if it was true.

"I heard—l heard that he had a wife living. I heard that he was in desperate straits—that he had romped through tin whole of his grandfather's fortune, and that lie was de- pending on his marriage with my sister, who had a fortune of her own, to keep the Jews at bay. I heard that, and at first I couldn't belie.v3 it.. Then I went _up to the 'Hall to _ _ _

see Stephen himself, and he denied it ve- hemently. "It was a pack of lies, he declared. He admitted that he had got into a bad set, but said he had broken from them, and it was be- cause of that—because he was trying to get rid of them—that they had become his ene- mies, and were trying to undo him. "I didn't believe him. There was some- thing in his face that branded him 'liar, somehow—something in his eyes—something in his manner that set all my blood boiling, that filled me with unspeakable hatred and loathing and horror as I thought of my poor, sister Ruth. Liar ! I think I can see him now, swinging his legs from a table, brandish- ing a cigar, and leering at me—ah ! heaven help me ! How that picture haunts me." .He took a turn up and down before he spoke again, and then he went on, without a glance at Ethel: '1 had only .Ruth in all the world," he said. "She was a delicate girl, fragile, dainty. .Ah, poor little Ruth ! I had pro- mised my mothcr when she was dying that 130 harm should come to Ruth—that I would. guard her with .my life. So .1 would. So I did. But I couldn't guard her against a scoundrel like Stephen Henderson. I couldn't keep her out of his clutches—l couldn't pro,/ tact her from a snake like that.

" She was desperately, foolishly, hopelessly in love with him. I had no chance with h3r. She would have believed him against all the world—even against me. " I saw Stephen before I told her what I had heard, and he sat smiling impudently at me, swearing it was not true. " Well,' I said, I can't let it rest. am :going to London to-night to make in- quiries, and if it is true—if • any part of what I have 'heard is true—you will not marry my sister. I will shoot you like a dog first ! ' "He lifted his head and glanced at me.

a little uneasily. She had never yet faced Mrs. Dunston without a feeling of awkward- ness. She could not help feeling that alis hated her, resented her being at the Hall, and never entered it without rememlering all she had lost.

It was, of course, only natural, but Were Was something in Mrs. Dunston's face which Mrs. Verriker instinctively disliked. Now she shook hands with Julia with some curiosity. They had been frequent visitors at the Hall of late, and she could not he noticing that their visits grew more frequent as the day of Geoffrey's return grew nearer. Now he was scarcely back, and they were there already. "We couldn't help coming," Mrs. Dunston cried. "We were so anxious. And that dreadful wreck—do you know, for three days we felt certain the boat was lost."

She was looking into Geoffrey's eyes. Julia stood beside her, but she was looking at Olga, and her sharp eyes were devouring every detail and every inch of her face. She saw how beautiful it was. She saw how dif- ferent her dark hair and eyes and the curve of her. lips were from her own, and her heart dropped sudl3nly. She shook hands with him, moving her eves from Olga's face to his almost mechani- e'ally, and her lips trembhd suddenly as she turned away from him again. The butler brought chairs. Mrs. Dunston managed to find a seat opposite Olga, and her hard, btight eyes searched the girl's face. "Do you know that you are quite roman- tic ? " she said. "You can guess how excited We are over you.. Fancy Sir Geoffrey bring- ing a bride from Australia. You are an Aus- tralia.u, are you not ? " _

Olga shooli her head. The faintness seemed to be. sweeping over her ,again. "No, I am English," she said. " English? " Mrs: Dunston lifted her head in surprise. "Amo you? Then had you been out in Australia long?" "Not long," said Olga.
Mrs. Dun-ston hesitated an instant. It .seemed to Olga as if her bright eyes had power to search her through and through, and sho shrank a little.

"Well, I suppose you are both very glad to be back?" Mrs. Dunston was saying. 'And it is sOmething to be the .only two survivors, though, by the way, I did hear that there had been another person saved. Did you see that in this morning's paper? " . Olga sat suddenly, sharply upright. "Someone else saved? she repeated, harshly.
Mrs. Dunston's dark eyes looked squarely into hers.
"Yes,' she said; "a man, supposed to be a passenger from th, Stella , was picked up by a sailing boat a day or two ago. He was unconscious."
Olga was clutching the arms of her chair. "And did he speak?" she asked.
Mrs. Dunston s'hook her head.
-" Then," Olga cried, "how do they know he was from the Stella? How could they toil?"
gettln.7 down from the table, and standing with his eyes level with me. "'Oh, you are going to London,' he said, 'to-night

-- , - "'To-night,' I answered. , "He smiled again. 1 remember how that, smile -irritated me. It seemed to defy me -- to mock me. "Well, I went up to London, and before r went I tried to make Ruth promise not to sea or speak to him while I was away. I told Ler I had heard something about him, and going to to make inquiries about it. It was a- mistake to tell her. I should not have done so. It • set her against me—she could not. understand even that I should for. a moment. suspect anything against Stephen. She hated me for suspecting him. She was indignant - Poor little Ruth ! "I reached London late that night. I spent next day in making the inquiries I wanted. learnt that everything was true. He was 5 gambler, a spendthrift, a drunkard, and be was already married. "I came back 'armed with proofs. I went' straight to the Hall. People said afterwards that they had met me in the town, looking like a madman, and that I stared them. in .tile, face without seeing or recognising t.:em.. know that I did; and then someone saw 1110 hurrying to the Hall grounds, and told Bulb, and she followed me.

"I went straight to the house. It N‘.119 summer—just such another evening as this hot, and still, and breathless. "I was hot when I reached the Hall. I re- member wiping my face as the butler shew3u me into the billiard room.
"I found him there, playing with a man named Perry—Sam Perry, who looked like a jockey. "Stephen turn3d when he saw me, and hig face, took on at queer look.
"'Back alreaay? ' he asked. 'satisfied.'
'You are soo3
I -went straight up to him, and struck him in the lac?. To see him there, smiling, liar and scoundrel that he was, and to thiqE of ril:c sister believing in him, worshipping him, sent me mad I think.
"He fell back, and then shouted something' at me.

"What I shouted back I don't know, but. Sam Perry afterwards swore that I said 1 " shoot him if h 3 ever attempted to see my 515 ter again. I had a pistol in my pocket, and.r took it out, without knowing that I did so, and put it down on a table. At that moment I meant to shoot him. I was mad. I should have shot him, I think,, but at that instant Ruth herself appeared at the open window. "I can se 3 her now as she came. I went up to her, and put my arm round her. "'You must come away,' I said. 'You must' not speak to him again, Ruth: It is all true every bit true. He is a scoundrel, and not fit for you to speak to.' - "She wanted to know why, of course, and when I told her she w3nt straight up to him, and looked into his face. " Is it true ? ' she asked
"'You know it isn't,' he answered, and then she turned to me, and the look she gave M 3 turned me to stone.

" I believe him,' she said. " ' But I have proof !' I cried. 'Ruth, 1 can shew you—l can prove to you that he is a; scoundrel and a knave, and already married. "I saw hatred ame in her eyes. She lookad at me coldly. _ be-
" ' I don't want .to see,' she said. lieve him.'
"I saw his leering, mocking eyes over her head. I saw his face, his dastardly face, triumphant, exultant—l saw him bend to kiss her, and I made a dash for him.

"They checked me, but if I had had the pistol in my hand then. I should have killed him. - But they got me away—Sam Perry, I think, got me away out of the window. "I went home, and waitad for Ruth. When she came I made her listen to me, and I told her what I had done, and what I had dis- covered. Then I shewed her the proof of his marriage, and that convinced her against her will, and it killed her ! She was never strong. She fainted twice, and when Dr. Collins came he shook his head rather. gravely. We should have to taka care, be said. Then she asked to see Stephen for the- last time, and I could not refuse her. ." could not resist her, and aftar dinner that night I walk,* back to the Hall to, fetch him.

"I was a fool to go. I hated myself for yielding so weakly, but I had never bee able to deny poor little Ruth anything, ad her faca went with me across the fields. "Poor little Ruth ! I only saw her aziga ce, and that through prison bars." (To be continued.)

ment,Stringer reached 6 and had a majority of s,but his opponent crept up and reached 9 to Stringer's 8, only to .be throWn behind by a double a minute rater. Stringer stayed at 10. Massey therefore won by a margin of s—not bad after being 5 behind at the commencement of the game.

_ T. Ellison, who last year won the individual merit championship of Lancashire and Cheshire,placed some notable achievements to his credit on Saturday. He took part in three matches and was victorious in each. Playing for Lancashire and Cheshire against York- shire, be defeated J. West by 21 points against 15 points. In the Works Competition against Richmonds he beat his opponent, R. Bennett, by the odd chalk, 15 against 14 points; and in the Warrington and District League against Warrington Bull's Head at the Farmer's Arms, Fearnhead, he was successful over W. Simister by three points, 21 against 18 ; his opponent was leading six without and then 13 against 8, uatil finally Ellison drew level and ran out winner after a splendid game.

A. Scott, of Warrington Cemetery has also been displaying great form. By virtue of his splendid victory in the Lancashire and Yorkshire match oti Saturday of 21-10 over A. Howarth, Yorkshire individual merit winner this season, gained the gold medal which is given to the Lancashire player with the best aggregate against the Tykes in the two games.
T. Ellison, also a.member of the Warrington Ceme- tery Hotel team., secured the gold medal for the highest scored in the matches with Staffordshire.

A large roach caught by ir. Johnson, an enthusiastic fisherman, from the Old Quay Canal a few weeks ago, is now on view in the aquarium at the Bank Park.

On Thursday afternoon the Borough Police held a fishing competition at Preston Brook. Sport was very slow, the only fish of any size being caught by the following, who were the winners :-1, P.C. F. Plumb, 12oz. Odrms. ; 2, P.C. Gibbs, soz. 14drms. ; 3, P.C. Hankins, 4oz. ldrrn.

The "jolly anglers " society held their annual fishing match on Saturday last at Agden Bridge when 26 members fished. The members left the society's headquarters at the" Bowling Green '! House, Liver- pool-road, about 1.45 p.m. and arrived at Agden Bridge at 3:30. A start was made at 4 o'clock and theAlembers fished for two hours. There were not many fish caught and the first prize was captured by Mr. P. Rooke, the weight of pis catch being Hoz. 12drams. The other prize winners were :-2, W. Rooke ; 3, W. Bate; 4, S. Thomas; 5, E.Kendall ; 6, T. Rigby; 7 and 8, R. Pooley & J. Ellison; 9, E. Lucy; (10) J. Battersby and (11) J. Evans. After the match a substantial tea provided by Mr. Lea, the proprietor of the "Boat House" Inn, Agden, was partaken of by the members. After tea a side game of howls was played when Mr. W. Robinson's (vice- ' president) team beat Mr. W. Charnock's (vice-presi- dent) team by 5. The return journey was. made through Ileatley and the members. arrived back at headquarters about 9.30 and sat down to a light supper provided by Mr. and Mrs. Campbell, after which Mr. W, E. Clare (vice-president) in .the unavoidable absence of the president (Mr. F. T. Bennie) thr2ugh illness, gave out the prizes to the successful competitors. A vote of condolence for the absence of The President was proposed and seconded, and Mr. R. Pooley in making the proposition said that he was sure that all present that evening regretted that Mr. Bennie was not amongst them, and that it would be everyone's wish that he would have a speedy and peimanent recovery, (Applause) Song - and rezita- tions were rendered by the inimitable J. Oultram who kept the compiny in high glee. Concertina solos and duets by the Bros. Brobbin were also highly appre- ciated. The usual votes of thanks, &c., then brought a ploasant day's outing to a close.

div.head: NOTES ON GOES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GOES AND ATHLETICS.
Cricket.

Newton, who occupy the lowliest position in the West Lancashire League table, visited Warrington on Saturday and were not so easily accounted for as one might have supposed from their season's record. They fought gamely, and Warrington had their work cut out to win. However, they were equal to the occasion and ran out victors by a margin of 30.

Newton had first turn at the wicket and their venture realised 125. T. Cooke, who batted with great confidence and dash, amassed 41 before Podmore accounted for him with one of his puzzling slow deliveries. Podmore did very useful work with the bill, capturing three wickets at a cost of 21 runs.

Warrington did not make a promising start, for although H. Callon led off with a faultless 31, he was not well supported and five wickets were down for 88. A fine stand by B. Silcock and J. W. Pearson placed the issue beyond doubt. Both batsmen played with caution and runs came slowly. Silcock contributed an invaluable 18 and Pearson, by one of his best dis- displays of the season, kn)cked up 23, for which he was warmly cheered.

Warrington 2nd, triumphed over Newton 2nd, for the second time this season. The feature of the match was the magnificent innings of J. W. Bain- bridge who secured 58. H. Speakman (15) and F. Richmond (19), also batted admirably for their runs. D. Plinston did effective work with the ball, main- taining a good length and capturiwg six wickets for 32 runs. For Newton C. Gee took four wickets for 13 runs and C. A. Bodmer was the top scorer with 36.

St. James's continue their triumphant career in the Warrington and Disirict League and the ch in- pouslnp seems a 'certainty for them. On Satur ty they disposed of the " Guardian " eleven withut much difficulty, C Holt being the most successful. batsman with 21. A. Green accounted for five wickets at a cost of 20 runs, and V. Tole took two for two. -Clarke,for the printers, bagged four wickets for 19 runs.

Whitecross Social made a -poor display against Walker's Brewery in a match which was notable for small scores. The bowlers had a fine time, Edwards capturing six wickets for five runs and J. Rylands three for eight runs for the winners. H. Wright and C. Lavell did practically all the bowling for White- cross, taking two wickets for 12 runs and six for ten respectively.

Rylands Bros. and Cheshire Lines ,Engineers tried conclusions, the wire men gaining the advantage by 19 runs. Sanders gave a fine display for his 31. McGowan, for the winners, took five wickets for eight rnns, and performed the hat trick with the first three balls sent down. F. Jolley secured three for 22, and Jewkes one for four. For the Engineers Deeley captured four wickets for 20 runs, Monks two for .eight, and Chamberlain two for 26.

In ;the Warrington and District Junior League Howley registered a victory at the expense of Orford, W. Warburton (16 not out) being the highest scorer. R.Gifford and S.Caldwell bowled in grand style, taking four wickets for three runs and six for nine rues respectively.

Rylands' Recreation experienced an ignothinious defeat at the hands of Holy Trinity, for they only put up the miserable icore of 7 against their opponents' 75. For the winners James was the most successful batsman with 28, and H. Fleming took eight wickets for three runs.
Sankey trounced St. Mary's to the tune of 125, Bradburn batting well for his 61 which included six fours. Forster took four wickets for 4 runs, and Webb six for nine.

---- \ There was an exciting encounter between Warring- ton and Birkenhead Commerical Travellers, the Warringtonians winning by a single run. A. E. Cole did good work for Warrington,his innings realizing 20.

Grappenhall entertained Seedley and gained the victory with five wickets in hand. B. Ellis dis- tinguished himself with a fine not out innings for 25. Carter took two wickets for no runs, whilst Watson took five for nine.
Warrington Municipal Officers' Guild were defeated by Altrincham Wesleyan 2nd to the extent of 15 runs. Berry and Stuart did well for the Warrington team, their respective scores being 31 and 24.
Sankey Wire Mills suffered a reverse at High Legh Lymm were victorious over Ashton-on-Merse3,, J. W. Gibbon batting brilliantly for 48.

Bowling. The semi-final in the Warrington Works Bowling Competition was played last Saturday, when the result, which was anticipated somewhat, showed that Whitecross and Rylands No. 1 are to try conclusions for the Finlayson Challenge Cup.

Spectators of the final match on August 7th on the Bowling Green at Bank Quay will witness some very fine games, as both teams are determined to win. Whitecross have succeeded twice, and they are again the favourites. If they win this time the trophy will become their own property. Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P., and Mrs. Crosfield are to be present, and Mrs. Crosfield will distribute tile prizes. Crosfield's Band will be in attendance.

In last Saturday's matches, Whitecross easily triumphed over Rchmond's. Although Richmond's had an advantage of 20 at the start, they were beaten by a handsome majority of 43 points. All except two of the Whitecross players were successful in reaching the desired number-15. That the match between the leaders of the teams (T. Ellison, Whitecross, and 11. Bennett) was about the best was a fact that will be seen from a short description •of the play. Ellison gained five whilst his opponent was three behind, Ellison ran up his total ,• to nine, whilst Bennett only added one. Bennett increased his score rapidly, reaching eight before Ellison could move. Later they peeled at 11. This in the face of such a margin against Bennett in the early stages was a grand dis- play of bowling. However the Whitecross captain got a lead and maintained it, winning by 15 to 13.

Another good game was that between J. Horton (Whitecross) and J. Smith. They peeled at four, and then the latter gained an advantage and increased his figures to ten whilst Horton had to be content with six. Smith kept a lead all the way but was only victorious by two points. A. Warburton for White- cross easily vanquished W. Rigby, winning by a majmity of 13 points.
The match between the Corporation mad Rylands No. 1 was fairly close, but Rylands were better repre- sented, and the result was that although 5 points behind at the start Rylands won by 15.

R. Knight (Rylands) and W. Newns (Corporation) provided an interesting game. They peeled at 7,8, 9, 11 and 12. Then Newns added a double, only to be followed by a double by Knight. With the next wood Newns was proclaimed victor.

J. Shaw (Rylands) beat J. Cooper by 15-6, thus scoring a win by a splendid majority of 10. G. Shaw (Rylands) and C. Newey played a good game. They equalized at 5, and later Shaw secured on advantage of 10 to 7, but Newey pulled up and with a fine piece of work was able to peel at 10. Then Newey got ahead, and remained there, winning by 15 to 12. At first it appeared as if A. Stringer (Rylands) were going to beat J. Massey, but those who had set their hopes on such a result were doomed to disappoint

div.head: Swimming.
div.p: Swimming.

. , The cold and wet weather which has been so prevalent of late has had a bad effect on the takings at the local _plunge • baths in Legh-street, as only the hardier swimmers have inulged -in the refreshing exercise.

The Warrington polo team journeyed to Woolton on Tuesday night and were beaten to the tune of 8 goals to 3. The players put their defeat dotNnto the small- ness of the Woolton baths which hampered their efforts and combination.
Pemberton was unable to play on Tuesday night and his place was taken by W. Dunn. The local team was C. Woods, H. Woolstencroft, S. lace, C. Turner, 'W. Dunn, R. Pepper, and R. Beaman.
The first works squadron race of the season will be swum on August 24th, and the second on -September 7th, leaving thp final tie to be competed for on the gala night, September 23rd.
A. friendly match between Warririgton and Widnes will take place at Widnes on Tuesday night.
Rugby Football. The Warrington Football Club haye arranged their first practice for Saturday next, August 7th

The fixtures for the season have now.been published and are pretty 'much the same as usual. Leigh set the ball rolling at Wilderspool, and with Bolewski on their side and Frawley and O'Malley in the home ranks, this should be a specially interesting match. Warrington ought to get some useful points in the first month, and make amends for the disastrous start a year ago. Supporters of the club will note with satisfaction that the match immediately preceding the first round of the NAL cup-ties is at home. That mid- week visit to Halifax last February was a disastrous one for the Warrington Club. -

The" Sunday Times " of Sydney, June oth reports fully a match between New South Wales (mostly members of the Kangaroos tourist party) and a New Zealand team. The match was 'played under N.U. rules before 15,000 people aud was won by • the home side, 20 to 21 points. O'Malley captained the 'Sydney men, and Frawley played a brilliant game on the wing with llosenfeldt. 'their running, passing and re-passing frequently brought down the house, and resulted in four tides.

The 24th annual Amateur Athletic Sports promoted by the Warrington Rugby Football Cluhtwill be held on Monday next,on the Wilderspool-road ground,when prizes to the value of £BO will be competed for. A record entry has been secured which includes A. E.M. Rowland the New Zealand walking champion.. The following is the number of entries for the various events :-100yards, 59; 220 yards, 60; 410 yards, 36; 150 yards (scholars), 28 ' • 880 yards, 43 ; 1 mile "flat, 39 ; 1 mile bicycle, 31; 2 miles bicycle, 25 ; 1 mile bicycle novice, 22 • 600 yards obstacle, 30 ; 2 miles walking, 19; making a total of 392. Given line weather a large crowd is expect3d. The Borough Brass Banct will be in attendance.

div.head: ROYAL LANCASHIRE SHOW.
div.p: THE ROYAL LANCASHIRE SHOW.

Merryweather and Sons, the well-known Fire Engineers, of London and Greenwich, have at their Fire Station, near the Fountain in the main avenue, one of their patent" Fire King" patten Steam Motor Fire Engines. This machine has a capacity of 50 gallons per minute and is of similar design to those built by the firm for :—London (6), Liverpool (5), Edinburgh (2), It is capable of travelling at speeds up to 30 miles an hour and of taking a gradient of 1 in 6. A patent improved oil fuel burner is fitted, and when, as is usually arranged, steam is kept up in the boiler, the machine can be instantly turned out to a fire, on receipt of a call.

div.head: MORE ADOPTED CHILDREN WANTED.
div.p: MORE ADOPTED CHILDREN WANTED.

The committee of the Lambeth Guardians, appointed to arrange for the transference of" nobody's children" from the poor law schools to families anxious to adopt children, on Wednesday reported at the meeting of the Guardians that they had no further children at present to recommend for adoption, although the applications from persons desirous of adopting children had been numerous.

Since the formation of the Warrington Civic League of Help a special ,committee, compasecl of the Rev. W. Bracecamp, Mr. C. E. Parker, and Mr. B. ITownroe, has been searching far and wide in order to find a suitable secretary. All quarters likely to be of service have been appealed to, from Canon Scott Holland, of St. Paul's Cathedral, to the head of the Quaker settlement at Woodbrook ; from Pusey House, Oxford, to Toynbee Hall, Whitechapel. At last the special committee discovered Mr. Wilfred Rowland, v‘ho was brought before the Executive Committee the other afternoon and unanimously elected secretary of the League at a salary of £2OO per annum. Mr. Rowland is a man of wide experence in social work. He was for some time financial secretary at Mansfield House, Canningtown, and is the intimate friend of the gentlemen who first started Leagues of Help in this country. His work has extended to Lancashire, for last year he conducted an investigation on behalf of the Free Church Council into the state of the Free IChurches in Liverpool. Mr. Rowland, who is thirty- six years of age, has served on boys' employment bureaux and has also been prominently identified with the National Home Reading Union. As a Commis- sioner in South Wales he dealt exhaustively with the question of "The advantages of social ;nstitutes as counter-attractions to public-houses." He is an Acceptable speaker and is well accustomed to conducting public meetincrs, while his book on the Free Churches of Liverpool has com- manded a great deal of attention owing to its thought- ful and moderate tone, Mr. Rowlands is of a very tactful, unassuming manner. He is at present tempo- rary warden of .Mansfield House, Canningtown, but will probably start work in Warrington in September. It is greatly to be desired that the citizens of Warring- ton will do their best to help Mr. Rowland in the great task which lies before him. The League of Help is not attached to any special denomination or party but as the name denotes, appeals solely to civic spirit. Of even more value to the success of the undertaking than donations and subscriptions is the personal help which Warringtonians can give. Mr. Rowland can only achieve the objects which the League has in viewl if his organizing ability is assisted by the united efforts of a large body of helpers who will be willing to serve on committees and come into intimate con- tact with cases of distress which unfortunately occur in such large numbers in winter. All lovers of social progress will ivelcome Mr. Rowland as a force for good in the town. He will have his offices in rooms which are to be rented from Messrs. Hesketh and Son, opposite the General Post Office.

As to the method by which the League will seek to accomplish valuable work, it I% expected that com- mittees will be formed in the wards where the greatest distress prevails. The object is to organise charity and charitable effort; not to distribute other people's money but to see that money is given in the proper direction. Under the present conditions it frequently happens that the charitably-disposed are imposed upon Quite recently a . girl sought relief from a local lady, stating that she lived in a certina street in Warrington and was badly in need of help. The lady, after considerable inquiry through the clergy of the town, discovered that the girl did not live in the street named. However, the girl came to see her again, and confessed that she had told a lie in the first instance because she had been in the Work- house and did not want the fact to'be known. She was helped, but later it was discovered that the second statement was also a fabrication and that the girl had never been in the Workhouse. If the Civic League of Help had been in full working order, the lady would have been able to apply to the secre- tary and obtain reliable information. Particulars of cases of distress will be filed, and there will be excep- tional means of finding out where money ought to be given or what particular form relief should take. There will be no distribution of doles from the offices of the League, for the main purpose of the organization is the dissemination of advice. There will inevitably be expense attaching to the work, and a public appeal will shortly be made to the inhabitants of Warrington to contribute to thesupport of what promises to be a very useful addition to the beneficient institutions of the town.

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, JULY 31sT, 1900.

There ara some parts of ALL-NIGHT the proceedings of Par- SITTINGS. liament in which the public at large cannot be_ expected to feel more than a most casual interest. They are technical; they are not eaeilY intelligible even through the medium the most extended reports, and they have reference to theEmanner in which Parliament 'ehall conduct its own business. One of these Deculiar intervals presented itself on Wednes- ;3l°3T. We shall nevertheless ask our readers give attention to it for a few minutes..at east, for it _is illustrative of the present ,13°11tical situation. Stated broadly and with 'revity. the case is this: the character of the opposition to the Budget has made it 11,ccessary to hold all-night sittings. All Qiscussions in Committee in the House of '%tnrnons are presided over, not by the 'l3eaker of the House, but by the Chairman Committees or one of his deputies. It is °Dvious that the Chairman of Committees cannot remain in his place uninterruptedly through the whole of an all-night sitting. As matter of fact, however heroic and enduring Chair man may be, the chair has frequently be taken by one of the deputy-chairmen. explanation may seem wearisome, but nust necessarily be carried a little further. ,t 'ere are tinies when the deputy-chairman arniot exercise the powers which could be Izercised by the chairman if he were present ati_t the same time and were confronted by ge same circumstances. He cannot, for listance, accept the closure except under ellain specified conditions. It follows

from this that during a very prolonged sitting there must be intervals- during which on Opposition can act against the sense of practically the whole House ; it can do as it likes ; in fact, it can deliberately waste as much time as it likes ; it can set reason and all rules of ordinary conduct at defiance. This condition of things the Government has been driven to amend. My. ASQUITH proposed an amendment to the standing orders which proposes to confer upon the deputy-chairman all the powers at present at the disposal of the Chairman whenever he is called upon to occupy the chair. This is merely reasonable, as every- body must admit, It is never agreeable to the head of a Liberal Government to move such amendments to the standing orders as mist restrict the perfect freedom of Parlia- mentary proceedings ; but experience has proved beyond question that restriction is necessary, and common-sense declares that a power which is given to the Chairman o! Committees should also be conferred on his deputies. And now it becomes necessary to see what can be said on the other side, and a great deal is always said on all such occasions. What was Mr. BALFOUR's case against the proposal which was carried on Wednesday night? He said that the reason for the course of action proposed by the PRIMEMINISTER was obvious. It was because it was beyond the physical capacity of any Chairman to stand the strain which thei Government had imposed in the past and intended to impose in the future. He himself did not deny that the strain under the existing system was too great for the Chairman, but whatever was too great for the Chairman was too great for the mem- bers. Were they going to have two Chan- cellors of the Exchequer, or was Mr. LLOYD" GEORGE in these all-night sittings going to

delegate his powers to somebody else? And so on and so on. There was not a syllable of pity for Mr. LLOYD-GEORGE, who has stuck to his post like a hero. The point is that these all-night sittings, which weary out everybody, are a consequence of the con- duct of the Opposition. They are not ordained by the Government; they are made neces- sary by the situation. The Government does not want to sit up all night, neither do its supporters. But what is the situation? It was inadvertently explained by a Tory mem- ber who talked about this being the usual time for preparing to bring the session to an end. And so it is; but there is no prospect of bringing the session to an end much before Christmas, for the House of Commons, despite the all-night sittings, will next week still be engaged with the early stages of the Finance Bill.

The chapter of War- THE ROYAL rington history dealing VISIT. with the recent Royal visit is not yet closed. On the whole this is a matter for regret. There was a feeling of disappointment engendered by the Royal visit itself, but that was solely because we did not see enough of their Majesties. The diffi- culties which have arisen since originated in the proceedings prior " to the Royal visit and might easily have been smoothed over with a little tact on the.- part of the Mayor. An explanation was certainly due, for instance, both to the Town Council an the town in regard to the present of a diamond necklace to Princess Victoria. The matter was, perhaps, hurried of necessity, but when a Committee was appointed to select the gift that Committee should not have been ignored, and an explanation subsequently refused. Even to-day the Council and public know nothing officially except that the necklace was bought, presented, and cost £l5O. As a result of this unconstitutional procedure, the Mayor has been requested to call a special meeting of the Council to discuss the minutes of July sth. He has refused to do so, and five members of the Council have taken matters into their own hands and convened a Council meeting for Thursday evening next. Altogether it is an unhappy sequel to a great occasion. The deadlock might have been avoided, as we say, by a tactful recognition of the rights of the ordinary members of the Council to an explanation of what had been done in the name of the Maya and Corporation of Warrington.

We thought the idea CAPITAL 00ING that British capital ABROAD (?) was "going abroad" to any alarming or even disquieting extent had been exploded as a myth or a party-political bogey. Mr. Lloyd-George's raid on the hen-roosts of the rich and redundant was going to denude the country of capital. So said the opponents of the Budget when first its bold legislative proposals were made public. The tale was credited in some quarters, for a very short time—just long enough for the reflection to carry weight that the taxes on land, for instance, instead of driving capital out of the cour4try would, by their encouragement of specula- tion, enterprise and productivity create a very welcome outlet for capital at home. Much to our surprise this week Captain Crosfield, in the course of his enthusiastic National Service propaganda, has repeated the assertion that English capital is going abroad." This time it is not the Budget that ,is to blame, but our insecurity as a country against foreign aggres- sion. Unless we arm at all points and train like Marathon competitors our nervous capital will take to itself wings and fly away abroad. It has even begun! Some of Captain Crosfield's friends are investing their money abroad, "convinced of the dangers which lie ahead of this country." On the whole it is ' a sad spectacle, and renders inevitable the conviction that between patriotism and pocket the principles of some estimable people are liable to become confused. There is one thing we should like to ask. If Old England is so totteringly insecure, which blessed spot abroad is safer?
The South African

THE SOUTH Constitution was intro- AFRICAN MIRACLE. duced on Tuesday in. both Houses of Parlia- ment. Lord Crewe showed no eagerness to arrogate to the Government any undue share of credit for the miracle which has transformed South African politics from a weltering chaos into harmony and progress. And Lord Lansdowne paid the Government the tribute which Lord Crewe did not too greedily claim, but which ungracious critics have grudged them. At the same time Lord Crewe took the opportunity, as was only right, to emphasise the confirmation which

the trend of South African affairs has given to the wisdom of that belief in the virtue of responsible Government which has always been a firm article of the Liberal creed. The new era dates from the courageous resolve of Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman to grant at once a full measure of Colonial self-government to the late Republics. We do not forget, and South Africa will, not forget, how that brave act of his was opposed and denounced by the Conservative party. It has been justified in threebrief years. No act of British policy has ever so enhanced our prestige throughout the civilised world. While at home, the Liberal policy of trust in the people was never more strikingly justified.
Mr. Balfour, stung per- MR. BALFOUR'S haps by a realisation JUSTICE. of the absurd. incon-

gruity of the position which he took up when he attacked the Government for not having rushed into heed- less expenditure upon more Dreadnoughts before it was known that they would be necessary, while he refused to be a party to the provision of the revenue necessary ,for carrying out the existing programme, has at last confessed to his own view of the way in which the money in national defence should be found. Speaking in the City on Tuesday, Mr. Balfour proclaimed his adherence to the policy of raising the revenue for Dreadnoughts and the like by taxing imports. That as everyone knew, was always Mr. Balfour's only alternative to the Budget, though he was reluctant enough to make the avowal. It is, according to Mr. Balfour, sheer spoliation to ask the very rich to make a contribution towards the cost of their own and the community's protection out of an unforseen windfall in the future, which they will owe entirely to the expendi- ture of the community. But to penalise the very poor, in their larder and in the little comforts of their poverty-stricken homes, is just and equitable. Mr. Lloyd-George's increment duties will not leave the rich ground-landlords one farthing poorer than they are to-day. Mr. Balfour's import duties will pinch those who are poor to-day and reduce them to the extremity of destitution. Therefore, shys Mr. Balfour, increment duties are shamefully unjust, and import duties are just and right.

Lord Lucas's announce- THE NEW ment that anew reserve RESERVE. , for the Territorial Army is to be constituted marks another step forward in the develop- mant of Mr. Haldane's plans for providing the country with an efficient Army for home defence. The force is to be made up of three sections, of which the first is intended to provide a sort of backbone for the Territorials on mobilisation. There will be a certain amount of wastage when the Territorial force is called up, as is quite natural and inevitable; and into the gaps in the ranks thus created will step these reservists officers who have done four years' service in his Majesty's forces since 1900—(a year selected, no doubt, to secure that all shall have knowledge and experience of the most modern conditions of training), and men who have done four fifteen-day camps or their equiva- lent. Ancillary to this fine body there will be the technical reserve formed of men skilled in various classes of technical work— such as railway and telegraph engineering, veterinary work, aeronautics, &c. And last will come the veterans—a corps in which may be inclu led men who have served in any branch of his Majesty's forces of the irregulars who did such good work in South Africa. Mr. Haldane's object is to ensure that in the time of need no material which may be of use shall be neglected, and that the War Office may have the means at such a time to turn to immediate accdunt the services of those upon whose ,training money has been spent, and who may be willing to take up arms again in defence of their country.

It is said on very good authority that the Government will carry the Budget through by the end of September. The Opposition are certainly not so full of fight as they were; all-night sittings and the results of recent bye-elections having had both a salutary and sobering effect upon the obstructionists. * * *

This week we have had a pause in the Parliamentrry discussions on the Budget. Everyone—including Mr. Lloyd-George, who has had an unexampled strain—had to have a rest. But what has been the result? Instantly there have been a cloud of silly rumours about the Budget being " dropped," "hung up," "Postponed." Don't believe a word of it. High Peak gave those rumours the best reply. So far from being "hung up "—except in the best position—the Budget is going as strong as ever. * * * On Monday evening Mr. and Mrs. Crosfield entertained at dinner at their residence, 39, Hyde Park Gate, the Grand Duke Michael and Countess Torby, the Prime Minister ,and Mrs. Asquith, the Rt. Hon. R. B. Haldane, Minister for War; M. Romanos, the Greek Minister; Mrs. J. A. Pease, the Hon. and Lady Cynthia Colville, Lord and Lady Acton, Captain and Mrs. Berkeley Levett, Miss Schilizzi, and Master of Elibank. On Tuesday they invited another party to dinner at the House of Commons to meet Mr. Maddison, M.P., and Mr. Vivian, M.P. * * *

The consideration of the Finance Bill will be resumed after the Bank Holiday, and will be taken from day to day. The next point to be d9alt with is the "Undeveloped Land Tax." What is that tax? It is a very just and moderate levy of one half-penny in the pound on the capital value—not of gardens, or parks ór playing grounds, which are all exempted, but of pieces of land on the out- skirts of towns which are held back from proper use. Everyone is familiar with such pieces of land. They check municipal development while the owners profit by it, and they form one of the main causes of so many people being herded in the slums. It is high time such land was taxed forthe good, and the halfpenny is only a modicum of what the country may eventually call up from this unexploited hen-roost." * *

Mr. J. Howes has been correcting a few Tory misrepresentations and we'would com- mend to our readers' attention the able and vigorous speech in which he answered the specious arguments put forward by a noble lord and others at the recent Bridge Foot demonstration. The hollowness of the tariff reformers' tactics in attempting to cast suspicion on the sincerity of Free Traders by pointing to the existing food taxes, was clearly exposed. Mr. Howes told his audience that every penny of these taxes had been put on by the Tories, and also that they were considerably heavier before Liberals swept away so many of the imposts which once pressed so harshly on the com- munity. Their work in this direction is not exhausted, and it will be considerably facili- tated by the passing of Mr. Lloyd-George's
splendid Budget which is daily becoming more popular with all who desire that the burden of taxation shall be more equitably apportioned.

The Bridges Sub:Committee of the Town Council has been dissolved. We could cry "Hurrah ! "—so little had it achieved. But its duties have been merged into those of the General Purposes Committee—which is nothing to enthuse about. Those new bridges are still in the air, and likely to remain there much longer than either M. Bleriot or Mr. Latham. * * *

The Liberal Association is losing no oppor- tunities of making the Budget clearer of understanding to the public, and for several weeks past the hoardings have been well supplied with pictorial argument and logic o 4 a convincing and illuminating character. Councillor Locker J.P., (the hon. secretary). and Mr. J. Howes jun. (the agent) can be relied upon to keep the constituency well posted up in the progressive politics of the day. •

* * • A new Town Councillor was elected on Monday, when Mr. G. N. Vernon (C.) was returned without opposition for the vacancy in Fairfield Ward caused by the death of Councillor Nield. People have been asking why the Liberals were inactive in the matter. The reason is that the new councillor's term will expire in October, and he will require to seek re-election on the Ist November. On that date the Liberals may feel that they have more justification for contesting the seat. ,k * *

General Purposes Committee meetings of the Town Council are frequently not happy gatherings, but there was one on Monday which had an unusual denouement. The agenda contained the report of the Reception Committee re the Royal Visit, and when this business was reached about a dozen members left the Chamber and deprived the meeting of a quorum. This was done, we understand, as a protest against the Mayor's ignoring of the requisition to call a special Council meet- ing to discuss those fateful minutes of the sth July. "The plot thickens," as the half- penny novelette would say. * * *

"The entries for the annual brass band festival which is to take place at the Crystal Palace in a couple of months' time already show signs, I am told (says the London correspondent of the "Manchester Guardian") of exceeding those of last year. It will be the aim of the promoters of the contest to keep the entries within reasonable limits, so that no class will be unwieldy in the number of - competitors. The Lancashire bands are never so numerous as those from Yorkshire or Lopdon, but there are always more of them in the competition proper for the Ithousand-guinea trophy. This year, as .before, several of the best Lancashire bands will be found in the first section, including Wingates, Irwell Springs, and Perfection. The competition promises to be keener than ever, because the modern policy of local authorities in paying bands to play in the public parks has made regular practice com- pulsory, with a general improvement in methods of playing. * * _ _

I have, during my twenty-five year's experience, received less aid from total abstainers than from any other class. All the best and most useful help I have obtained has come from the strictly moderate drinker. —Dr. R. W. Braithwaite, at the. Inter- national Congress on Alcoholism.

* * We are indebted to the Berlin correspon- dent of the " Daily Mail "for some interest- ing figures showing "how people of small means have to struggle for existence in modern Germany." These figures are to be found in a publication just issued by the Imperial Statistical Office, which a year ago caused 800 families in different parts of the Empire to begin keeping a systematic account of their incomes and disbursements. Every family received an account book in which it was requested to keep an itemised record of money spent bn food, clothing, fuel, medical attention, presents, education, amusements, &c. A teacher and his wife, without children, whose income was <EI4S, contrived to save Another teacher *and his wife, also childless, earned <EI6O and spent .El7l, their deficit was caused by them spending £25 more for food and a more for entertain- ment than the other teacher. A/married couple with three children, the father being a brewery workman, earned £BB and saved .E 7 10s. The family spends only £33 10s. on food. It is added that in order to accomplish the above results the most spartan economy was required, in most cases not a single farthing being spent unnecessarily. The statistics attract " especial interest in view of the new internal revenue taxes on varibus commodities which will -shortly come into effect, making articles such as tobacco, cigars, cigarettes, coffee, tea, sugar, matches, beer, cognac, and gas-mantles dearer." These facts are worth remembering when our own Tariff Reformers assure us that with a Pro- tective Tariff the cost of living is not to be increased.
