Special Council Meeting to be Held The Mayor's refusal to call a special Council meeting to consider certain questions arising out of the recent Royal visit and the presentation to Princess Victoria of a diamond necklace, has resulted in the following requisition being sent to the Town Clerk :7-- Warrington, 27th July, 1909. Owing to the Mayor having refused the requisition of 15 members of the Council of the County Borough of Warrington we, the Undersigned fiv6 members of the said Council, in accordance with the provisions of" The Municipal Cor- porations Act, 1882," hereby convene a meeting of the Council to be holden at the Town Hall, on Thursday, the sth day of August, 1009, at six o'clock in the evening, Business: To consider the thinutAs of the Council of thesth July, and to pass such resolutions thereon as the Council may deem neoessaryy . (Signed) JOHN Loan, • G. W. ,ThsErn, FRED 't. LASHFORD, JAMES HALLkWELL, THOMAS CHAN= R. A PROTEST. ,

At the meeting of the General Purposes Committee held at the Town Hall, on Monday afternoon,the report of the Reception Committee came up for acceptance. A number of members who had signed the requisition at once' left the meeting as a protest against the action of the Mayor in refusing to call a special meet- ing of the Council to consider the minutes of the sth of July.

Concessions on the _North-Western Railway.

The London and North-Western Railway Conapan-y have made important concessions to the signalmen, which have removed much of the friction caused by the recent award, and have given a great deal of satis- faction. They have agreed that the men called for duty in a higher-grade box shall receive the higher rate of pay attached to that box, and that lampsmen and men engaged in oiling points in the northern district, who hitherto have worked seven days per week, shall in future be classed as six,-day men, and be paid extra for Sunday duty. Only one candidate was nominated —Mr. George Newton Vernon, manager, 108, Man- chester-road, who stood in the Conservative interest and he was consequently declared elected. Mr. Vernon was proposed by Mr. Robert Bolton, seconded by Mr. Henry Maddock; and supported by Messrs. Frank Dunne, James Wood, Thomas Baldwin, Henry Houghton, George E. Clergy Daughters School. Many successes of pupils of St. Elphin's School for the daughters of clergy in the diocese of Liverpool, Manchester and Cheshire, wera announced at the school speech-day, held at Darley Dale, on Wednesday. The Bishop of Liverpool presided, ,and he was supported by Dr. Caton (who distributed the prizes), Canon Willis (Warrington),Canon Wilson (Worcester), Rev. G-. B. Thurston (Lymm), Colonel Buckton, Canon Bethel-Jones, Rev. A. G. Rawston, Canon Rountree, Rev. H. B. Blogg, and the Rev. H. V. Pigot (Warrington).—Dr. Caton referred to the good work the school was accomplishing upon the most approved and modern methods. He emphasised the importance of a full course of higher education, following upon primary education. Educa- tion, he said, was a splendid opportunity, when once gone would never return. Thoroughness and accuracy were essential, and that not only in the seemingly important matters.—The Bishop of Liverpool proposed a vote of thanks to Dr. Laton for distributing the prizes, and referred with pleasure to Miss Kennedy, the head niistress, for the success of her work at the school; also to Canon Wilson, who engineered the great scheme for the removal from Warrington to so delightful a spot as Darley Dale.—The Archdeacon of Blackburn seconded; and Dr. Caton, in reply, wished the school every prosperity. Tea and music on the lawns followed.

Picnic. The 3rd annual picnic in connectiGn with the employees of the above firm was held last Saturday. Gatacre was the place chosen, 70 making the "journey by rail. Arriving there, half the party decided to visit the beautiful country scenery that there is around this pretty village, the others participating in a bowling main on the green httached to the Bridge Inn, The winner was the old veteran bowler j. Clare who bowled well all through the main,' defeat- ing W. Bibby in the final. Other prize winners were J. Dolphin 3rd ;H. Pownall, 4th ; W. Smith, sth ; E, Gilbert, 6th ; H. Thornton, 7th; J. Gleave, Bth ; J. Welsby, 9th ' • PL,Clarke, 10th; Apploon 11th; S. Keene, 12th; E. Malone, 13th; E, Fowler, 14th; J. Hollinsworth, 15ih ;W. Aleock, 16th. After the main all assembled in the pavilion and partook of, tea, the catering being of the best. Then an impromptu concert was arranged. Songs were well given by the host Mr. Wilson, Messrs. W. Bibby, W. Rutter, R. Boscow, H. Lion, W. Smith; Duets by Mr. R. Clarke and J. Sadlow. During an interval Mr. R. Straw proposed a vote of thanks to the host and hostess. He said words utterly failed to express their feelings at being so well catered for and the adthirable, manner in which the party had been received. Mr. E, Gilbert seconded, Mr, WiNion briefly replied. The singing of the National Anthem brought to a close one of the best picnics the work- men have ever had. Warrington Cycling Club. The run to Sandiway on' Saturday was unfortu- nately marred by disagreeable weather, which pre- vented also what would have been a large attendance. A small party of members, however, made the journey by road while a respectable number chose the easier method of; travelling by rail to Hartford, At the outset of the afternoon the wheelers anticipated a wet time, but as the destination was reached the day brightened and the prospects of retaining dry garments looked more favourable. The stay was taken up by bowling and' a very enjoyable time was spent on the green. A return was made early in the evening, but the cycling section ran into bad weather before their arrival in Warrington. The President, Mr. Naylor, 'should have attended the fixture, but was unable owing to his being in the South of Eng- land. On Wednesday evening a match was played with the Widnes C.C. at Sankey which resulted in a win for, the home club by 32, the scores being Warrington C.C., ; Widnes C.C.', 38. After the bowling the visitors were entertained by a musical programme, provided .by members of the respective clubs.—The run on Thursday to Tabley was abandoned on account of the rain, this being another of the many Thursday runs which have had to be cancelled on account of the bad weather this season.—The club's arrangements for the coming week are :—week-end tour to Buxton and Derbyshire Dales ; on Wednesday the Club meet the St. Helens C.O. in a bowling match at Sankey; Thursday's run is to Altrincham.

div.head: TENNIS, CROQUET, AND GARDEN FURNITUE.— J. S. GARLAND, Bridge st., Warrington.—Advt. Warrington Children's Summer Camp.
div.p: TENNIS, CROQUET, AND GARDEN FURNITUE.— J. S. GARLAND, Bridge st., Warrington.—Advt. Warrington Children's Summer Camp.

The second batch of girls, numbering one hundred under the charge of the Misses Ellison, Taggart, Armstrong, Pennington and Broadhurst, arrived at •Prestatyn on Saturday morning where they were met by Mrs. Whiteley and Miss Emson. All were in excellent spirits. They marched to the camp where they were placed into sections for the various huts. Dinner was served and they were afterwards taken for a paddle in the sea. The girls then had tea and afterwards 'prepared their beds for the night. On Sunday the girls were early astir and after the usual morning's work they prepared for church. The Church of England section went to Meliden where special Children's Service was held. The Roman Catholic girls' were taken to Prestatvn. The remainder of the day was spent quietly in the camp grounds and on the shore. On Monday the Children waded along the shore to see the 'pierrots, whose entertainment was great)y enjoyed. The afternoon and evening were spent on the shore. On Tuesday the rain fell heavily for the greater part of the day. During the afternoon a concert given by the children, was held in the pavilion and was greatly enjoyed by. all. On Wednesday the girls were taken to view the beautiful waterfall at .Dyserth. The walk was thoroughly enjoyed, the return journey being made through the woods on the mountain side and all were quite ready for dinner when we., reached "home." On Thursday morning the pierrots were again visited, and in the afternoon the children were taken over the mountains and returning via Maiden in time for tea. Friday was a very busy day, the children assisting in preparing the huts for the boys who will arrive to-day. The children, who are all in good health, were very sorry to leavoAhe camp, having spent a vely enjoyable holiday, although the weather has been very unsettled the greater part of the week.

At the Bankruptcy Court on Tuesday last, on tiler application of Messrs. Arthur Browne and Co., the solicitors for the debtor,a receiving order was made by the Registrar, Mr. Ridgway, against John Thomas Heywood, of 72, Winwick-street, Warrington, clothier, and the debtor was adjudged bankrupt.

• Personal. Mr. and Mrs. T. D. Rollinson, master and matron of the Runcorn Union Workhouse, Dutton, have just been appointed master and matron of the Wolver- hampton Workhouse. At a special meeting of the Runcorn Guardians on Thursday their resignations were accented and high testimony was borne to the efficient work of Mr. and Mrs. Rollinson during their comparatively short stay at Dutton. Warrington Show. The annual show in connection with the Warrington and District Agricultural Society will be held in Walton Park on Thursday. August 10th. Prizes, cups and medals to the value of 4-.7100 are ogered for competition. There will be classes for hunters, harness horses, jumpers, shires, cattle, &c. Tuesday, August 10th, is the last day for entries.—The annual Walt= Flower Show will be held in 'Talton Park on the same day. The principal features will be the gardeners' classes for groups and collections of vegetables and cut flowers. Entries close =Tuesday, August 10th.—Schedules for both shows can be obtained from the Secretary, Mr. James Bainbridge, Walton House.

Off to Camp. To-morrow will se the departure of the local Territorials for their annual fortnight under canvas_ The site of the camp this year will be Cferwys, in North Wales. The country in this district being very rugged and mountainous, the thanceuvres, which will be on a larger and more exacting scale than hitherto, will test the stability of the" Terriers" to the greatest extent. A glance at the programme shows that serious business and not play wtll monopolise a great proportion of the time, but given fine weather the men will return full of health and vim. The battalion will parade at the Drill Hall at 12.30 (noon), on Sunday, and it is anticipated that the men will be well. on their way by two o'clock. They will leave the train at Holywell And march to Caerwys. The general idea of the manceuvres is that war had broken out in Eur Ope, and Great Britain is involved in it early in July. The Lancashire men are supposed to defend the Western part of tlie country against invasion. The brigade will be commanded- by Major-General E. C. Bethune.

Death of Mrs. Ellis Clare. Many of our readers will regret to hear of the death of Mrs., Clare, wife of Mr. Ellis R. Clare, which took place on Monday evening last at the Infirmary. Deceased was in fairly good health up tl about a month ago when she was taken ill with peritonitis, with the result that an operation was performed on Monday -morning. The operation was successful, and hopes were entertained that she would recover, but she passed away in the evening. The deceased lady, who was highly respected, was a regular worshipper at Bold-street Wesleyan Church. The funeral took place on Thursday in the presence of a large gathering of relatives and friends. The Rev. Thomas Miller officiated, and the mourners were :—First carriage, Mr. Ellis R. Clare (widower),Mr. Arthur Clare and Mr. Willie Clare (sons), Mrs. Whittaker (mother) ; second carriage, Mr. William Whittaker <brother), Miss Jessie Whittaker (sister), 'Mr. and Mrs. Dutton (brother-in- law and sister), Miss Nellie Kershaw (niece) ; third carriage, Mr. and Mrs. Walter Clare (brother-in-law and sister-in-law), Mr. and Mrs. Kershaw (brother-in- law and • sister); fourth carriage, Mr. and Mrs. R. Whittaker (uncle and aunt), Mr. and Mrs, W. Hillidge (brother-in-law and sister), Mrs. J. Moody (sister) ; fifth carriage, Mrs. Edwin Clare and Mr. John Clare (aunt and nephew), Mr. Fred Kershaw (nephew), and Mrs. Edward Spittle. Several wreaths were sent, including one from the Liberal Club, of which Mr. Clare is a member.

Sir Gilbert Greenell and his Tenantry. At the inVitation of Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., those farmers on the Walton Estate who " walked Belvoir Hunt puppy this year attended the Belvoir Hunt annual puppy show on the 22nd July. The following tenants participated in the day's enjoyment --Messrs. Wm. Weir, Win. Turner, H. Mawdsley, Thos. Warburton, R. L. Warburton, J. K. Priestner, Daniel Fowles, Joseph Billington, Fred Broady„Joseph Whitlow, George Mountield, E. Bretherton, Peter Moore, J. C. Edgerley, Thos. Cawley, John Cawley, Wm. Fowles, Thos. Whitlow, Wm. Blackshaw, C. Blackshaw, C. Goves, ThOs. Beckett, G. Beckett, and Thos. G. Williams. The party left the Cenfral Station for Grantham in a saloon carriage at 5.40. On reach- ing Grantham they drove to the Angel Hotel, where an excellent breakfast was served.' Breakfast over, the party were driven to the Belvoir Kennels, about seven miles away to witness the annual show el the puppies which were judged by the Rev. Cecil Ledger and Mr. T. Witmore, two noted authorities on foxhounds. The special prize given by Lady Greenall, to the walker of the puppy which was received at the kennels in the finest and healtkiest condition, was secured by Mr. Richard Cawley, of Newton-by-Daresbury. After luncheon the party inspected the hunters, kennels, &c., which were much admired, and then afterwards drove to Grantham station, arriving in Warrington at about 10.30.

CUP FINAL ,Ql_ TH_ OF GAMBLING. There was a crowded court at the Borough Police Buildings on Tuesday and Wednesday consisting mostly of forge workers who had assembled to hear the trial of Patrick Gill, aged 21, of Hoyle-street, who was charged with having on April 22nd, feloniously stolen the sum of £25 17s. 6d. the moneys of Thomas Warburton and others. After hearing the evidence on Tuesday the Bench (which consisted of Messrs. H. Roberts (Chairman) Alderman Bennett, C. Jackson Holmes, J. Rymer Young, Dr. Fox and W. Richardson) retired, and on their return the chairman said they had given the case very serious and careful attention and he regretted to say that they could not come to a decision, as they were equally divided. The casa would have to be re-tried. The prisoner was accordingly brought up on Wednes- day before Messrs. C. White (chairman), J. W. Hayward and Dr. Joseph, and the evidence was proceeded with. The Chief Constable stated that the prisoner was a native of Durham and had been employe 1 in Warring- ton during the last five years. For the last three years he had been employed as a labourer at Bowsey Forge. At the commencement of October last a Club was formed among the young men of the Bewsey district for the purpose of going to view the cup-tie final at the Crystal Palace at the end of the following April. It was arranged that prisoner be appointed the treasurer for the men's contributions which were is. each per week. He was assisted by a man named Rickards who also collected portions of the money and immediately handed it over to the prisoner. On April 23rd when the party were to have gone to London it was found that prisoner had absconded taking all the money amounting to £25 17s. 6d. with him. The police were informed and a warrant was issued for his arrest. Nothing was heard of the prisoner until the 17th mat, when he was arrested at Crook, near Bishop Aukland, in the County of Du-ham. Sergeant Meacock brought Gill to Warrington, who in answer to the charge admitted having taken the money. Mr. Unsworth who represented prisoner said before giving his speech for the 'defence he would like to establish Gill's good character. " Sergeant 3,leacock said he apprehended prisoner. When charged be said he did not think he was stealing the money. He intended to pay it back on getting a job. Witness had made inquiries RS' to prisoner's character at Bevvsey Forge and his workmates and foreman ,spoke highly of him as a workman. William Rickards, one of the prosecutors, said he bad no wish whatever to send the man to prison and the majority of the prosecutors did not wish to press the case. The Rev. Father Swarbreck said he had known Gill for over five years. He had always found him to be of a good moral and trustworthy character. He bad held small positions of trust and had given every satisfaction. Mr. Unsworth said he was going to ask the magistrates to take a lenient view of the case. Ile was gar, to ask them to deal with the case under the Probation of Offenders Act, of 1907. He implored them to deal mercifully with the prisoner and bind him over to come up for judgment if called upon. Gill was only a young man and bad been bromht up by an aunt, his father being dead and his mother living away. Unfortunately a year ago he got in the habit of putting small sums on horses, and having mixed his own money wit'h his companions weekly subscrip- tions, be found one day that he had made serious inroad into the club funds. Instead of going to his aunt and confessing what he had done be plunged still heavier, in the hope of winning back the money. Unfortunately he lost, and unable to face his companions he went away with the full intention of finding work and paying the money back. Concluding, Mr. Unsworth asked the magistrates not to make a gaol-bird of Gill, which would blast his future career, so that his fellow-workmen would not take his hand again. He felt sure that it would be a lesson to him. He bad promised never to bet on horses again. The Chairman (Mr. C. White) said they did not want to make a gaol-bird of the prisoner, and he was very sorry that ho (Gill) had got in such a mess. In binding him over for 12 months to come up for judgment if. called upon, they hoped it would be a warning to him. not to 'indulge in that pernicious and degrading vice of gambling again.—Gill was also ordered to pay the costs of the case (£3 125.)

div.head: Warrington Borough Court.
div.p: Warrington Borough Court.

SATURDAY.—Before Messrs. J. W. Ha 5 ward (chairman), A. J. Jolley and T. Pemberton. COST THE TowN RD.—Thomas Devereux, of no settled abode, was charged with running away from the County Borough of Warrington leaving his wife and three children chargeable to the Warrington Union.— Mr. Shearer prosecuted on behalf of the Guardians and stated that prisoner's wife and three children had been chargeable to the Union SinC 3 October last. Prisoner had gone away. they knew not where, and had not reported himself since. The prisoner's wife said she had been in the Workhouse for about 12 months and had not heard from her husband during that time. He lost his work because he was unpunctual. —Sergeant Stuart said he apprehended prisoner in Butterrnarket-street the previous night. He told witness that he had not been out of town at all and had been lodging at Cleeson's lodging house. On enquiry, witness ascertained that prisoner had only lodged there three nights.—The Chief Constable stated that prisoner bad been twice before the Court previously, for cruelty to his children and for neglect- ing to maintain one of his children in a reformatory school.—Prisener was sentenced to three months imprisonment.

MoNDAY.—Before the Mayor in the chair) and Messrs. W. Roberts, 11. Thornton, G. Pilling and W. Fulness. THEFT OF STRAWBERRIES.—Fred Archer, of no settled abode, was charged with stealing from the Market Place two baskets of strawberries, of the value of 3e., the property of Hugh McDermott.—He pleaded guilty.—The Chief Constable stated that the prosecutor was a wholesale fruiter, of Bewsey-road, and had a stall in the Market Hall. About half-past seven o'clock on Saturday evening he received a communication rind was in time to see prisoner run away from the stall with two baskets of strawberries. He gave chase and caught prisoner and gave him into custody. He was brought to the Police Station and charged and in reply admitted having taken them. Prisoner had been convicted of drunkenness, sleeping out, and theft of a carpet, for which be received a month's imprisonment. Conclud- ing, the Chief Constable stated that the prisoner was a man who seldom worked, and loafed about the railway stations.—Prisoner was sentenced to a month's imprisonment.

TUESDAY.—Before Mr. H. Roberts (in the chair), Alderman Bennett, Messrs. C. Jackson Holmes, J. Rymer Young, W. Richardson and Dr. Fox. ARREARS OF MAINTENANCE.—AIexandra Algie, of Albert-street, was summoned to show cause why he should not be sent to prison for non-payment of arrears amounting to £1 12s. 6d. in respect of his son, detained on the Ship "Clio."—lnspector Williamson stated that

in April last an order was made for 2s. 6d. per week for his son's maintenance on the Ship" Clio." Since the Ist June he had not paid anything. At present he was 13 weeks' in arrears. (21 12s. 6d.)—The Chief Constable stated that the case was a very bad one and the man made no attempt whatever to pay.—Tbe Bench decided to give defendant a month's time to pay the money, or in default a month's imprisonment.—Stephen Collins was summoned for arrears amounting to El Gs. He pleaded not guilty.—Defendant was ordered to pay the money or a month's imprisonment in default.—Thomas Donlan, Back Haydock-street, for arrears amounting to El 12s. 6d., William Vero, Dial-street, for £1 Gs. arr ars, were similarly dealt with. WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. C. White (in the chair) J. W. Hayward and Dr. Joseph. A FATIIRR'S NEGLIGENCE.—John Henry Beckett, of no settled abode, was charged with neglecting his family w hereby they became chargeable to the War- rington Union.—Mr: prosecuted on behalf of the Guardittns and stated that the prisoner was sen- tenced to a month by that court on the 3rd of Apt it for deserting his children, and on coming out, he had not been near his chi ld•en or paid anything for their maintenance. He had evidently determined that he would not do so. He W.t.9 in receipt of good wages, earning 304. per week on an average. Continuing Mr. Shearer said prisoner's family had cost the Guardians over £25 for their maintenance.—The Chairman, in sentencing prisoner to a month's imprisonment, said that he ought to be m..hatnel of him elf for not provid- ing for his family. Lie was a disgrace. If he did not provide for them on corning out of prison he would be sentenced to 3 months. -

WHOSE PANTS?—William Bradshaw,a stranger, was charged with stealing a pair of men's woollen pants from some person uoknown.—The Chief Constable stated that P.C. Holland was on duty in Bank Park on Monday evening when he saw the prisoner-lying on the grass. He afterwards saw a woman (who is at present in cusiody,.) rifle the man's pockets aud take the pants from him. The man was afterwards requested to give an account of how he got the pants and made two or three contradictory statements,finally stating that he had bought them from Wrexham. Consequently the Chief Constable asked for a remand for 7 days in order to ascertain the owner of the pants. He had circulated a description of them to towns within a thirty miles radins.—The remand was granted.
TiunsDAY.—Before Messrs. C. White (chairman), W. Roberts, J. Rymer Young, W. T. Williams and
Dr. Naden.

ONE MONTH FOR FREQUENTING.—Prances Ellis, an elderly woman, of Elizabeth-street, was charged with frequenting Bank Park with intent to commit a felony. —P.C. Holland stated that he was on duty in Bank Park on Monday night when he saw a man lying on the grass asleep and he saw the prisoner go to the man and rifle his pockets, taking his pipe, tobacco and matches. She then went to one of the walks and on satisfying herself that nobody was about, she went back to him and took a pair of men's woollen pants from his inside pocket and put them in a pocket under her dress.— Witness took her into custody ani brought her to the Police Station.—Prisoner said she found the articles on the grass when she was passing through the Park.— Prisoner who had been before the Court previously for drunkenness and frequenting, was sentenced to a month's imprisonment. THEFT OF PAPERS.—Edward Woraley and John Hargreaves were charged with stealing 52 copies of the Liverpool Express,' valued at 2s. 21. On hearing the charge Hargreaves said to the Clerk " They are worth Is. 51d. sir."—The Chief Constable stated that on Monday, the 12th of the present month, the prisoner Worsley went to the " Express " Office and asked Mr. Woods, the manager, who knew his character perfectly well, if he wo Id give him employment, as he wanted to go "straight." Woods gave him employment. On the Wednes2ay Worsley was given 52 copies of the " Express " for the purpose of supplying customers and collecting the money. Instead of that he disappeared, and nothing further was heard of him until the previous day, when he was arrested after coming out of prison for sleeping out. From a statement made by Worsley at the Police Station Hargreaves was found to be implicated in the affair and was arrested.—Hargreaves said he only had 61d. of the money.—Worsley said the money was spent on fish and bread and cheese.—Both prisoners had bad records, Hargreaves having thirteen previous convictions and Worsley eight.—They were sentenced to 7 days imprisonment each.

FRlDAY.—Before the Mayor (chairman),. Alderman James Evans, Messrs. A. J. Jolley, H. Thornton, W. Fulness and G. Piling. WANTED TO PAWN THE MANGLE.—Jaroes Lowe of \Vest-street, was summoned by his wife Annie Lowe for assaulting her on the 28th July.—He pleaded not, guilty.—Complainant stated that on Wednesday morn- ing about 20 minutes to 8 o'clock she heard someone in the back kitchen. On going to see what it was she saw defendant unscrewing the wringing machine and "taking away her living."—She stopped him and he then said he would have something and got hold of a saw and scratched her fingers with it. She had worked hard for him as he was out of work and would not try to get any. She had been married to him over 5 years. She had done everything to oblige and he had pawned all her clothes. A heated conversation then took place between the complainant and defendant and after quiet- ness had been restored the chairman said the case would be d'smissed.—Comniainant then appealing to the rolgistrates and said "What am 1 going to do." The Chief Constable " Turn him out." Complainant (eagerls) : "Turn him out, all right."

div.head: Presbyterian Services.
div.p: Presbyterian Services.

A Presbyterian service was held in Cairo-street schoolroom on Sunday evening, the prcazher being Mr. William Reid. of Sutherland, the neNly appointed minister-in-charge, whnse address was attentively listened to. He will take up his residence in Warring- ton in about a month's time, when a meeting will be hold to welcome him.

div.head: Memorials at the Parish Church.
div.p: Memorials at the Parish Church.

At the Livetpool Consistory Court on Wednesday, the Rev. Canon Willis, M.A. (rector of Warrington Parish Church) applied through the people's church- warden (Air. S. Taylor) for confirmation of the erection of a brass tablet on the north wall of the Boteler Chapel in the Church, with an inscription in memory of the late Rev. Edward John Willcocks, M.A., late head master of Boteler Grammar School (the consent of the patron, Lord Lilford, having been obtained) ; and also the erection of a brass tablet on the wi,st wall of the church beneath the gallery, with an inscription record- ing certain alterations and 'additions to the church. The applicants also sought permission to erect a screen at the west-end of the church, in memory of the late Cicely de Anyers Willis,a daughter of Canon Willis. The estimated cost of the screen would be .£6OO, and would be defrayed by voluntary contributions.—The faculty was granted.

div.head: Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church Choir.
div.p: Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church Choir.

Although the weather conditions in Wales on 1 slurs- day were not ideal the whole thy through, they did not prevent the annual trip of the above choir from being a grand success. At 8.17 a.m. the members of the choir and several friends left Bank Quay Station inn specially reserved saloon for the beautiful town of Llangollen and arrived there two hours later. At this time of the day the sun was shining brilliantly and the fine vantage point of Crow Castle was sought to take a panoramic view of the town and the surroulding hills. The dinner over the party went in pleasure boats along the canal to the Horse Shoe Falls which were greatly admired. Like most choirs on holiday they made use of their vocal powers 111 a variety of compositions. Coming back to Llangollen they had a drive in a char- a-banc round the neighbouring hills, and were very much impressed with their splendour and the beauty of the river. fhe return journey was commenced at 7.30 p.m. Warrington being reached at 9.30.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A.

There was a good open meeting at Wycliffe on Sunday, presided over by the Rev. John Yonge, who made feeling reference to the death of Mr. William Crossk ill, who for 1.1!i years bad worked on the P.S.A. Committee, and had for over 15 years been a member of the Brotherhood, lie had always shown a very cheerful and helpful spirit in the work, and his love for the P.S.A. was great. The Chairman proposed a letter of sympathy be sent to the widow and family of the deceased. The Secretary seconded, and said how deeply Mr. P.S.A. felt Mr. Crosskill's loss. The vote was taken standing. Mr. Ceecher Smith, of Manchester Y.M.C.A., gave the address upon" Who mind earthly things." Ile took lessons from three flowers, the oxslip, the cowslip, and the primrose, referring to the upward growth of the oxslip and the upward and beautiful growth of the primrose. lie pressed upon all the upward and LePutiful desires of life, and not simply the lower and earthly desires. Mr. A. Griffiths sang "I will sing of my Redeemer " and " Glory to Thee in his usual telling mander. Mr. Payton, Mus. Bac., presided at the organ. Mr. Yonge read a suitable lesson and the Secretary led the prayer with special reference to the Friend of the deceased brother. The closing hymn "Mourned whereso'er thou art" was sung with deep effect.

div.head: DEAN'S CHAUFFEUR PINED.
div.p: A DEAN'S CHAUFFEUR PINED.

At Kingston on Wednesday, Louis de Gasper, chauffeur to the Dean of Carlisle, was fined £2O and ordered to pay expenses. amounting to over RIO for exceeding the speed limit on Kingston Hill on June 26th. The speed was alleged to have been over twenty- eight an hour.

div.head: WARRINGTON GRAMMAR SCHOOL.
div.p: WARRINGTON GRAMMAR SCHOOL.
SPEECH DAY.

The annual Speech Day in connection with the Boteler Grammar School was observed on Thursday when there was a large gathering of the boys, their parents and friends, as well as many Old Botelerians, to witness the prize distribution in the Parr Hall. The occasion is always looked forward to with interest and pleasure, and Thursday's proceedings were character- ised by.the usual whole -hearted enthusiasm on the part of the pupils. The Rector -(Rev. Canon Willis) presided and was accompanied on the platform by the Rev. Canon F. J. Foakes-Jackson, D.D., Fellow and Dean of Jesus College, Cambridge (who distributed the prizes), the Revs. Canon Penrhyn, E. C. E. Carleton, and Horace Gray (headmaster), Messrs. W. Peter Rylands, H. Roberts, Vera B. Davies; and the members of the school staff. The proceedings began with the hymm " 0 Gentes Omnes," Mr. F. M. Darby, Mud. Bac., playing the pianoforte accompaniment. THE SCHOOL'S HISTORY. _

The RECTOR, addressing the meeting on the words "Look unto the rock whence ye are hewn and to the hole of the pit whence ye are digged," said it Waii just four centuries this year since the accession of Henry VIII. to the Throne. He was not a model of virtue, and yet we were told by Lord Bacon and by his enemy Pole that all excellent things might have been expected from him when he ascended the Throne at the age of eighteen. It was a wonderful time. The secret of the Universe had just been discovered. A new world had been discovered; a new language had been uneatthed, and they might say that a new religion bad been founded. A year after that (in 1510) Dean Collet fotm-led his first great Grammar School—the Grammar School of St. Paul. He spoke in his wonderful sermon in scathing terms of the vices of the clergy. He said that everything might be summed up in the words "The lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life." It was in order to change everything for the better that he founded the Grammar School of St. Paul. Sixteen years later Sir Thomas Boteler founded their own Boteler Grammar School, and it was founded, they were speciallly told, for the advancement of religion and learning. In 1880 a new scheme was formed, and those who drew it up had before them the constitution of 1526, and it was expressly appointed then that the religious teaching given in the school should be in accordance with the doctrines of the Church of England. In 1889, when a revision was made by the Charity Commsssioners, it was stated that the teaching in the school was not strictly denominational, but when a new scheme came out in 1908 it was recognised that on the written request of the parents who desired it their boys should have the whole teaching of the Church of England. and he (the Rector) was thankful to learn from the headmaster that three-fourths of the parents requested that their children might be so taught. (Applause). When he came to Warrington twenty years ago there were four notable nonogenariaus than living, namely, Lord Winmarleigh, Sir Gilbert Greene'', Canon Iharn and Mr. Beamont. Mr. Beamont said to him in that grave and onerous way in which he spoke "Sir, you have had some very distinguished predecessors. The Rev. Samuel Shaw was he idmaster of the Grammar school and Rector of Warrington for thirty years and the Rev. Edward Owen Wai Rector of Warriugton for forty years, and for fifty years headmaster of the Grammar School. They were all distinguished scholars, eloquent preacher, and strict disciplinarians." To come down to the present time, they had lost just lately the Rev. E. J. Willcocks, who for thirty-seven years was second master and headmaster of the school. He was a great° friend of all boys and much loved by all who knew him. (Applause). His successor was the Rev. Horace Gray, who had been with them for between oue and two years —(ipplause)—and who had, they trusted, a long career before him. They hoped it would be a most successful and prosperous one. (Applause).

div.head: BOTELER SCHOLARS.
div.p: BOTELER SCHOLARS.

The RECTOR announced that the following Boteler scholars sere elected at a meeting held the previous thy :—B.Browne, E. A.Tbomss, R. W. Weaver,F.O. Stans- field, G. Woodcock, C. H.Lyes, E. Jeffrey, L. W. Weaver, and W. Maginn. An examination for the election of two Boteler scholars from the elementary schools would take place in September.

div.head: HEADMASTER'S REPORT.,
div.p: HEADMASTER'S REPORT.,

The Bev. HORACE GRAY, in presenting his annual report, said the school was fulfilling in a very real way her part as the most import int centre of secondary education in the town. In his report of last year he dealt with certain changes that were to be introducel subject to the approval of the Board of Education. This having been granted, they had this sear been able to place the various members of the staff in charge of those spbjects which they had specially made the own. Asa direct consequence

div.head: BETTER RESULTS
div.p: BETTER RESULTS

had been obtained. The value of such arrangement, however, would be more clearly seen in the course of the next few years, a hen the boys in the lower forms, nurtured on this principle, should have found their true place in the highest forms of the upper school. Various structural alterations in the time table bad been made and, if experience served one aright, would be recom- mended in a fuller degree when the number of boys reading the classics as a school subject found their true proportion. In this respect it would perhaps be said that they had erred on the side of caution. They had, however, thought it advisable to move slowly rather than to introduce any very drastic changes. Of those who had recently enteric' the school, their environment had naturally suggested what was termed

div.head: MODERN Eb-UCAtION
div.p: A MODERN Eb-UCAtION

—a curriculum in which scientific subjects played an important part. Thus as the year advanced, these bad found a more recognised place in the curriculum, although possibly they had not been fully appreciated by the cla.ses taking them. The reason for this might be the limitation and weakness in the application of mathe- matical knowledge. This next year he confidently expected to see this difficulty eliminated as the spade work had been done and tbe subjects would be more kindly received and appreciated. One might well define this mathematical weakness as the line of least resis- tance. There were some boys who showed decided mathematical ability and who if they elected to follow that branch of study should earn distinction. On the other hand the reputation of the school as a

div.head: CLASSICAL SCHOOL
div.p: CLASSICAL SCHOOL

bad been fully maintained if not largely enhanced. Bat they must not close their eyes to the fact that the number of boys who were reading with the intention of proceeding later to the Universities was small in comparison with the number of those on the modern side. The school had in the past merited classical exhibi- tions at the ancient Universities, and he trusted would in the near future adi to her honours in that field, but they must remember that schools similar in constitu- tion to their own found opportunities in other directions. Natural science and mathematics should claim their share and with the staff as at present com- posed, if tho material was forthcoming, those honours could, be confidently asserted, most certainly be won. Thus it was that he asked aspiring parents to entrust such material to them and the school would do her part. But let him say at this point that the school as an institution expected a corresponding outlay of energy and interest on the part of the pupil. One would seize an opportunity like the present to urge upon boys that they had a very real duty to perform towards the school and that they would exert themselves to the utrgost to fulfil that duty. Turning to more genial topics, the past year had not been without its successes—in fact the

div.head: HONOURS GAINED
div.p: HONOURS GAINED

by present boys must be well received by old Botelerians who continued to manifest deep interest in the school and all tint concerned her welfare. They would be interpreted by them and by the friends of the schools as indicative of the fact that some very vaftiable work had been done. Sterling, the held boy, was soon lost to them, his success in a very severe com- petitive examination in December last causing this, his place in the Civil Service examination under the Junior Appointments Scheme, 37th out of nearly 180 candidates, being a most honourable one. He NVII4 now engaged in the Estate Duty Office in London, where they had no doubt that he would do ureful work. Another success in the Civil Service examinations had recently been obtained by Hayes, also direct from the school, who was placed 26th out of more than 700 candidates in the boy clerkships and scored excellent marks in all the subjects that he offered. Further a new feature had been introduced by the entrance of one of their boys, Carruthers, in a recent Public SAool scholarship examination. They were pleased that his efforls met with success and hoped that his career at Christ's Hospital would do credit to the trainitr, that he had received at the school. During the Christmas term they passed Bunch, ma. in the preliminary examination for chartered accountants. _ _

_ . Over and above all these honours, he felt that a school of their type must be proud of the achievement of Hands, the present head of the school, who n was in March last elected to a open exhibition in modern history at Downing College, Cambridge. This result was most gratifying, seeing that Lein(' only specialised in this wide subject during the past year. They took that opportunity of publicly congratulating him and to wish him every success in his University career. lie left them ready to take up at once his fripos work i as he recently secured a first-class n two parts of the Previous Examination. One result of this specialisation was to be seen in the absence of his name from the prize list, but his work for the school had merited the award by the governing body of the Beamont scholar- ship of ihe value of £5O for three years. Once again the results of the Oxford Local exiimina- dons were most pleasing, the list being considerably above the average. Ten boys were placed in the first class honours list among them no less than 14 distinc- tions were distributed, p of which were for religious knowledge. Remembering that those boys who had in the previous year passed the Senior Local were not again entered,such a record must be held to be extremely

satisfactory. He would venture to draw the conclusion that such could only he the outcome of sound work. Besides these examination successes, a large number of boys had been enabled to take up suitable positions in various professions. As concerning the Old Boys, a number were now in residence at the Universities and were only in the middle of their courses, so that they bad this year no final successes to relate. They gathered that they were all prospering and doing well in their inter- mediate examinations. Dutton, the school exhibitioner, had'just secured a first class in his College Mays and had been elected to an exhibition of £3O. He was at St. John's College, Cambridge. As in former years the school had just been examined by the Oxford Delegacy, the Rev. Canon W. G. S. Wbicker, M.A., ex-scholar of Corpus Christi College, Oxford, having been with them all the past week. In his report he stated that the school was in a satisfactory condition. The work was more concentrated than it used to be and had, he thought, improved inconsequence. The HEADNI4-STER also dealt with the recreations which assisted the boys to pursue their mental labours with greater vigour, and in which rapid strides had been made. Although they were minus .the provision of what many schools enjoyed—playing fields adjoining or in close proximity to the school buildings— they had utilized to the full the kind provision which the governors had made for them. Mr. Gray expressed his thanks to the staff for their hearty co-operation and suppsrt in and out of the school. Many of the improvements which had been remarked were traceable to the zeal and self-sacrifice on the part of his colleagues. The boys had almost in all cases made an adequate response. A spirit of unanimity had pervaded the whole and he must heartily thank the members of the staff for their staunch.support. They wished to express good wishes for Mr. Sinclair, the junior master, who was about to enter upon different duties in a new sphere. They had secured in Mr. Grew., late scholar of Magdalene College, Cambridge, who had just graduated in the historical tripos, a man who-from the scholarship point of view would fully maintain the school's high traditions. In conclusion the headmaster thankei the governors for their unfailing support and extended a hearty welcome to his old college tutor, the Dean of Jtsus College, Cambridge. (Applause).

div.head: TUE PRIZE LIST.
div.p: TUE PRIZE LIST.

The following is the prize list for 1909 : CLASSICS.—VI. Form, Browne, ma.; V. Form (Classical), Woodcock ; V. Form (Modern), Welsby ; IV. Form (Classical), Fergason,ma.; IV. Form (Modern), Fern; HI. div.head: PRESENTATION TO THE HEAD BOY.
div.p: PRESENTATION TO THE HEAD BOY.

The Rev. H. GRAY said he wished to recognize, on the part of the school, the work of the head boy H. Hands) not only in his learning but in the unobtensive spirit in which he had worked since he became head boy. He thertlore asked Canon Foulkes-Jackson to present on behalf of tee school a small memorial to
Canon Foukes-Jackson then bawled to Mr. Hand 3 a handsome pair of silver candlesticks. CANON FOAKES-JACKSON'S ADDRESS.

Canon FOAKES-JACKSON, having distribut3d the prizes, delivered an interesting address. lie said it was a peat honour for any boy to belong • to so ancieut a foundation or for any towa in the kingdom to own a school so ancient, honourable and distinguished as the Boteler Grammar School. In this progressive age we did not look so much to whether a thing was ancient as to whether it was of any use. We thought more of efficiency and vigour than anything else. Their school, ancient as it was, had one of the greatest advantages of youth—that one was able to deal with anticipations for one's future and to anticipate great things for opeself without any concern to what was strictly probable or even feasible. He dare say there were some of his younger friends present who were destined for most respectable, honourable and regular careers, but who hid great hopes that they might one day command a pirate ship or take to the road, or some equally adventurous method of life for which their present education was hardly qualifying them. (Laughter.) At any rate, they might feel the enthusiasm of youth and imagine great things for the school. Somehow or other it was not so foolish as it seemed to imagine great things, because that was one of the ways to attain them. A school renewed its youth whenever anew headmaster was appointed,and if ever a school ought to renew its youth it was the Boteler Grammar School since Mr. Gray had undertaken the duties of steering it. (Applause.) Mr. Gray was a very old friend of his. He (the speaker) remembered him in his own college at a very difficult period of its history, when it was going through a great transition, and he remembered how well and honestly Mr. Gray worked to bring about a general improvement in the place. He was a pers-in of con- siderable influence, for in those days he indulged with considerable success in a game called cricket. (Laughter and applause). Mr. Gray might be trusted by those who had great hopes for 'the Warrington Grammar School, to guide it into a very brilliant and successful future. (Applause). Continuing, the speaker said he considered the school had a right to entertain the ambition to become

div.head: ONE_ OF THE LEADING PUBLIC SCHOOLS
div.p: ONE_ OF THE LEADING PUBLIC SCHOOLS

in Lancashire, and pointii—NalC-I;.;Ve-re.-ir-e-a-tly in its favour were the convenient situation of Warrington, which should attract pupils from a wide area, the great prestige of the town, and the antiquity of the school. He proceeded to speak of the value of the public spirit created by schools of that kind, for if a boy belonged to a good school he felt a sense of dignity and responsibility which was a great help and guide to forming his character in after-life. There,was also the determination in a good school, whether it was at the beginning of a great career or at the height of it, to maintain a truly good and honourable tone. If they wanted to mike a school a first rate school and worthy of its traditions, they must do all in their power to maintain a healthy tone—honesty, purity, good manners, courtesy and all that was meant by gentlemanly con- duct. There was one danger attached to a day school. The boys who attended it were apt to be less self- reliant than those who went to: a boarding school One reason was that when one was away at a boarding school and anything unpleasant happened one had to bear it in silence —which was a very good thing. But when boys could go home in the evening and consider 01l the little grievances of the day there was a danger of losing a certain self-reliance. He appealed to parents to take the side, in many cases, of the master against the little boy. The elder boys could take care of themselves but it was the little boy who was such a dear little chap and no-one must say a word against him or vex his dear little soul, even when he was naughty. (Laughter); They must give him time and let all these little things go by, remembering that it was all part of the discipline of the school and that the discipline of our public schools in Warrington was to make boys into good boys and then turn them into good men. (Applansal. They must have some of the rough and tumble of school life. The speaker referred to the success of the boys' club in connection with the school and said be had elk° noted with pleasure the development of laboratories and their admirable tables for carpentry. Was it too much to hope that in the lap of the future there lay a prospect of a school standing in more—be would not say agreeable surroundings because nothing could be more beautiful than Mr. Rylands' works —(laughter)— but in more open space so that there would be more opportunity for the development of the laboratories and workshops and the provision of a larger playground, although Mr. Gray told him that the present ground was a most admirable pitch. (Laughter.) To make a school thoroughly efficient, it was necessary that it should be a rather costly burden to a town, but an efficient secondary school, taking a first-rate place, was a burden which, if costly, well repaid anything that was spent on it. The town of Warrington seemed to him, from what be beard, to be a MOST PROGRESSIVE AND PROSPEROUS PLACE, to be constantly developing, and to have shown great enterprise in a great variety of businesses and manu-. factures. In that case it was most important that the education of those who would have to take the lead in the business of the town in the future should be as

good as possible, and that they should be given as many opportunities of improving themselves in every way as possible. lhough his interests had never run on the scientific side, .he realized most tremendously the importance of two things—the thorough teaching of science and of modern languages. On those- two things a great deal of the commercial prosperity of England as a manufacturing country must necessarily depend. But their's was a Grammar school and De Quincey, in in his "Confessions of an Opium Eater" gave a good definition of the word. Grammar did not mean the horrid thing that they connected with it; it did not mean the parsing of words, the analysis of sentences, or the almost indecent irregularities of the horrible verbs (Laughter.) Grammar meant literature—literature of every kind—and he thought it might be expanded so far as to mean all learning that hsd not directly to do with the way they got their living. It was a most remarkable thing that the people who had been most generous to learning bad been men mho had been enti-ely devoted to business all their lives and the places where learning had flourished most had been in business centres. The reason why business men set such value on learning was that they saw the great importance of something that would refresh the mind and enable them to turn from the cares of the day to other thoughts, something that would remain a happiness to people when many of the good-things of this world had gone. We might strive after money; we might make it, but he believed those who had been most successful knew what a precarious thing a man's fortune really was,and how easily it might be lost. Our health and strength might go, but there was an enor- mous pleasure left for those who had cultivated some taste and some of the intellectual pleasures of the mind. Perhaps that would seem to th 3 boys to be "rot,"—(lauehter)—but he assured them that it was not. They would find more happiness in many of the things I they were learning now than they would perhaps find in , anything else. (Applause). The Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON, in proposing a vo‘e of thanks to Canon Feakes-Jackson, referred to the tie which hai so long existed between the old Universities and the Grammar Schools. Long before people talked about children passing by gradual ascent from the elementary school, through the secondary and higher grade schools, to the University, many a youth found his way through the Grammar School of his own town and district by means of scholarship to the University. It was true that the scholarships was a form of charity but it was the glory of the Church that it had made charity a thing that might be accepted without dis- honour and, associated as those scholarships were with every honourable distinction, there was ne class of the community that did not feel the possession of those prizes to be a coveted ambition. ,_
Mr. C. S. BURGESS seconded and the vote was heartily passed.
TUE PLAYS.

Three short plays were then given by the boys and were very appreciatively received. The first was in French and was entitled "Non-Coupable "(Not Guilty). It was written by Mr. F. C. Herzog, modern language master at the school, and proved highly entertaining. The parts were taken as foliowq :—Tirepont (gentle- man), B. Browne; Dnbourg (lawyer), J. Bunch ; Tic, W. F. Wersby ; Jean (Tierpont's servant), G. H. Masln. l'hen followed a Greek play—scenes from "The Acharnians " of Aristophanes, the performers being : Dicteopolis, H. Hands LLamachus, E. A. Thomas; countryman. R. W. Weaver; messengers, attend- ants, &c., G. Woodcock, C. Hayes, L. W. Weaver, 11. Blackwell, W. Maginn, E. Jeffery. Lastly the audience was entertained to scenes from "The School for Scandal," the following being the cast :—Sir Peter Teazle, T. C. Murphy; Sir Oliver Surface, S. C. Owen; Charles Surface, P. 0. Stansfleld ; Rowley, A. Lee ; Careless, W. C. Kewley ; Moses, P. Eyre: Sir lit:rry Bumper, J. L. Smith.—ln each play the boys acquitted themselves admirably, and the audi- ence expressed approval by applauding vigorously. The usual cheers having been given, the boys dispersed for their summer holidays.

div.head: NATIONAL SERVICE LEAGUE.
div.p: NATIONAL SERVICE LEAGUE.
ANNUAL MEETING AT APPLETON
HALL.
Judge Criticises the Prime Minister.

In the beautifully-situated grounds of Appleton Hall the Warrington division of the National Service League hold its sixth annual meeting on Saturday afternoon. The kindness of Mr. and Mrs. Lyon in inviting the members to meet in such pleasant surroundings is highly appreciated, and there was an excellent attend- ance. In the early part of the afternoon the outlook was unpromising and there were several heavy showers, but later the sun shone forth and a happy time was spent in rambling about the well-kept gardens. The meeting was held in a large marquee, and NVJS presided over by the Earl of Stamford. The house party con- sistsd of the Earl and Countess of Stamford, Baroness Ritter-Gruensteyn, Judge Hans Hamilton Lady Brooke, Rev. and Hon. C. F., Cross, Mr. and Mrs. Cecil Parr, Mrs. George Egerton-Warburton, Mr. and Mrs. Ussher, Rev. Percy and .Mrs. Stewart, Miss Cicely Thorpe, Mr. Bazeley and Mr. Weld. Amongst others present were: Appleton, Alderman Bennett, the Rev. H. B. and Mrs. Blogg, the Rev. G. C. Briggs, Mrs. and the Misses Broadbent, Colonel and Mrs. Buckton, Mr. and Mrs. Burgess, Councillor Broadhurst, Mr. and Mrs. Coiling- wood, Mr. and Mrs. J. J. Crosfield, Captain Crosfisld, Mr. and the Misses .T. E. Davies, Mrs. Edelsten, Mrs. Brereton Fairclough, Mr.H.Greenall,Mr. E Hall, Messrs. W. N. and G. Hutchiugß, Mr. Lister Kaye, Captain Mott, Mr. and Mrs. Pierpoint, Rev. H. V. Pigot, CJuncillor H. Roberts, Mrs. Stack, Major and Mies Strachan, Mr. B. S. Townroe, Captain Waring, Mr. and the Hon; Mrs. Willis, Canon Willis, Mr. Max Woods.

The Chairman said the members of the National Service League understood that they had got a duty towards their country in addition to metely getting things out of their country. It was rather too much the fashion to ask : What advantage could they get from the Government? When they got advantages from the Government it meant that they were getting them over Brown, Jones and Robinson, that they were getting them out of their neighbours, after all. He th,iught a better feeling was : What can Ido for my neighbours and for my country? For a lung time past they had talked about the rights of citizens, but they had not talked so much about the duties of citizens, and that was the point which the National Service League was trying to bring home to every head and heart in England. Warrington had responded well to that cans() and he knew the good work done by Captain Crosfield and others was constantly qu)ted as an example to the rest of England of the efficient work done in the stirring of the people to a sense of their duties. The president of the division (Mr. T. H. Lyon) had given him a message to deliver, "Warrington we. are showing their loyalty now as they did 109 years ago, when the country was daily expecting to be invaded by Napoleon's army assembled at Boulogne. The Blue Cap Regiment was created by my great uncle and his nephew, and my father was one of the subalterns. The men werenot highly drilled, but they meant defending their hearths and homes." Alluding to the progress of the movement, the Chairman said they were enlisting the support. of Liberals as well as Conservatives. That was a point upon which he was very insistent—that the League was

div.head: NOT A SECTIONAL OR POLITICAL CAUSE
div.p: NOT A SECTIONAL OR POLITICAL CAUSE

but a national cause. (Applause). He had urged his colleagues to keep that point continually in view. Of course, on the political field it might be the fash7on to denounce Liberals as traitors to their country, but in the business of life they found they were all very good friends indeed. (Laughter). Even in the House of Lords and in the House of Commons the Unionists and the Liberals got on very much better than one would think from the language they used in the country. (Laughter). After all, he thoeght they all tried to regard the real interests of the country. They did not think each other traitors, as a matter of fast, and they were very thankful there were a great many oppor- tunities of working together, as upon an occasion like that. That would be a very treasonable thing to say if there were an election coining on— (lauthter)—but he thought they would take his remarks in the spirit in which they were meant in' the present circumstances. He happened to stand rather in the centre between the two parties, and so he felt entitled to make such remarks. The Chairman went on to refer to the activity of Lord Roberts in the cause, remarking that in his conduct of the Bill in the House of Lords, he showed no sign other than of youthful vigour and perennial enthusiasm on behalf of the subject which he had made one of the great subjects of his life. It was a gratifying surprise to see how small was the majority against that Bill. It would have been too premature to have swept the board at once, but the result showed that members of the House of Lords had been consider- ing this important question carefully and had come to a pretty strong conclusion. He always felt that the House of Lords was like a jury. They could pick out any dozen men, gat their opinion, and they would get somewhere about the right result where their interests were not immediately concerned. On a question like this they had moderately sensible men debating a national question which did not immediately concern their own interests, and their conclusion showed how far the cause of national service had advanced among the average minds of the nation. After claiming for national service that it was a truly democratic movement, Earl Stamford said it was invaluable for civic life as well as for military life. (flear, hear.) Men were better for business, they were more intelligent and more amenable to reasonable dis- cipline, and they were better able to appreciate indus- trial needs than those who bad not gone through the course. They were also better men physically than those who thought their athletic work consisted only of standing with their hands in their pockets watching football and cricket matches and so on. They had got hold not merely of the art of war,but of the arts of peace as well. (Hear, hear.) One heard son.etimes of the evils of militarism. The best way to avoid them was by universal military training. (Hear, hear.) Generally the most peaceful and good humoured man was the trained boxer • he was not a quarrelsome individual at all. He (Earl Stamford) was a man of

peace, but he was bound to acknowledge by the force of circumstances that if they wanted peace they must be prepared for war, and that a really pacific spirt,' attained to by thorough preparation for hostilitielf (Applause.) WARRINGTON ? CHAPTERS. WARRINGTON'S ATTEMPT ATTEMPT AT SHIP-BUILDING.
THE ILL-FATED "JOHN TAYLEUR."

Most of the old inhabitants who have told their life stories for the interest of the readers of the "Examiner" have mentioned the launching of the Warrington ship "John Tayleur." The occasion had great local magnitude and circumstances combined to make it a striking event. We remember the "John Tayleur " to-day as a piece of local enterprise, and as a chapter in the sa,d annals of the sea, and in both aspects the subject has interest. OCEAN VESSEL BUILDING.

The firm of Messrs. Tayleur, engineers, of Warrington,conceived the ambitious project of developing a new branch of industry; nothing less than the building of iron ocean-going vessels. It was felt that the Mersey at Warrington was fitted for the launching, and that at their works at Bank Quay,they could successfully build vessels of large capacity. It was in the early fifties that the pro- ject was entered upon. The discovery of gold in Australia had occasioned • a wild rush of emigrants to the Gold Fields, and passenger ships were in great demand. In 1852 the "John Tayleur " was planned and began to rise in the stocks, a long well- designed and graceful vessel of about 2,000 tons burden. She was designed for a steamer but it was found that engine builders were busy: Unwilling to wait,the builders decided to rig her as a sailing vessel and send her upon a first trip under sail. As a sailing ship she was the largest of her time and there was considerable local pride that the town was to give the world a record vessel. October 4th, 1853, was the day fixed for the launching and the river banks presented an animated appearance 'as the hour for the great event approached. It is small wonder that expectations ran high, for the success of ' this first iron vessel might mean an import- ant industry for Warrington. We have searched the local records with considerable care, with a view to giving our readers the best description of the event. Much snore interesting than any of them is an account furnished by the kindnese of Mr. Corbett, the Borough Engineer of Salford, and we propose to print it as giving,a very happy and lucid picture of the events of the day as they impressed a schoolboy witness. Mr. Corbett was, in-1853, a scholar at the Friends' School at Penketh. The boy § had seen the lofty skeleton form take shape and heard the riveting with which she was clothed in her iron skin. They were now marched to the river side to see her take the water. PENKETII SCHOOL BOY'S ACCOUNT.

This is how the incidents impressed him : The river was at its utmost height in a full spring tide, showing a wide• area of waves where usually cattle- grazed on the marshy lowlands. Just after high water the "John Tayleur " was successfully Launched, and as the tide-stream quickly turned and ran very rapidly sea-ward, the ;Teat ship, floating very high out of the water, came rapidly towards us. I was short-sighted and could not see the launch 31early. I heard the excited comments of my comrades and was wondering when the ship would come within my limited view. Still looking towards the shipbuildinyard I had forgotten that the river's course was round a bend to• our left. My mistake was noticed by my teacher, Thomas Cartwright, who gently turned my head in the right direction,. Instantly I was startled by the sight of the high, sharp bows of the ship close at hand, and apparently rushing right on to us. My alarm was warranted by the reall circumstances, for there is a somewhat sharp bend in the river course just there, and we were on the outer side of the bend. The " John Tayleur " had a steam-tug lashed on either side, helping to steer her course, and the pilot had under-estimated his difficulty in turning the long ship round this bend. The consequences were very nearly being very serious, for the great ship' swung close to the sloping river bank just above the wall where we were; and she pushed her little steam tug, probably some 300 tons in weight, right up on to the bank. The stronghawsers snapped like threads, I suppose the tug on the port side backed with her full power, and by only a few feet clearance the ship escaped from crashing into the stonework, and passed rapidly along with the outgoing tide.

div.head: AN ANXIOUS MOMENT.
div.p: AN ANXIOUS MOMENT.

"Then occurred one of those incidents of quick, sound judgment, firm command and prompt obedience, whicri might on occasion win a great battle and earn a nation's grati- tude for some military commander, but which are quietly passed over, time and again, as merely every-day duty among engineers and their workmen.

The Manchester, Warrington, and Garston Railway ,was then in course of construction close by, and hundreds of navvies, with their foreman and engineer in charge, were watching the "John Tayleur "go by. Piles of slender scaffold poles lay some fifty yards away. When the steam tug was pushed on to the river bank, and the great ship nearly followed her, there was a sudden cry of alarm; but almost immediately a loud firm voice announced the scheme of the clear-headed engineer, and with instant obedience the navvies ran to the scaffold poles and brought them at a run to the water side; every moment was valuable, with the tide running down so fast; each pole was firmly grasped by a score of strong men. Many scores of men with poles worked side by side methodi- cally as if they had been drilled for this special work; the poles, like so many boat launching poles were thrust against the side of the stranded steam-tug, and at the word of command, all together, they thrust the tug down the sloping bank into the water, many of the men wading deeply to make the thrust effective; and in far less time than it takes to tell the tale the tug was paddling along at her best speed to over- take the ship and resume her duty.

div.head: SCHOOLBOY'S PREMONITION.
div.p: A SCHOOLBOY'S PREMONITION.

"My school chum, Jim Thompson, and I I had together made a fair-sized model ship, and arranged to launch her there and then; but there was no time to attend to so small a matter when such great events were hold- ing our attention. That evening, wfien we were having our recreation time in the large schoolroom, Jim Thompson busied himself quietly in a corner for some time. Presently some boys came to me in a rather scared and and indignant state, to call my attention to what Jim was doing. He had got a piece of black-faced cardboard and was making a drawing on it .by scratching white lines through the black facing ; and a very terrible drawing it was, for it represented the fine new ship "John Tayleur " being wrecked on a rocky coast, amid wild waves. Some of the boys were angry with him and I think they , seized and demolished his ill-omenedpictqre. "A few months later the master, Samuel Evans, read to us from the newspaper, with suitable comments; how the "John Tayleur " on her first voyage, had been wrecked on the rocks of Lambay island, near Dublin, on

January 21st, 1854. She had left Liverpool on January- 19th with 579 passengers, going hopefully to the goldfields, on board, and of these only 296 were rescued. Of the 100 women on. board,sad to relate only.three were saved.
"I need not enlarge On the too-hurried outfit, the incompetent crew and other things which conduced to this awful catastrophe."
LORD KELVIN ON THE WRECK OF THE " TAYLEUR."

One good purpose was served by the sad event. The building of iron ships was a new industry and it was not realized that the metal used in their construction might influence the mariner's compass. The "John Tayleur " is believed to have gone upon the rocks because her compass was deflected and the circumstance called the attention of men of science.

Mr. William Thompson, afterwards Lord Kelvin, wrote an interesting letter to the " Times" on the subject. He gave it as his opinion that the vessel had been built with her head towards the north, and therefore the hammering of her rivets had knocked what we may call northern magnetism into her whole fabric, that her compasses had been adjusted as usual, to allow for the particular condition of her fabric. His surmise that she had been built with her head towards the north proved to be correct and his theory was accepted as the true one. He went on to suggest that in sailing southward down the Irish Channel the battering of the storm waves had knocked out her original northern magnetism, and had reversed her effect on her compasses, thereby deviating them so as to mislead her captain, and causing him to steer 9, false course on to the fatal rocks when he thought he was going safely down the channel. The problem was taken up in earnest and Sir William Thompson, after many years of study, produced in 1876 the very ingenious compass which is now in common use. It has fine magnetic needles in a light frame and two compensating balls of soft iron and adjustable magnets. It is our one ray of solace in contemplating the wreck of Warrington's great and only triumph in'shipbuilding,thatout of the disas- ter cane one of the most useful of inventions. 'Space does not permit us to quote other local references which we have gathered on the subject of the "John Tayleur," but in selecting the account of Mr. Corbett we give the one that seems most attractive, and trust that it may interest our readers as a reminder of an almost f?rgotten local industry. A.M.
