div.head: MR. HENRY WHITHAM.
div.p: MR. HENRY WHITHAM.

I may add to the above captioun, "and, not too well told." When one sits down to write an account of the events of his life it may at least be presumed that what is offered will be of interest to the reader. lam not sure this will be the case in the present instance. In my case our Editor's request "would 1 oblige" at least safeguards me from thecharge of egotism.

I am afraid I have been rather an unpleasant person, butting in Where those around me might think a still tongue would bring a more peaceful life. However this may have been it was decided, and not„at my request, that I shciuld make my debut upon this plane of varied activities in Halifax, Yorkshire, on the 30th of. September, 1839. My schooldays, such as they were, began to be strikingly apparent in Manchester, to which city my parents, Richard and Sarah Whitharn had moved.

A word or two as to my parents. Father ' was born in Huddington Barracks, Scotland. His father, a soldier, being, along with my grandmother, located in that focality when the event took place. An honourable dis- charge, now in possession of my brother Dyson,shows that he left the ranks two years previous to the notable one of 1815. My mother,a Dyson of Highburton, Yorks, was of the Yeomany class,, her father farm- ing his own land, and being engaged in other activities, to which I may refer further on. As I have said, my earliest remembrances are of school life in Manchester. The strik- ing character in Handforth's Academy, Oldham-road, was Mr. Benjamin Handforth. He was a large man, strong of muscle, and,as I remember, his chief occupations were as he walked between the forms, to sharpen our quill pens and rather too often to invite his scholars to the floor. While one pupil "made a back," the culprit prepared to save his trousers from being injured while he doubled himself across it, and the cane, not too thick a one, was plied by the burly ruffian. No wonder I was never a Tdcent writett In the forenoons we had ten minutes for play-time and this we mostly used in displaying the scars and weals of scholarship. We were supposed to learn our spelling,geography, and grammar at home, and the morning's first work was to form a sort of crescent around the desk with the stalwart in the centre. If the young scholars of to-day could have a few moving pictures and thus see more graphically than I can describe that first half-theur's process of making the young idea shoot they would shake their own hands for pleasure that they were not born seventy years ago. "Hold your hand up ;" an upward swing of the cane,higher, another swing ; and if the cane split, the culprit to go out for anothpr, and it must be a- thin cane, not too thick or some more caning. Imagine the rest. I did not remain long at this school. , My next effort to make a man of myself was at Mr. Ferguson's school, situated on Copperas, near Shude Hill market. The fish market now covers the site. This pedagogue was notable chiefly for the avidity he, dis- played. in absorbing the contents of the Family Herald," the thin green-backed monthly Charles Dickens was then delight- ing the reading world with. I have not done with the school question, but I must note ether events. About this time the Chartists' cause was fading away. . It seemed as if all they had urged had been side-tracked. The French Revolution was giving lesson to the world's workers, and those who put their

ears to the ground might have heard fearfu rumblings. Then, as now,only a few heard and noted with concern the coming storm. At that time I attended a Sunday school in Lever- s treet,off Ancoats,and my father worked for R. Johnson at the Dale-street wire mills,and lived at Collyhurst. To reach the school on Sunday, or the mills during week-days, my way lay through New Cross, and many a time have I stood at that Cross drinking in pure Radicalism. Scores of times have I, as a kiedy, wandered among the factories of Ancoats, and known and seen mere babies forced to join in the making of cotton goods. Children were important assets then as they are to this day in the economic system of buying in the cheapest and selling in the dearest markets. Little children swept your chimneys in those days, and as a consequence of all these cheap but nasty ways of money making, it came about that I found one day my way across the city was blocked. New Cross in all four direc- tions, looking up Oldham-road or down Oldham-street, up Ancoats-lane or 'down Swan-street, soldiers and cannon only could be seen. At that time the New Cross end of Oldham-road was Well supplied with cellars, in which were huddled crowds of the poor and poverty-stricken. Around the tops of these pest holes were iron grids, and over these guards and steps I had to climb and make my way to school and mill. Years after these events John Bright put into words the idea that had long, long years before been formulated in the-Radicals' make-up, 'Force is no remedy.' These words might have been said years before when the Cheshire cabbage cutters made the site of the present Free Trade Hall historic. In these eventful years, my father's employer sent for him into the office and questioned him as to his relationship with a John Whitham who had some years before passed away. It seemed that a considerable amount of property was struggling to get into the market, a good title could not be given with it; so it happened that when the circumlocution office had done its work, father .was declared heir-at-law. Father engaged in "the traffic." Ife,like his son could not take life easy, and to the traffic he added a tobacco shop, and old Tim Bobbin, Roch- dale-road, was the location. I couldn't say if it was a paying venture or not, anyhow his path was crossed by a man named Burgess, who had a son-in-law with a fishy name. The two persuaded him to realise on his property and go into the wire manu- facturing business. The charmer charmed successfully, the move ending in a wire mill being established at Almondbury near Huddersfield, and a farm being taken at Shelly, a village about seven miles from the same town. Something of a change this for myself, but off to school I was sent again. Shelly school was, at that - time, notorious for its strict discipline : it outdid the Handforth. Academy to an extent that forbids my dealing with it.. It was allowed that Mr. Bedford was a good scholar, but his methods failed entirely in instilling anything intq my thick skull. I remember at this time the book "Uncle Tom's Cabin" being issued and my mother buying me a copy. I also remember my school days came to an end, and I was given a horse to care for. Dear old Jerry, many a mile we travelled together, leading coal, Up hill and down; through hail, rain and sunshine. That too passed away, and then I found myself learn- ing how to spoil wire, and under one whose son is now, I think, one of Warrington's business men. Were I to make use of a few " If's " now, and shape out a few phrases it would make no difference, not a bit, things happen and that's all there is to it. I remember going into the house one summer's evening and seeing my father and mother, the latter crying, standing surrounded by a few of the neighbouring farmers. The debacle had come, we were ruined, and a forced sale was going on. Limited liability was an unknown quantity at that time. The charmer had charmed all the money. out of the business and skipped. As I under- stood the situation,' father attended to the wire drawing end of the business and Burgess to the money, and clerical end, of which father had no more knowledge than I at that time. I should add that a practical farmer had charge of the farm all through this short and sour episode in my life. On the evening referred to, this man and I started out with two cart loads of furniture, and early the following morning we found ourselves at Owlerton, a suburb of Sheffield, and just under the walls of the horse- barracks. I think it right to say here, there was no need for any of this panic; a cooler head, and a slight knowledge of the world and its ways, would have carried father back into smooth water. Kisniet ! Now is the beginning Of a very ugly 'period in my life's story, and one• that is never to be effaced so • long as I live. Father having domiciled his family and looked around, foun d one of his old acquaintances of the name of Yates. Together they planned to start a wholesale yeast business. Father found the money, not much of it I fancy, and Yates found the skill. 1 well remember the trudg- ing up and down Sheffield streets and the unsatisfactory reports turned in. The venture collapsed, Yates disappeared, and father found himself again in a dilemma. Looking through the advertisments one day he came upon one that gathered me into its horrid grasp. A whitesmith of the name of William Amory wanted an in-door apprentice. He also wanted £lO as a premium and seven years' service. I was taken to this man, and exhibited of course. I should be about fifteen at the time, and I cannot to-day understand how several of the items contained in the indentures could have been drawn up by an honest lawyer. There were two of us bound at the same time. The other, like myself, was a big strong lad, a farmer's son. Big and strong as poor Jack was, the horrid, nay the fearful life we were forced into, soon, very soon, sent him to his grave. The memory of poor Jack has always been one that I. have cherished. We agreed well together, and I think his parents came to look upon me as a welcome addition to the family circle each week-end. My own family soon left Sheffield and moved to Birmingham. I fancy there are few now who know what it was to be an indoor , apprentice fifty years ago. I had three years of it, and I had all the hell I want during those years. The mistres's was a Roman Catholic, and a constant attendant at early mass. I had, as home work, to clean the shoes each morning of master, mistress, and daughter. Jack had to make the fire, and clean up the hearth, and we had to be in the smithy at six o'clock. We had to take the place of strikers, no other man but the smith and lathe men being kept. It was heavy work, hammers, Vices and dies for silversmiths being the chief work. The master was a sodden sot of a' drunkard. The mistress was the greediest and meanest woman I have come across during the whole course of my life. I think I must have been a bit tougher than Jack. She starved him into his grave; I weathered the long storm, as I have weathered others since. She would cook good food for their table; we at a side table could only squint at it. It was a regular thing for her to keep, during the 1 summer months, pies and bread until mouldy, and when we broke the bread, or took the pie from the plate,, it would almost hang

together with mould. One morning a basin of stuff was placed before each of us that caused a disturbance. With our spoons we turned it over, but we could not name it. We asked what it was, and were told to eat it. We would not, and at once left the house. Next morning it was there again. My friend Jack was no fighter, and so I had to tackle the situation. I took the dish of stuff out with me, and on it being examined it turned out to be bacon rinds that had been cut off their breakfast bacon and saved 'Until she thought there was sufficient to make a meal for us and then it was stewed. This incident caused me a lot of trouble, and I put it before the men in the Workshop, and the master taking to my side led to a perfect uproar in the house and started him on the spree. Another incident: There was - plenty of good food in the house, and gener- ally a ham and a flitch in the garret. We took the opportunity to help ourselves to this. Posting Jack on the watch, with a knife in hand I was soon aloft where I found the flitch cut level, and from end to end, and - the ham cut on the level around. This didn't daunt me. I followed in the wake of the previous carver, and we had a few good meals before we were found out. We found on the cellar door the legend No ham this morn- ing,' and I wrote under 'Very well.' It was soon after this that Jack died. My troubles commenced in real earnest now. The master was seldom sober. He would come into the shop half drunk and send me out for jugs of ale, and I had to deal it out to the men. On one of these drunken bouts he told the men the ham and beef story, and fine fun there was when he pointed to the hero. I must move on, I'll fill the "Examiner." From now on until the end he was rarely sober. One evening I had been out to my father's, or, on my waty there, when, suddenly remembering I had the door key in my pocket, (I ought to have left it at the daughter's who had recently married,) I hurried back and called for madam and together we went home. She Went in at a side door, I going forward to the back yard, and there I found the master hanging from the rails of the top yard. I gathered him up on to my shoulder and did some yelling, enough to bring madam out of the back door. Seeing the situation see brought a knife, cut the long length of silk he had used and I carried him into the house. Delirium tremens followed this, and about now my parents left Sheffield and moved to Birmingham, leaving me with my future in such a state that few can imagine. Certainly I had no home,and most certainly I saw no likelihood of a trade. The wonder is how I ever escaped becoming a member of the criminal class. There was a -short interval, very short, of soberness. During this interval my life was a perfect hell. He was all fondling and slobber with the madam; would belieVe all she told him. My work was all behind the anvil using the sledge hammer ; a wonder I didn't sample the master's work. He broke down again, and was at it some weeks. One evening we were called across the street, the master was hanging in a stable, and I and a butcher cut him down and carried him into the house. Some more delirium, and on with the drink again. Attached to the works were a number of small cutlers' shops. In each shop was a small fire grate used for melting glue. The master one night while drunk, entered one of these and lay across the hearth. A cinder rolled out and against his elbow, burning it, but not so much. During the night he raised the neighbourhood. We had to bring him home, get him to bed, and I then had a few days such as seldom falls to a lad of under seventeen. The smith, a big strong man, and I had to keep guard over this maniac. He would make for the door, or the window, yelling murder, and people from the street would force the door to see what was the matter, and during all this his arm was approaching mortification. When the drink died out of him he lay in his bed quiet enough for me to be left alone with him, and I was alone with him when he died. Yes, I alone, and neither wife- nor child would venture near him, and I was reading the Catholic service for the dying and he was buried as a Catholic. •

When we returned from the funeral lat once asked for my liberty. It was denied me and I was shown my indentures where it said I was bound to William Amory and his heirs and assignees, and so on. I stood it for a time and,during this short time it was that I came across the writings of John Page Hopps, a Unitarian minister. I devoted a lot of my time to the study of polemics. At this time I first saw and heard C. Bradlaugh in a debate with the Rev. Brewin Grant. The next time I heard Mr. Bradlaugh it was in a debate with Dr. Mackie in the old Music Hall in the Market Place. To Sheffield again. I began to be restive, I was being treated worse than a dog, and remember all this time my wage was sixpence a week, when I got it. I deter- mined to run for it. I should say here that my parents knew little or nothing of the life I was leading. It was the day before Xmas that I asked the smith to pawn my watch for funds to take me to Warrington. I remember as I travelled I expected at each station to see a man in blue ready to take me back. When I landed at Warrington jt was snowing heavily. I had the address, 41, Orford-lane. It was dark and just about as miserable outside as F was inside. I got to Orford- lane, but no one knew Richard Whitham. At length I found out that the last gas lamp was opposite 41. Above " Dick " Siddall's shop there were few houses, but Mr. John Rylands and I had what seemed to me a long lonely walk befow I stood at that lamp, saw that number and knocked at that door. To hear my dear mother's voice ask "whose there ?" to answer "me," and to hear her voice again saying to father "It's our Henry," was but a short prelude to being folded in my mother's arms. I may pass over the next few days. All in good time a lawyer's letter arrived. If I did not return at once to Sheffield the police would come for me. No use, I had to go back, and back I went, determined not to do one stroke of work. No, I did not, and would not touch hammer or tool of any kind. There I stood like a pillar of wood. How the next two weeks went on I cannot say. More than this, the men would stand about laughing, and the madam would, now and again, come in and call me all the names she could think. No matter, I would not work, and soon I cleared out again and off to Warrington. I knew my way this time, I had begun to see things. This time father went to Sheffield, and by paying another .£lO down I was liberated. I shall have to talk again about this grimy old town. In the mean- time I was at home with three sisters and a brother,and I wanted a trade. My father on landing in Warrington started work at Edersten's wire mills, Town's End. When I landed he was working for Rylands Bros., so he applied for me as an apprentice. The men wouldn't have me; they said I was too old. They raised quite a disturbance and threatened to strike. Mr. John Rylands dared them to do such a thing, and they did not take the dare, and I was put to a block. Then a strict boycott was put on Dad and his unfortunate big lad. It was a wonder the dear old folks didn't go off it and take me with them. (To be concluded next week).

div.p: THREE MONTHS IN INDIA, SYRIA, AND PALESTINE.
By Truda H. Crosfield.

div.p: (ARTICLE IV.)

I certainly never met one who was not utterly convinced of the necessity for training the young men of England to arms, so that they shall not stand by and bite their thumbs in helpless ineptitude and'rage when peril, which comes as a thief in the night, threatens the Empire as it surely will, sooner onater. _

div.head: RAIN AND PAROKEETS.
div.p: RAIN AND PAROKEETS.

There was a links at Sialkhot, not so good perhaps as those of Calcutta or Chitta- gong, but easier to play on than the one of hard-baked earth laid out by my cousin at Cawnpore, where the " greens " consisted of squares of white sand, watered with kerosene to keep them from flying away! Whilst play- ing one aftetnoon at Sialkhot, a tremendous thunderstorm burst above us, and at once the down-streaming rain brought the feel of northern climes with it. The rain had been terribly needed, however, for another ten days of dryness would have done for the crops that year, and brought famine on the people. So we gladly saw it pour for two days, after which everything looked glorious. There was quite a large garden round the bungalow, in which Captain Innes was suc- cessful in growing sixteen kinds of vegetables. These were much attacked by green paro- keets, especially the peas; but when we went out with an airgun the parokeets positively perched on the highest trees to squawk at the gun, and then flew off! • AGRA.

From Sialkhot I had a long night and morning journey down to Agra, where Miss , Moreland was awaiting me at the hotel. From now on began ten of the most crowded days of sight-seeing that I have ever put in. We worked as hard as though we were in for an examination, and even Sam, who did not sight-see, for he knew it all before, was worn out when we reached Bombay. Our first duty of course was towards Taj Mahal, that most exquisite tomb in all the world. We saw it splendidly, white as any pearl with its four white minarets around it, far down the curving bank of the lordly Jumna, as we gazed from the terrace of the fortress-palace. To describe this palace would be wearisome since it resembled that of Delhi, but excep- tion must be made for the Jasmine tower, a small octagonal chamber of marble, inlaid with scrolls of jasmine flowers and leaves done in transparent stones such as carbuncle, , agate, jasper, malachite and many others. Walls it had none, for they were replaced by openwork marble screens, and here the "light '

div.head: LAHORE FORT AND CITY.
div.p: LAHORE FORT AND CITY.

Who should be quartered in Lahore fortress but a company of the South Lancashire Regi- ment! A blue-eyed boy private, who showed us over Akbar's great fort, hailed from Warrington itself. The rest of the battalion were in cantonments two miles away; and there was something pathetic about that lonely little company kept in the fort, resolute and active though they looked. They were never allowed into the city; for the Punjabis are a proud and warlike race, and any friction might have most serious con- sequences. We were much impressed with the big, fierce-looking people who filled the narrow streets of the bazaar. Of a very different type were they to the Hindus further South. Latticed balconies overhung the bazaar on both sides, and, from them peeped the veiled women whom we would much have liked to see.. As to the European quarter of Lahore, it is largely a standing witness to the architectural skill of Mr. Lockwood Kipling,father of the genius whose pen has delighted millions. Mr. Kipling, senior, has attempted to blend Hindu and Mohammedan architecture, two very differ- ent quantities, for the first is all square, slim and ornate, the latter round, ponderous and plain. The result is several highly interest- ing-looking public buildings. We of course visited the celebrated Museum of which, I think, Mr. Kipling has been curator; and saw the botanical garlens, where are also many splendid specimens of animals. Amongst -these were white peacocks in a big mire enclosure. The male birds positively spread their superb tails and turned round and round, slowly, so that we might see them. Two miles away, across a bridge of boats, stands the enormous and ornate tomb of Jehangir, spn of the great Akbar, and father of the equally famous Shah Johan. A splendid-looking, crafty old Sikh was in charge, and got a big tip out of us, for the tomb (he said).

div.head: GOLDEN SIKH TEMPLE.
div.p: THE GOLDEN SIKH TEMPLE.

Amritzar is but an hour away in the train, and everyone who can, goes over there to see the celebrated Golden Temple of the Sikhs. It stands in the midst of a square lake, and the blue-green waters leave a black and white marble terrace on. all sides. A long marble pier extends to the centre of the lake, and terminates in the square temple itself, whose copper sides aie covered with gold leaf, and shine almost unbearably in the sun. The place reminded me of Chinese pictures of pagodas set in lakes, and we saw nothing like it anywhere else in India. We traversed the marble bridge, and walked round the

div.head: WHITE PALACE, UDAIPUR.
div.p: THE WHITE PALACE, UDAIPUR.

golden walls, listening to sounds of chanting within. When we entered, it was to see a painted and gilded hall, two-storeyed, but open to the roof in the centre, whilst a stair- case and galleries ran round the sides. The Sikh priest read passages from a huge and ancient volume, open before him on a low desk, behind which he sat, tailorwise ; and on either hand squatted half-a-dozen choristers who intoned the chants. I fear we rather "held up" the ritual by asking to see the Sikh treasures, which are double- starred in "Murray," and sound magnificent. Our guide, before we could stay him, inquired of the head-priest, whilst all the choristers stopped chanting, and gaped. He replied haughtily that the treasures were not there, and anyway we could not see them without a special permit from the Governor. So the treasures went unseen ; but we climbed the usual minaret, in this case about 14 storeys high, or so it seemed to my knees, and had a wide view over the chief city of the warlike religious race which produced that great ruler, Maharajah Runghit Singh about eighty years ago.

of the palace," Shah Jehan's beautiful wife, must often have sat to catch cool airs wandering from the north, and have gazed upon the site above the blue-green river, where her glorious tomb should rise.

div.head: SIALKHOT.
div.p: SIALKHOT.

From Amritzar our paths diverged. Miss Moreland went to Simla, whilst Sam and I journeyed up to Sialkhot, a northern Punjab town within twenty miles of the Cashmir frontier. All round the horizon, vast chains of snowclad mountains raised their jagged and steep-sided forms. I suppose these peaks were mostly fifty to eighty miles away yet they seemed to tower even at that distance, as I watched them from the train; and small wonder,for they are 17,000 to 20,000 feet high, whilst Sialkhot lies on a dead level plain. There is something quite different in the very air of the Punjab, once north of Lahore. It is something northern and solitary, which reminded me of nothing so much as the Normandy plains in early spring, when the wheat is just showing green above the furrows, and the air is still raw and thin with the winter rains. I had come up to spend some days with a cousin whom some Warringtonians mu remember as Miss Edith Blaiw, before she married Captain Innes. They lived in cantonments of course, a mile outside the city proper, which is said to be full of sedition,small place though it is. The country is as flat as your hand; but the roads have superb surfaces, there are plenty of trees, and above all, unlimited space for parade grounds, of which I think they told me there were ton!

div.head: SOLDIERS OF THE EMPIRE.
div.p: SOLDIERS OF THE EMPIRE.

It was a splendid sight to see the Black Watch, to which Captain Innes belongs, swinging down the long field at the run, or forming fours and wheeling in the centre; a sight to give pause to the siditious rascals who pour forth their literature against the best Government India has ever seen. 'Yet what a handful those steadfast troops are, set there between the swarming millions of India, and the fierce tribes and possible hosts of enemies beyond those frontier hills! There are, of course, the civilian whites to back them, for there are no two ways of thinking about military training in India. Men know there that you must be strong to .uphold justice and maintain truth with your

div.head: LOVELIEST TOMB IN THE WORLD.
div.p: THE LOVELIEST TOMB IN THE WORLD.

The tomb itself is a miracle of marble- inlay. But then everything in Agra is; even the fish at dinner was inlaid with slabs of beetroot! We visited the Taj Mahal by day and again by night, when it looks best of all. There was a moon, reflecting in the long narrow tanks which led up from the huge gateway to the huger dome. Tall black cypresses and °other trees were grouped on either hand. A little hot breeze whispered through them, and roses scented the air. Beyond glimmered the enormous marble dome. We climbed one white minaret, but the sun had so heated it by day that even at 9 o'clock at night it was gaspingly hot inside. Interest there is none Within these great Indian mausoleums,except for the marvellous inlay on the straight narrow tombs, and the open-work marble screens around them. Otherwise there is but the vast size of the empty dome and galleries to admire.

div.head: AKBAR'S PET PALACE.
div.p: AKBAR'S PET PALACE.

Our second day was devoted to seeing Fatepur Sikri which no one should miss if possible. We motored out 20 miles along a dusty road and then beheld the celebrated rose-red walls, 7 miles in extent, which I enclose Akbar's favourite palace. Its court- yards are now empty, and solitude has fallen ' on its beautiful buildings; for the water in a brackish lake, now dried into a swamp, proved too bad; and the great Akbar left the city on this account even before it was finished. But every building seemed to us a perfection of beauty. They were all of rose- red sandstone which seems to suit the pale blue Indian sky like nothing else. No damp had discoloured them, nor lichen grown in the carvings. They were perfect in outline as when Akbar sat there 350 years ago and played pachesi, a kind of chess, with beauti- ful harem slaves as pieces, in the courtyard paved as a chess-board. We saw the gallery supported on a much-carved, pillar from which branched four _gangways of stone; here Akbar was wont to sit in the centre and argue religion and philosophy with four learned men, one at the end of each gangway. There is another house, all doors and turn- ings, where tradition says the court played hide and seek; and the most beautiful build- ing of all, we thought, was the Panch Mahal, or "five palaces," a five-storied, open-sided series of floors, which acted as nursery and women's quarters. The sides were hung with curtains, and on the hottest days there must have been a faint breeze to be caught on the topmost stories. We certainly enjoyed one as we lunched lip there and gazed down on the beautiful silent palaces, glowing with colour in the hot sunlight, till it was ,a relief to turn the eye to the green swamp and maize fields outside the city walls.

div.head: NATIVE STATE.
div.p: A NATIVE STATE.

From Agra a night journey took us to Jeypur. The name of this celebrated native state is spelt in many Ways, and its appear- ance has been compared to Earl's Court. There is a most unreal look about the wide

streets. The two-storeyed houses are all covered with pink stucco, and scalloped along the top! As Hinduism reigns supreme here, no animals must be killed, and we saw thousands of pigeons feeding in great whirring flocks on .the grain which is scattered for them near fountains. Elephants frequently stride along the streets with half-a-dozen men seated behind the mahout or driver, each holding on to the other, or else safely seated in a howdah. The city gates are a scene of much buying and selling, chiefly of vegetable produce ; and the people, being Hindus, wear gaily coloured clothing. Dust is everywhere ; a dust which chokes throat and nostrils. The dryness of the air literally seemed to wither one's skin for we were on the edge of the great Rajput desert; and water is terribly scarce, even in ordinary times. Ido not like to think of what Jeypur must be when the monsoon fails it.

div.head: PRESENT DAY PALAQE.
div.p: A PRESENT DAY PALAQE.

We visited the Maharajah's palace, after duly obtaining a permit from the Residency. The palace contains much tawdry furniture and the usual glass decorations. But there were some superb carved brass doors, about 16 feet high, shining almost unbearably in the sun, and the gardens would be beautiful but they were untidily kept, and no water ran in the stone-flagged runnels laid for it. In the fernery we met a princeling, six years old, and already his large, languid black eyes seemed full of insolence. At the end of the gardens there is a large pond, half overgrown with sedge and bushes, and only to be styled lake by courtesy. Here live the muggers" to whom former victims used to be thrown. We purchased a piece of raw beef, and an old man raised the cry of" Ao, mugger." But none answered; so another man calmly descended into the brushwood and began lay- ing about him with a stick. We were divided between fear that the mud or the mugger would swallow him ; but neither happened. A black log floated through the water towards us, and there on the bottom step of our ghat rose a bottle-nosed crocodile with wicked, stupid little eyes, and a,truly awful stench of mud. Ordinary drains were not to be compared to it. As the long snout opened we had a vista down a hideous white throat, pulpy, and saffron-yellow in the deptla. Then the raw meat went in and the great mouth closed grinning upon it.

div.head: ANOTHER DEAD CITY.
div.p: ANOTHER DEAD CITY.

Amber, the former capital, lies five miles away, and we drove out to the hill gateway and here mounted an elephant. I think our's must have been a very old one, for he only shuffled along at a maddeningly slow pace, do what we 'would. I beat him violently with a parasol, leaning over the howdah, but he did not hasten his steps by a hair's breadth. We must have taken 40 minutes to go a mile, and the sun at three o'clock was unpleasantly hot. Amber lies in a rocky defile. The hills have splendid jagged out- lines and steep sides, and it was an ideal fastness,—the palace upon the crags,the little town below. But bad water hero as else- where, brought the city's life to a close. The palace is long and irregular, crowning the heights above the little lake. It is painted white from end to end and is handsomely built. A favoUrite ornament to a room is to cover its sides with crushed glass, which produces a sort of dove-grey blunted transparency. The windows look down steeply into the little blue-green lake ; and on the other side the open courtyards face the desolate and rugged hill sides,seamed with long and straggling walls. As we drove back through Jeypur, a mild full moon was shining, and under its rays the rose- coloured cardboard houses seemed more unreal than ever.

Jeypur is famous for its precious stones, its native weapons and curios; we had, of course, a visit from several vendors in the verandah of our little native hotel, and by judicious bargaining got several necklaces of jade, pink agate, and lapis lazuli reduced to quite tempting figures. But I must hurry on to Ajmere, where we spent next day after another night journey.

div.head: AJMERE.
div.p: AJMERE.

This city is chiefly famous because of the Mayo college for sons of Rajahs. Lord Mayo designed it to be an Eton of India and each pavilion is more pleasing than another. We saw no students however, as it was mid-day, and our driver told us they were all taking a siesta. Ajmere's greatest beauty is •the Anasagar lake. One drives through the pleasant green gloom of a wood, to emerge on a grass terrace edged with marble-pavilions and a balustrade against which the clear brown waters of the lake corhe fretting and splashing. That peat- brown water and the hills around reminded one of a mountain tarn at home in our western isles. We drove to the sacred lake of Pushgar, seven miles off, that afternoon, and saw groups of grey monkeys swinging in a clump at the end of boughs or leaping lightly from tree to tree as we passed by. They were eating wild plums, which here grew in abundance, and it seemed a remark- ably easy and pleasant existence despite the melancholy expression of their faces. The sacred lake did not differ in much from others, except that ancient pavilions belong- ing to the Hindu rulers of India tottered round its banks; and that the fish, being scared, lost all fear of man, and rushed in such a whirlpool to catch the grain we threw them that they flapped each other out of the Water. A LITTLE PARADISE.

Another night journey, and we were crawling up a branch line to Udaipur next morning. Small wonder if this little paradise is but rarely visited. The branch line took five hours to do about forty miles; and on all sides stretched a stony plain covered with aloes and withered grass. But the low jagged rims of hills gradually rose and encircled the small but famous state whose boast it is that no Maharajah of Udaipur ever bowed before a Mohammedan Mogul. For this reason the Prince of Udaipur to this day wears two swords at his belt. We put up in a simple but clean dak bungalow a mile from the city, and were bumped there in a a tonga that afternoon to see the, palace. It is really three palaces, all painted white, and standing_high on the bank of the lake which is Udaipur's chief glory. Islands stud this lake anti on two of them are small marble palaces, one of which sheltered Shah Jehan when he was a wanderer on the face f India. We entered the palace yard through a towering gatehouse, and beheld elephants chained up on either side, whilst flocks of pigeons (as usual) were whirring and peck- ing over grain scattered in the centre, One elephant had lain down on its side to permit the mahout to rub its forehead with pumice stone. The stone was as large as a round loaf and the man laid on with both hands,but the elephant never moved an eyelid. , His forehead had been daubed with paint which was now being removed. Splendid dogs, and the usual tigers were here, and we saw one or two important looking royal relatives, • including a small prince dressed in pale pink. The Maharajah sent to request us to visit his mother's palace first as he was using his own rooms. When we visited these later it was to find them filled with the ugliest and most massive kind of mid-Victorian furni- ture. We crossed a marble court, round which the rooms were built; and when I put

up my sunshade I was respectfully requested to put it down 'as the Maharajah was present.' We went for a row to the islands afterwards and I shall never forget the fierce yellow afterglow over lake and islands when the sun had sunk behind the jagged purple hills. It reminded one of Pallanza or Lake Maggiore.

THE SLAVE-GARDEN AND BUDMASH BHILS. Next morning we drove out in our tonga to the slave-garden, uninhabited now but filled with thousands of flower pots, in which blossomed roses, mignonette, stocks, and Indian flowers. The sight and smell of them was doubly welcome, because flowers are so rarely seen in India. We drove on to an upper lake; and here my cousin elected to climb asteep little hill for the sake of the shrine which crowned it. I went for a walk up a shallow defile instead and passed three wild- looking country folk with whom I exchanged salaams. Suddenly I heard steps running, and turned to find Din Mahommet, our driver, much excited because of the country- men. • " They budmash (bad people) Bhils ; draw arrow—so--take silver chain—so and excellent aoting accompanied each remark. Din would have been perfect in pantomime; he was much tickled by the quandary he had been placed in because Miss Moreland was up a hill, I in a valley, and his tonga and horses in a third place

div.head: CHITOR THE GLORIOUS.
div.p: CHITOR THE GLORIOUS.

We left Udaipur by the afternoon train, and regained Chitor junction before sunset. This famous fortress has the finest and most tragic history in India, but it would take too long to narrate. We lost no time in hiring a tonga and driving up the long inclined road which winds up the steep face of the great rock plateau on which the city stood. It is two miles around the top and must have been well-nigh impregnable. Most of the houses are gone, and the temples damaged, but
INDIAN SERVANT.

splendid beyond words rises the great tower of Victory, nine stories high, and covered with beautiful Hindu sculpture on every available spot. It was erected in 1450, but is recent compared with another tower of Victory, only a third its size, but dating from the Bth century ! We climbed both of them despite the wind, and the carving inside was as fine as that without. Then we hurriedly drove down the long road and away to our dak bungalow, for darkness was coming on. 'ln the twilight, the ruined Chitor stood out starkly'above the outline of the hill, and its solitude seemed to befit the brave dead who had guarded it.
"SAM," THE INDEFATIGABLE

div.head: BOMBAY.
div.p: BOMBAY.

We were up by candlelight at four! Night journeys had quite lost the charm of novelty by now, and we had a long and grilling day in the train. The main thing I remember was that we stopped at a station called Nemutch for breakfast; that each egg we opened was bad, and the coffee an atrocity, •and that we thought the name of the place singularly suited its restaurant ! The night was stifling, for it was now the 9th of March. We had the windows open, and all night the dust blew in on my hair, till in the morning it was nothing but a mat! About six o'clock we awoke to glimmering swamps and rounded hills, and the flat, muggy air of Bombay. This queen of cities is handsome, as it forms a sweeping curve round the bay to wooded Malabar Hill ; and the lights of the shipping as seen from the Yacht Club lawn at night, are fairylike. But the languid heat overcame us after the dry air, however hot, of the high inland plains. We visited the famous caves of Elephanta, and wondered what mysterious race carved out those gigantic and awe-inspiring faces from the solid rock. They are beautiful, but wild in expression. The great pillars of the rampant lions guarding a flight of steps make it an unforgettable shrine. Then we packed a last time,,said good-bye to the faithful Sam, and our kind friends in Bombay, and on a Saturday morning boarded the P. and 0. Persia, bound for Port Said, and from thence for Syria and Palestine.
(To be Continued).

div.head: USE OF STIMULANTS.
div.p: USE OF STIMULANTS.

'A stimulant can do no more than draw on the reserves; it borrows for one hour what must be paid back the next hour. No horse owner will believe that whips and spurs can be substituted for oats and hay! And so it is with men and women; no amount of stimulants can take the place of good food, well digested. When appetite and digestion break down and you feel weak. nervous, prostrated—perhaps after an attack of influenza, as was the case with Mrs. Emma Dimmock—you need Mother Seigel's Syrup, the remedy that cured her. It does not spur you up and let you down afterwards, but it restores the lost poWer to your stomach, liver and kidneys, so that you can digest your food, and get from it the substantial nourishment that Nature intended you to have. Mrs. Dimmock lives at Leavesden Green, Watford, Herts. Not long ago she wrote us :—" In 1902, after a serious operation, and before I had.regained my health, I was struck down by a violent attack of Influenza. The result of that was utter loss of appetite, great weakness, nervousness and Indigestion. In a little while I lost three stone in weight. After four months illness and treatment I tried Mother Seigel's Syrup, and by the time I had taken eight bottles of that medicine, I was as well as ever I had been in my life. And now, more than six years after, my health continues as sound as I could wish it to be." _

There are the plain facts. Mrs. Dimmock needed strength, and she found it,_tecause Mother Seigel's Syrup enabled her to digest-her food. Then that food nourished her in the true natural way. div.head: OPEN-MR POLITICS.
div.p: OPEN-MR POLITICS.
MR J. HOWES REPLIES TO THE TORIES.
The Question of Food Taxation.

Another largely-attended and enthusiastic meeting promoted by the Warrington Progressive Labour Lc ague was held at Bridge Foot (near Arpley Cannons), on Monday evening. Mr.J. Elwell presided and was accom- panied on the platform by the Rev. C. Harvey Cook, Councillor Skelland, Messrs.J. Howes, E. Wynne Jones, S. Wright; J. Morton and J. Howes, jun. (hon. secretaries). _ _

The CHAIRMAN said they bad reason to congratulate themselves on the great victory that was won in the High Peak division of Derbyshire. (Applause). Not- withstanding all the efforts of the privileged and retrogressive forces—oven the Duke of Norfolk and his "dear Profumo"—(laughter)—the Liberals bad Main- tained their position. (Applause.) It was amazing what energy and vitality these men exhibited when the Government began to talk about putting taxes on the things which appertained most closely to them. They could tax the necessities of life, in fact they could tax anything so long as they did not tax what belonged to the wealthy and the landed aristrocracy of this country. The speaker contended that it was only right that the men who possessed great wealth and bad the ability to pay should contribute in proportion to their means. They talked about Dreadnoughts but when it, came to meeting the bill they wanted the wsiskingnien to pay for them. Continuing, Mr, Elwell urged his hearers to stick to Free Trade which had placed us in a position of pre-eminence in the industries of the world. Under 50 years of Protection our trade increased by '22 millions.. but under 50 years of Free Trade it had increased by 190 miliions. What Free Trade had done for the industries they wanted to extend to the land, so that the people could live on the land and benefit, instead of flocking into the towns and overcrowding various industries. They wanted those who bad been forced off the land by the big landlords to come back and help to produce the necessities of life. Protectionists. talked about wealth leaving the country. In the past ten years we had imported 480 millions of gold and silver and expertise.: only 432 millions. Therefore,arguing on the lines of Protectionists, it must be assumed that we had made a profit of 48 millions. One of the speakers at the tariff reform meeting last week said that 363 million pounds worth of goods came into this country, and only 180 millions went cut. He (Mr. Elwell) considered that a very good exchange. Ile would like to get Is. for every 6d. he expended, but not only did we get that, but according to the tariff reformer's way of reckoning, we had also an increase in the amount at the bank as the imports of gold arid silver considerably exceeded the exports. (Applause). Mr. J. llowss, who had a hearty welcome, began his speech with a bria allusion to the Liberal triumph in the High Peak division. There they met their opponents in big force, but the progressive cause 'obtained the victory. (Applause). Ile understood that the meeting held At Warrington last week in support of the Budget was the largest open-air meeting ever held in „Warrtngton, and there was a clear indication that the men ot Warrington were as firm with reference to the Budget proposals as the people in the other parts of the country. (Applause). The Tories bad a meeting which he hoped satisfied them, to celebrate the birthday of Air. Chamberlain. At the present time he (Mr. Howes) felt, very uneasy about saying anything personally about Mr. Chamberlain. Chamberlain was a great fighter when he fought for them and ho said some very strong things against the Tory party. Whin he left the Liberals he said equally strong things about them. -Unfortunately he was now prostrate and for the time being could fight no more. Therefore they had no desire to attack him; they would rather see him in the arena again. (Applause). At the Tory meeting they had a

REAL LIVE LORD. It was not very often they got that treat in the open (Laughter). Somehow, after all, lords were hot- house plants and they were not like the hardy Radical of whom it was said :—" He loves the air and sky ; left out he thrives, and taken in he dies." (Laughter). This noble lord was dealing with the present conditions' of what he called "free imports "and he said "The man who :et up a factory abroad bad the foreign market secured to him and the English market open to him, while the man who set up a factory in England had tho foreign market closed to him and he had- to • fight for -his own existence, even at home." It was wonderful how We did it ! (Laughter). But the idea of trying to persuade sensible people at this time that a statement like that Will a fact! Ho wished the noble lord would point to a single foreign market in the world that was closed to us. Every year we sent our goods into every market in the world. Ns matter how strong their tariff walls, the elasticity of our Free Trade system allowel us to blow holes through their tariffs, awl despite their attempt at prohibition, British goods entered and British ships hovered round their coasts. Last year Germany took £41,000,000 worth of our goods; United States, £0,000,000; France, £23.000,000; Argentine Republic, £17,000,000; Italy, £11,000,000; Belgium, £12,000,000; :Japan, £12,000,000; China, £12,000,000; Russia, £11,000,000. That was the way they kept our goods out of the market. (Laughter). Ho would like to ask the noble lord if he could point out another country that did a similar trade with the rest of the world. We simply

BEAT ALL THE WORLD. (Applause). Why did those noble lords tell these fairy tales? The hereditary peer did not know much of the world in which be lived. They might send a man to college aad teach him all the languages living and dead, and those which never ought to have lived— (laughter)—he might come out and do the Grand Tour, and then be totally ignorant of the conditions of the people of this country. It was a dangerous thing for a noble lord who was not up in politics, to come and address a large open-air meeting in a town like this, because he could so soon be found out. (Laughter.) _Germany bought as many goods from us in a year as Canada and Australia put together. We allowed Canada and Australia to send us what they liked, when and how they lilted, and the cheaper they sent goods the better we liked them. They put tariffs on our goods and would not allow their 'people to buy them cheap. But the people did buy our goods, and they bought them dear, because their own Government put taxes on. If foreign Governments imposed taxes to make their people buy goods dear, was that any reason why our Government should do the same? The noble lord also said: "A few months ago- when the mother country, was in need of ships, the people of the Colonies came forward and offered three Dread- noughts. We knew perfectly well that one nation was building Dreadnoughts in rivalry to our fleet, and the question for us to settle was whether we wry() going to trade with the people who built Dreadnoughts against us or those who built Dread- noughts for us.' His (Mr. Howes') reply was that we were going to do trade with both. So long as they wanted anything that we had got to sell we should sell it, because uhore the customers were, there should the goods be also. Lord Weimer said "Their opponents sometimes said that if we were to give the Colonies a preference it would be necessary to tax the food of the people." Lord Wolmer was evidently a little bit vexed at the placard which they put out, giving Mr. Chamberlain's message. There was an old saying that "The truth shall make you floe" but when they applied it to the Tories they should ray" The truth will make you vexed." (Laughter). His lordship attributed the statement to " their opponents." They did not want to claim credit for utterances which were not their's. They gave Mr. Chamberlain the credit for the state- ment in question and when the noble lord said it was absolutely untrue ho was flying in the face of his leader. His lordship said "That statement was abso- lutely untrue. Free Traders had taken a certain state- ment of Mr. Chamberlain's about putting a TAX ON THE PEOPLE'S FOOD; they had isolated it from the rest of his speeches and made a perfectly misleading and unjust use of it." Of course, they must necessarily isolate the quotation from the speeches, but they did not do it any injustice. They gave the entire quotation and did not wrest it from its context. Mr. Chamberlain during the debate on the question in the House of Commons said," I will give my-opponents the benefit of this: if you give a prefer- ence to the Colonies you must tax the people's food." That statement was entire and complete and moreover it was perfectly true. The Colonies sent us a lot of our foodstuffs and it was said by tariff reformers that we ought to induce them to send more. We gave them open ports and let them send what they liked. What could an do more? But there were other countries who sent us sometimes some foodstuffs cheaper than the Colonies could send them and we had got sufficient sense to take them from the man who served us best. The only way to help the colonies was to tax the food that came from other countries—and that was what the Tories wanted— in order to let in food from the Colonies in greater abundance. If we were silly enough to do that, the Colonies could send us what they liked at a higher price than they sent it now. No-one could pay it but the consumer. Now we got our goods at the bottom price always. Even at the last failure of the harvest, and when a Yankee was trying to corner wheat, although the price of bread went up, we were at the bottom price. When bread was dear we got it cheaper than any other country in the world, and when it was cheap we got it still cheaper, so that Free Trade always benefited us. His lordship further stated: " Under our system of Free Trade, the food of the people was taxed to the time of 13 millions." There was a great history concerning that 13 millions, and he wondered if this noble lord knew it, and if he did, whether he thought his audience knew it One of two things must have happened, either the noble lard had a low opinion of his audience and imagined that they did not know the history of it, or else he did not know it himself. He (Mr. Howes) proposed to take the latte: explanation, as he did not suppose the noble lord wilfully tried to deceive. Lord Weimer said that although this was a Free Trade country the food of the people was taxed to the tune of 13 millions. Every penny of that taxation which was now on their shoulders was PUT ON BY TIIE TORY PARTY; they must never forget that. Not a penny of it was put on by the Liberals, and although they had to-day 13 millions of taxes on these articles, a few years ago it ma 30, 40 aud 0 mUliona.But the

Liberal patty had swept away a lot of thopi_ and in doing so had benefited the Tories as well as DT Liberals. (Applause.) If they got this Budget throug: they would probably be able to take more taxes ("" (Applause.) Lord Wolmer said : " Tariff reformer: promised that for every penny they put on wheat .0 meatimported from foreign countries, they were goiti to take an equal amount off tea,coffee,sugar and cocoa. He HotAes) wished they would tell us how n3811_,51 pennies they proposed to put en. Such a scheme ro Lord Wolmer promised was a juggle. div.head: DISTRICT
div.p: DISTRICT
PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

There is no lack of light entertainment at the Hippodrome this week, the programme being such as to make the two hours pass pleasantly and rapidly. Alburtus and Millar are entitled to hearty praise for an amusing turn entitled "A scene-at the fair ground." A cocoa-nut " shy" is erected on the stage and though there is only one customer he proves such an adept at throwing that he clears the row of dolls at lightning speed. The same individual and the girl in charge indulge in a club-juggling duet which brings down the house, and the lady also displays enviable powers as a cornetist. Little Lily Shaw stands only about a yard high, but she is a wonder and well deserves the title of "'rho Pocket Vesta Tilley." Dressed immaculately as a dude she sings popular songs in a clear voicie with quite the Vesta Tinley air. Perrier's ventriloquial turn is the most novel of its kind yet seen. One is in the middle of marvelling how Perrier manages to use four voices with such effect when there is a startling denouement. The dolls are quite out of the ordinary, and must be seen to be appreciated. A comedian capable of causing roars of laughter is Ted Low-en ; even his little vulgarities pass muster by the grace of undtniable humour. Minnie Warner, the rubber girl, dances and contorts herself in wonderful fashion, and Stevens and Brett shine in their burlesque duo. The Sisters Desmond are amusing as character duettists, While the Palace Pictures claim the attention of every eye. Each week they seem, -if possible, to be better. A extra turn, which was one of the most popular of the evening, was introduced by Cummin and Seaham.

WOOLTON v. WARRINGTON

The Liverpool League match was decided at Woolton on Tuesday evening. The home team defended the deep end in the first half, but wore superior to the Wirepullers. Fred Jackson, though playing in the full back position, twice beat Woods with terrific shots, which scored at the corner of the goal, and R. Lott and J. Martin scored for Woolton ; while Beaman and Turner registered two goals for Warrington. This was the score at the interval. On resuming, uninteresting play was seen for some time. Then Woolton settled down to business, and goals were added by J. Martin (2), Jackson and Lott. lace oLtained Warrington's third goal just on time. Result :—Woolton, 8 goals; War ri og ton 3.

div.head: Education in Agriculture.
div.p: Education in Agriculture.

The Lancashire County Council offers free educa- tion to farmers' sons and daughters and others engaged or likely to be engaged in agricultural pursuits who are residents or ratepayers of the Administrative County of Lancaster, and in addition makes an allowance in aid of board and lodgings in Preston, or for travelling xpense% thereto. The classes are held at the Harris Institute, Preston, and the session lasts from about the last week in September to the middle of April in each year Education, with board and lodging, is given in. butter-making, cheesemaking, milk sterilization, breadmaking, and poultry keeping, free of cost, to students attending the Dairy School, at the County Council Farm, Hutton near Preston. Instruction in butter-making and Hutton, is• givem where required in the county Tree of cost. Lectures and advice are given on agriculture, horticulture, poultry keeping, veterinary hygiene, and beekeep- ing. Valuable scholarships and exhibitions are ()tiered annually.

HILL CLIFFE AND S TOCKTON HEATH UNITED BAND OF HOPE.-1 he annual trip in connection with the above took place on Thursday, when upwards ,of 120 members and friends visited New Brighton. The party accompanied by the Rev. J. S. Hughes (vice-president), and Mrs. Hughes and several members of the committee left the Wesleyan Chapel in special buses at 8.15 for the Central station where they were joined by the mem- bers and friends of the Bold-street Wesleyan Band of Hope, who spent the day with them. They journeyed to Liverpool by the 8.50 a.m. train, special carriages being ptovided. On arriving at the wtport the party proceeded at once to the landing stage where they embarked on the ferry boat to New Brighton. the passage down the river being much enjoyed. Upon arriving at their destination the members were 4-Lken to the Caf6 Royal where lunch had been provided. Afterwards the youngsters at once began to avail them- selves of the usual seaside pleasures of wading. sand digging, etc. Others visited the Tower grounds where the many attractions provided amusement for all. The lift ta the top of the tower, flying machine and scenic railway received a full share of patronage. The new promenade was greatly admired. From here a good view of the attempted "invasion" of the Mersey was 'obtained, rrany of the visitors watching the cruiser and two destroyers proceeding up the river to be repulsed by the watchful artillery who were repeatedly firing off the cannons on the New Brighton battery. At four o'clock the party re-assembled at the Caf6 Royal wbere a substantial tea was served to which full justice was done, the catering arrangements of Mrs. Bmith being admirable. After tea the weather (which up to now had been all that could be desired) suddenly changed and rain began to fall. At seven o'clock a start was made for home, the day having been too short for some of the youngsters who were reluctant to return. Stockton Heath was reached a little after nine, all expressing themselves highly delighted with the day's proceedings. The arrangements for the comfort of the party reflecting great credit upon the Committee and the energetic Secretary, Mr. G. Whitfield.

_ SCHEME TO COPE WITH OVERFLOW. . _ A SEWERAGE QUESTION. The Clerk read the report of Mr. Diggle with refer- ence to the overflowing of water which ought to go into the sewers. The report contained the following: After having spent a considerable amount of time in ascertaining the facts in connection with the Syphon and obtaining particulars in reference thereto from the engineer of the Manchester Ship Canal at Warrington, I now find myself able to report definitely upon the matter. As no doubt your committee is already aware a very large quantity of surface water finds its way to the syphon which no doubt is the primary cause of the flood in time of very heavy rainfall, having regard to the fact that there exists no screening arrangements in front of the syphon. It is in my opinion highly probable that the capacity of the syphon has become diminished by means of debris which has been passing into it. In all syphonic arrangements of this kind I invariably attach a screening arrangement at the entrance to prevent the accumulation of debris upcn the invert of the syphon. The first thing to be done is the cleaning out of the syphon, and I should be glad to have your instructions to put this in hand. Upon receiving your instructions I will apply to the Manchester Ship Canal Company for their consent and assistance in the matter. Under any circumstances there ought to be a screening arrangement at the entrance to the syphon, and having regard to the fact that there are no less than four number 12in. pipes or sewers discharging into the entrance to the syphon, there ought to be provided an additional storm outflow to discharge into the Ship Canal to relieve the Syphon in times of very heavy rainfall. I have upon two occasions interviewed the engineer of the Manchester Ship Canal upon thie matter, and upon the first occasion he resolutely declined to allow any storm overflow to discharge into the Ship Canal on account of the dredging which he considered would become necessary to keep the Canal free from accumulation of debris at that point After a subsequent interview with the Engineer's assistant (.11r.Congreve) I came to the conclusion that the Manchester Ship Canal Co., would be willing to accept such an arrangement pro- vided that ample means were made for intercepting debris by a screening arrangement at the entrance to the syphon. My estimate of the total cost including the reconstruction of the existing manhole with screen and storm overflow arrangements and the necessary 18in. iron pipes between the storm and overflow manhole of the Ship Canal is approximately £l7O. This does not include the cleaning out of the syphon. It is of course probipmatical, but cannot be large. Mr. H. .1. Westbrook: Oughtn't something of the cost to fall on Lower Walton?

Mr. J. Hallows: What about Appleton? The cost is too heavy for Stockton Heath to take on. • The Cbairman : Our own surveyor has got a scheme of his own, which will cost nothing. Mr. Brown wanted to know whether the Ship Canal Company could object to any scheme they had of putting the sewage into the canal. The Clerk said the Ship Canal were willing to provide for the sewage. On the proposition of the Chairman, it was decided that a special meeting Of the Council be called when the Clerk returned from his holidays, and that the scheme of their own surveyor be presented to them.
GAS LAMPS.

Mr. Whitley moved- that the minute respecting the number plates on the gas lamps be rescinded, as the initials were rather objectionable. ?.'jr. Bcuchier seconded and this was agreed to. In the place of that resolution, Mr. Whitley moved that numbers only be put on. Mr. Hallows seconded and it was carried.

_ Mr. H. J. Westbrook said that the gas lami.s in White- field-road were not lighted on Saturday night at 10.35 and on t•unday at 10.30. Mr. Whitley: lhere is a llot of truth in that. Continuing he said that the lamplighte had got too much to do. He started in Warrington,went to Walton and then he MT() to Stockton Heath. Mr. J. H. Clarke said they were not getting ,the full amount of the gas they were entitled to. He moved that an intimation be sent to the Warrington Corpora- tion that the lamps were not lit on these dates at the time stated,and they expected sore reduction in their charges. div.head: NO HOUSES TO LET.
div.p: NO HOUSES TO LET.

After Mr. J. H. Clarke had submitted the report of the Building Committee Mr. Hallows said that there were 6 young couples going to get married and they could not find a house to lbt in Stockton Heath.
FIRE ENGINE.

The Clerk read the minutes of the Fire Engine Com- mittee which proposed that the words "Fire &Minn " be painted on the side of the sheds, and also that a board be affixed to the fire station with a notice "In case of fire ring bell, which hangs at the corner of the Police Station." It was decided that where the water mains were of less diameter than Gin. and the other mains in the same street were on the high pressure, hydrants shall be transferred to the high pressure mains, and that it be ascertained how many hydrants will want transferring and what the approximate cost would be. The tender of Mr. Worrall for fixing 12 enamel plates to the fireman's residences, after the permission of the landlords, was accepted.

div.head: SPEED OF MOTORS.
div.p: SPEED OF MOTORS.

Mr. Whitley gave notice that he would move a resolu- tion at the next meeting of the Committee which would deal with the excessive speed of motors. Ho observed that the speed the motors went along Walton- roed was outrageous. It was a wonder that there had not been some serious accident.

div.head: SWING BRIDGE.
div.p: THE SWING BRIDGE.

Mr. Browne mentioned that they got no waver to the qtiestion of removing the water off the Swing Bridge. The Chairman said the Warrington Corporation were taking the matter up. He had seen an account of it in the paper. Mr. Browne moved that they make enquiries of the Corporation and write to the County Council asking them to assist them in the matter. This was carried.

div.head: Lymm.
div.p: Lymm.
OLD BOYS' CRICKET MITCII.—The OM Boys cricket match in connection with Lymm Grammar School was player' on Saturthy afternoon with the following result :—Lyrura Grammar School 112, Old Boys 23.

GARDEN PARTY AT LYNIM.—A pretty garden partf and fête was held at Foxley House, Lymat, the residence of Mr. and Mrs. Champ, on Wednesday afternoon, in connection with the Primitive Methodist Centenary Fund. The function included afternoon tea (which waa given by Mrs.Champ)and served in the field adjoining the house. There was a good number of willing ladies and gentlemen helpers who did their best to see all had a good time. The whole of the gardens were thrown open, and there were a number of little side shows, including shooting gallery, palmistry, etc. There were about 150 people present, the weather being most favour- ablP, and the whole proceedings terminated very success- fully. LYMM URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL.

1e monthly meeting of the above Council was held on Thursday evening in the Council offices. Mr. 0. G. Smith presided and there present : Messrs. J. Davies, W. Ewart, R. H. Gotobei, F. Warburton, F. 0. Moston, G. L. Welford, %V. G. Groves, W. Nlullard (clerk), D. Donaldson (gas manager), D. Mort (surveyor), and Dr. De Junge (medical officer.)

div.head: TELEPHONE POSTS.
div.p: TELEPHONE POSTS.

The minutes of the Road Committee showed that a letter was read from the National Telephone Co., asking the Council to agree to certain poles being placed on the west side of the road between certain points, instead of all the poles being erected on the Basterly side. It was propesed by Mr. Mosten and seconded by Mr. Davies that it be a recommendation to the Council for the Clerk to write and inform the Cop-pany that the Council could not agree to any alteration of the position, but adhered to the resolution passed at a meeeting'held on the 24th June last. At the same committee meeting a letter was read from the Superintending Engineer of the Post Office Telegraph enclosing sketch of position of a pole and stake and asking the Council to give their consent to the fixing of stove. On the proposition of the Rev. G. B. Thurston, and seconded by Mr. Groves, it was recommended to the Council that the Clerk write and say the Council decline to sign the consent asked for.

STEPS AT BEtOOKFIELD BRIDGE. A letter was read from the Manchester Ship Canal Company as follows: "Proposed steps at Brookfield Bridge. In reply to yours of yesterday, herein I have to say that the request of your Council for provision of access from the highci ay to the tow-path at this point cannot possibly be entertained. The tendency Is to discourage such means of access in the interest of public safety, there having been so many drowning cases owing to such trespass." The minutes were passed unanimously. DEPUTATION REPORT.

Mr. Davies gave an able report upon the Urban District Council Conference at Ilkley. Mr. Davies was accompanied to Ilkley by Mr. Mullard (clerk). On the proposition of Mr. Groves and seconded by Mr. Welford, a vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Davies for his report. .

HEALTH REPORT. Dr. De Jonge submitted his medical report, which showed that during the quarter there were 14 deaths, an annual rate of 11•28'per thousand of the population, estimated at 4,950. During the quarter there were 28 births, 16 males and 12 females. This gave a rate of 22.56 per thousand of the estimated population. Eighteen cases of infectious diseases had been notified.

LYMM LANE CROSSINGS. Mr. Warburton stated that this crossing had been, in his opinion, left iu a dangerous state. He enquired if the Surveyor was satisfied with the present condition of the crossing. The Surveyor said the crossings were in a very unsatisfactory condition. On Wednesday be went and saw the crossing, and it had been temporarily made safe. Mr. Foot, the chief engineer, bad promised that the matter would be attended to on Tuesday next.

div.head: Moore.
div.p: Moore.

Smoot CHILDREN'S TREAT.—The annual treat to the scholars attending the day schools at Daresbury, Moore, Hatton, and Preston Brook took• place on Saturday afternoon, a visit being paid to Overton Hills, Frodsbara. The children were conveyed by train at two o'clock from Daresbury and Norton stations, and at 4.30 tea was supplied at Mersey-view. After tea Sports of various kinds for prizes were well contested, and a very pleasant evening was spent. Many rambled along the hillside, and at eight o'clock all proceeded to the station, arriving in high glee at Norton and Dares- bury a little before nine. The weather proved most favourable, making'the treat one long to be remem- bered with pleasure.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
ST. HELENS JEWELLER ROBBED.

At St. Helens, on Saturday, Elizabeth Aspinall, charwoman, was charged with stealing jewellery, Mr. J. C. Mason, of 41, Church-street, said that for about nine months Mrs. Aspinall bad acted as charwoman at the shop, and also at his residence, 79, Keswick-road. On May 28th, he received a consignment of Jewellery, which bad been repaired at Birmingham. Three or four days later some of the jewellery disappeared. A fortnight later a brooch ma missed, and information was given to the police. Mrs. Aspinall was suspected. Ultimately, Detective-sergeant Curran found one of the articles, which had been sold by the prisoner, and the woman was arrested. Mrs. Agnes Green spoke to buying a George IV. lion shilling pendent from her for 3s. 6d. When charged, the woman said she was guilty, but it was her first appearance, and she was very sorry. The Chief Constable said the woman had worked very hard for years to keep her family. Her husband was a drunken, lazy fellow. The home was clean, but ay.solutely devoid of furniture. There were five children. The bench decided to deal with the case summarily, and tined the prisoner V.!, or twenty-eight days.
SECTARIAN QUARRELS. SEQUEL TO ST. HELENS PROCESSION SCENES.

Four men who were arrested on Sunday evening during the brief row which took place in Higher Parr- street, when the Orange procession with two drum and fife bands was returning from Parr to Liverpool, were brow,ht before the magistrates on Monday.—James Lovalt, carter, of 42, Netherfield-road South was the first defendant charged with breach of peace. Constable Featherstone said that when he was escort- ing the pilkession along the street at ten minutes past six a disturbance broke out. He saw Lovatt dash into the crowd and a seault a man. Witness went to him, upon which a wan out of the procession came to them pulling a bayonet out of his trousers pocket. He was told to get on with the

procession, and Lovatt was locked uo.—Prisoner said he was carrying coats for the bandsmen and walking by the side of the road when he received a " belt " in the ear. He was struck several times by women and men.—Lovatt was ordered to find sureties or go to gaol for 28 days.—Michael Battle, of Langtree- street, pleaded guilty to causing a disturbance.— Constable Turrill said that Battle rushei into the pro- cession and assaulted the Orangemen, striking right and left. He arrested Battle, or there might not have been much left of him.—The Mayor: What did you do it for ?—The Chief Constable : It was simply because they were of different colours in religion. He - was a Catholic.—Battle was ordered to find sureties or 28 dAys.—James Craig, of 32, Langtree- street, was dealt with in a similar manner.— In the case of Michael Duffy. Pocketnook-street, Con- stable Bate said the three defendants were part of a gang that had been assembled in this street for some time. When Duffy was arrested he was followed by the crowd who shouted," Well done' Michael." Before the procession arrived at that point he heard Duffy and others saying what they would do.—The Mayor said they were determined to put down that snrt of thing. There was not much religion about people who followed others about to fight them. Duffy would have to find sureties for twelve months, or go to, gaol for two months.—Later Thomas Kelly and James O'Donnell were also charged with breach of the peace. Constable Merrill said that O'Donnell was the worse. He was seeking bother all afternoon. The Clerk : It we s a sort of continuing skirmish all the way along the road? Merin : Yes.—Both men are bound oven—James Lovatt, carter, was ordered to find sureties for two months or go to geol for twenty-eight days for breach of the peace. Michael Battle and James Craig were similarly dealt with.—Michael Duffy was ordered to find sureties for twelve months or go to gaol for two months.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
MANAGER'S SCUFFLE WITH WORKMAN.

At Runcorn, on Monday, John Henderson, manager of the Widnes and Runcorn Transporter Bridge Company, was summoned by James Shaw, a motor-driver, for assault. Shaw said he had been driver of the trans- porter car since it started four years ago. On the 19th inst., as be was leaving work, Mr. Hendersen told him he could not pay him 30s. a week to go greasing, and be must go and get his money. He refused, as be did not think Mr. Henderson had the power to dismiss him. He went into the toll-house, and defendant followed him and said he should not go out until he had received his money, blocked up the doorway, and when he tried to get under his arms Mr. Henderson clutched his throat with both hands and butted him on the face. His nose was severely injured. The defence was that when Mr. Henderahaw discharged Shaw the latter got into a frenzy of temper and put up his bands and made a rush at Mr. Henderson. Mr. Henderson caught Shaw by the coat and pulled him to him so that be could not get in a swinging blow. It was possible that the hard rim of Mr. Henderson's bat had caught Shaw's nose, but there was no butting.—Defendant was fined 10s. and costs (12s. 6d.) or fourteen days.
