div.head: N.S.L. OPEN-AIR MEETING.
div.p: N.S.L. OPEN-AIR MEETING.
Captain Crosfield and Foreign Investments.

The Warrington workers of the National Service League are emulating the example of the various schools of politicians in appealing to the public by means of open air meetings. The first gathering of the kind was held at Bridge Foot(near Arpley Cannons)on Wednesday evening. When the proceedings opened there was a very meagre attendance, but this was augmented as the evening wore on, until it reached between 100 and 200. Mr. J. H. Smethurst presided and was supported on the platform by Captain G. R. Crosfield, Councillor Broad- hurst, Mr.J. Elwell, Mr. B. S. Townroe, and Mr.J. IT. J. Hampson. The Chairman having briefly commented upon the non-party character of the movement, Mr. J. Eewm.i. delivered an address in which he stated that the utterly defenceless condition of England during the South African war caused him seriously to consider the question of national defence and to join the League. It was generally admitted that the defences of this country were in anything but a satis- factory condition, and in proof of that they had the findings of the Royal Commission which sat a few sears ago. Also they had the efforts of Mr. Brodrick,Mr.Arnold Foster and lastly of Mr. Haldane, who in introducing his Territorial Army scberGe said that its success was the only solution which stood between this country and conscription. From the ethical point of view there, was all the difference in the world between preparation for military aggression and preparation for military defence. It was defence which the National Service League aimed at. The proposals of the League need not and would not, in his opinion, create a love of war for war's sake. There was nothing so antagonistic to a spirit of jingoism as the feeling that those who created a 'Tar would be the first to take part in it. A professional army and a more or less illiterate electorate were far more likely to create war and to cause us to drift into war than a nation in arms, where every man might be called upon to serve the morrent hostilities commenced. If we e ere thoroughly prepared for warno power would attempt to invade our shores or to take advantage of the If we had the privileges and benefits of citizenship we ought also to be prepared to take our share of the res- ponsibilities and duties. (Applause.) Councillor BROADHURST contended that the opinions of experts went to show that England was in danger and he particularly warned his audience against the possibility of German aggression. Dealing with the state of our defences at the time of the South African war, he said that if we had been fighting an enterprising army, the British Empire would have been in a most I perilous condition. Speaking after nineteen years service in the Volunteers, he testified to the value of military training from the physical, mental and moral standpoints. Questions were invite, and Mr. D. Purcell, an ex-soldier who has served in India, asked it it was proposed that the young men who CAMe forward to serve their country should have the benefit of the franchise?

Captain CROSFIELD said the National Service League and its President (Lord Roberts) had not laid down anything in connection with that question. Speaking for himself, and he believed for the great bulk of the members of the National Service League, they would to entirely in favour of giving the vote to all those young men who came forward to train themselves so as to defend their country. They believed it to be a true, just and sound policy to have the rifle in one hand and the vote in the other. He promised to raise the question at the next meeting of the Council of the League. A vote of thanks to the speakers and Chairman was proposed by Mr. J. H. J. HAMPSON who considered that national training would conduce to habits of order and cleanliness and to a more 'wilted nation. _

Captain CROSFIELD, in seconding, said he wished to impress upon the meeting that the question concerned the workingmen just ;as much as the rich men, and perhaps more, and that it was affecting them at the present time, although perhaps they did not realize it. Niore than one of his friends who were convinced of the dangers which lay ahead of this country were invest- ing their money abroad'. Speaking generally they knew, whatever their politics might be, that the mo re capital they had in this country and the better it was. Why, even the Socialist did not want capital to go out of this country ; he wanted it to remain here. so that he could collar hold of it. (Laughter). It was in their interests to see that capital was invested in this country. The more capital they had, the more trade went ahead, and the more wages would go up. The qnes- tion of whether capital was invested here or not largely depended on the security of the country. If the capitalists thought that people were getting so slack and careless about national defence, that, as some- body said the other day, they were sunk in "pot- bellied equanimity "—they would say, r We shall be attacked in the 3 ears to come" because we were not properly prepared and trusted entirely to the Navy, and therefore they would invest their money abroad. What we wanted was a sound second line of defence which should be as the backs and goal-keeper behind the forward line—the Navy. The League said we could not do it by such a military makeshift as Mr. Haldane had devised—a makeshift by which he said we would only give rerious training for war when the danger bad come. Was that good enough? They would never get three or four months' training given to each man at

the age of eighteen or nineteen, unless they made it the law of the land and each man did his share. That was the only fair and just way. (Applause). • Mr. TOWNROE sopported and the vote was agreed to.

div.p: EAS S

BRITAIN'S WORKERS

Ventilation in the School and Home. Sir,--I was pleased to see your notes on the Medical Officer's report to the Education- Authority and especially the emphasis put upon the inadequate ventilation-in our schools. There are a few things which conduce so much to the health of children as well as older folks as a plentiful supply of fresh air, and there is no tonic which can be procured at so low a cost. Like all the best blessings of life it is -1' without money and without price," all that has to be done isto do away with the obstacles that shut it out. But -our own observation, which is confirmed by the Medical Officer's Report, shows very clearly that our townsmen, as a whOle, have not assimilated this fact. We do not act upon it in our homes, our schools, or places of public meeting. Our teachers only half believe in it, and our education authority cannot be aliie to it, or they would not have so long tolerated our badly ventilated schools. The Education Com- mittee are actively engaged in seeking to improve the physique of the children, but at the same time the condition of the schools in the matter of ventilation tends to neutralize their efforts. What is required is a spread of knowledge of the importance of fresh air amongst the inhabitants generally. What was said of 1 the school is true also, and perhaps to a more dangerous degree, of the home. Many of the children sleep in rooms from which the fresh air is systematically excluded. Let- anyone walk through the town during the sleeping hours and count the number of bedroom windows that are open, he will scarcely find one in a hundred. The idea is altogether too prevalent that open windows are liable to introduce colds and other complaints, whereas it is nearer the truth to say that open windows would prevent colds and lessen the liability of disease. This I have confirmed by the experience of my own family. People harbour all conditions which render themselves liable to consumption and its developments, and then, after it has got a firm hold, send the patient to a sanatorium in which the prime condition of cure is-an abundance of fresh air through open windows and ventilators, night and day, Surely if this is to gheck and erradicate this terrible disease it would be more sensible to employ the same method to prevent its inception. Various popular and erroneous notions are current on this subject. .For example it is believed .by many that the night air is laden with carbonic acid gas and ought therefore to be kept out as much as possible. The fact is, in a bed- room in which only one person is sleeping and from which free air is excluded will contain from the various exhalations of the body ten times as much carbonic acid gas as the ordinary outer air. I can confirm what has been the experience of those who sleep with open windows, (preferably the top sash) that they sleep better, wake fresher, are less subject to colds, and are more immune from other diseases. Draughts can be obviated by some simple screen, put those who are accustomed to fresh air do not Suffer from draughts, and find such a precaution, which may be desirable at first, unnecessa6. The bedding ought to be warm and not too heavy, blankets are much preferable to the heavy counterpanes so often used. Children, and indeed' all, should be taught to breathe through their noses and sleep with their mouths shut. A PARENT .

div.head: Budget and the Distribution of
div.p: The Budget and the Distribution of
Wealth.

Sir,—The Budget seems to be a" star" turn in the theatre of national politics, and at present the words budget and politics are synonymous terms. At Bridge Foot last week an enormous crowd assembled to listen to the Member for the borough, Mr. Harvey, M.P., and others deal with its details and incidentally the public were asked to support" a splendid budget. Being conscious that I am a worker taking a lively interest in and looking to politics for righting the social evils from which the workers suffer, and after listen- ing to and also reading the speeches in the "Examiner,"l come to the conclusion that the Budget is a good and bad one—good in comparison towards -what we have had, and bad in comparison towards what we ought to have. The policy of the drafters of past Budgets seems to have been to put as much taxation upon the workers as they would stand, Liberal and Tory alike. The monstrous injustice to levy any taxation at all upon the workers is a violation of any laws of equity yet conceived, especially when we consider that, according to Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman, we have 13 millions of our people living on and below the verge of starvation. Apart from any reason for justice it is an economically unsound policy, because we know that the best paid workingman does not receive a wage which we may call an elegant sufficiency. To reduce the worker's wage or purchasing power of his wage by taxation or any other method is to reduce his standard of living. To reduce his standard of living is equivalent to reducing the physical condition of the people, and physically unsound people are poor producers of wealth. But-circumstance demands a revised source of taxation, and the Government is compelled to levy more taxa- tion upon the rich than hitherto. The label- ling of the Budget as vindictive strikes one as being miserably insincere small talk. For we find that according to Mr. Chiozza Money, M.P., out of a population of 43 millions and an aggregate annual (1906) wealth production of £1,710 millions, 5 million people take £B3O millions and 38 million people take £BBO millions. A further division finds that 11 million persons take £585 millions, 31 milli,on persons take £245 millions and 28 million persons take £BBO millions. I also find that in 1906-7, 21,000 persons left at death £2BO millions out of £290 millions, and. that 4,172 left £2lB millions out of £290 millions. lfy contention is that whilst we have such an unjust distribution of wealth the poorest ought not to pay a farthing in taxation. The extra taxation upon tobacco is unjust, the taxation upon tea, sugar etc. is anpma bus, and-instead of putting further taxation /upon tobacco a progressive Government ought to be taking tolls off tea and all commodities used by the poorer class. However much I try I cannot join in with the enthusiasm displayed for this Budget. To say we are going to tax the rich £6,000,000 may seem great to accepted ordinary politics, but to the new idea wanting to see something done this only shows how little he may expect from orthodoxy. Why, this sum could be obtained from the surplus wealth left by 13 men who died in the Budget year 1906-7 and then it would be possible to make 15 men millionaires with what was left. The Budget, like the Liberal and Tory political :ideals, is paltry. Listening to Mr. Crosfield convinced me more than ever of the nebulosity, and the utter failure of the, Liberal mind to grasp any idea of the needs of the times. His reply to the question about his vote upon unemployment was halting and evasive. What use is it to me reducing unemployment to a minimum. Competition for employment reduces my standard of living. Competition for employment is the whip used to force me to accept totally insufficient wages, which at once cuts me off from any possibility of enjoying those things which go to make life human. The problem of unemployment to me is one of abolishing it. I believe a reduction in hours of labour all round and an increase in the purchasing power of tha.workers would solve the unemployed problem. But Mr. Crosfield being a" bit of capitalist" perhaps does not favour these things, for unlike cheaper land it would not raise dividends. So the Government's juggling with the unemployed question and Mr. Crosfield's lackadaisical attitude upon it do not make me very hopeful. Like past Governments the workers will get as much as and no more than they can squeeze out of them

div.head: SUDDEN DEATH OF COUNCILLOR
div.p: SUDDEN DEATH OF COUNCILLOR
W. B ROBERTS.

A. painful surprise was created in Warrington on Monday moening when it became known that C oun- calor W. B. Roberts had passed away with tragic ' suddenness the previous evening. It is but a month since Councillor Roberts retired from the position of head brewer to Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co., Ltd., and left Stockton Heath to take up his residence at Bleak House, Lymm. On Sunday afternoon he was visited by Mr. C. G. Stone, who has succeeded him as head brewer at Wilderspool, Mrs. Stone and Dr. Adams (an old friend and the family doctor) and was then in his usual cheerful spirits. At about seven o'clock he-...„ left home in a motor car, accompanied by Dr. Adams and Mr. and Mrs. Stone, with the intention of spending the evening with the two latter at their residence, Brook House, Wilderspool Causeway. It was noticed that he got into the car with some difficulty, as he was suffering from asthma, but once the journey had begun he chatted and joked with his friends, and although at his request the pace was slackened, there was nothing to give rise to alarm until the party were nearing Stockton Heath swing bridge. Mr. Roberts then told the driver to increase the speed and to get to Brook House as soon as possible, and it was seen that he was seriously ill. He was assisted into the house, placed on a chair and examined by Dr. Adams, but he was beyond, medical aid, and death took place from heart failure at six minutes to eight o'clock. Mr. William Brittain Roberts, F.C.S., was the son of the late Mr. J. W. Roberts, of Ravenscroft Park, Barnet, and was born in the year 1859. On leaving school, he went to Messrs. Watney, of London, to learn the brewing business, and he also studied chemistry under the late Professor Southby, -of the same city, with the object of thoroughly qualifying him for his work. He was afterwards with Messrs. Mitchell, of Birmingham (now Mitchell and Butler). and Messrs. Robert Bent and Co., of Liverpool. Twenty-three years ago he entered the service of Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co., Ltd. and fulfilled the duties of head brewer in a way which earned the confidence and regard of the firm as well as the esteem of the employees. On his retirement on July Ist of the present year, Mr. Roberts was granted a liberal pension for life, in recognition .of his faithful services, and it is a pathetic circumstance that he lived such a very short time to enjoy his rest from active work. The staff presented him' with a handsome solid silver salver, bearing the following inscription :—" Pre- sented to W. B. Roberts, Esq., by the office staff of Wilderspool Brewery, and his colleagues, on his retiring from the position of chief brewer for Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co., Ltd., in whose service he was engaged for 23 years-1886-1909." The workmen under his immediate supervision, at a dinner given to them by Mr. Roberts, presented him with an addvess, the text of which reads as follows :—" W. B. Roberts. Esq. We, the employes of Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co., who have been under your immediate super- vision for the period of '23 years, durine, which you have been engaged as head brewer, and from which position you are about to retire, take this opportunity to congratulate you on your attainment to a position which enables you to pass the rest of your life in retirement. We also desire to- express our sincere and heartfelt appreciation of the many kind acirs, as well as the unfailing courteay, which have always characterized your treatment of every workman under your charge. We wish you and yours health, wealth happiness and long life in your retirement, and trust that this token of our esteem and the small rose bowl accompanying it may serve to keep a sweet place in your memoryfor all your old employes. June, 1909." It was only of late years that Roberts had taken part in Public life. He entered the Town Council in 1907 as one of the representatives of Howley Ward and was a useful member of the Education, Finance and Estates, Street Improvement awl Lighting, Water, and General Purposes Committees. He was pro- minently associated with the Order of Freemasons and his sudden death is deeply regretted by the brethren. He was initiated a member of the "Lodge of Lights " (148), about 22 years ago,- and passed through the chairs. He was qo of the founders of the " Friendship" Lodge and walk:nstalled as W. 1.1. He was also P P.G.D. of West Lancashire. Mr. Roberts, who was a staunch Conservative and Churchman, was of a generous disposition and was always willing to support deserving objects. He took a great interest in sport and athletics and was one of the vice.presidents of the Works Bowling Association as well as president of the Bull's Head team.

Deep and heartfelt is the sympathy with the widow and only son in their tragic bereavement. Quite recently the son, Mr. Victor Roberts, underwent an operation and is still confined to bed. At a meeting of the Warrington and District Licensed Victuallers' Association held at the Saracen's Head Hotel, Wilderspool, on Tuesday afternoon, Mr. Joseph Shilicock (vice-president) presiding ,in the absence of. the president (Alderman John Evans), a vote of condolence was passed with Mrs. Roberts and her son in the sad loss they have sustained in the death of Councillor W, B. Roberts, who had been an honorary member of the association for many years. Mrs. Robert Pierpoint, speaking at a meeting of the Warrington ,Women's Unionist and Tariff Reform League on Thursday, evening, made sympathetic reference to he late Councillor W. B. Roberts, who she said, was a real good stannch Conservative.

div.head: Saturday, July 31, 1909.
div.p: Saturday, July 31, 1909.
THE INFIRMARY. New Honorary Assistant Surgeon Appointed.

A special general meeting of Governors of the War- rington Infirmary and Dispensary was held at the Infirmary yesterday afternoon, Mr. %V. P. Rylands (Chairman of the Board of Management) presiding at the outset in the absence of Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart. (President of the institution). Mrs. Garnett, who wrote apologising for non-atteniance' stated that she was still very much concerned about the lack of Sunday services for the inmates of .the institution and would do anything in her power to obtain what she felt to be so much required. • Apologies were also received from Mr. John Fairclough (who heartily supported the adoption of the proposed new rule), the Rev. R. E. Letheren and Mr. Gcorge Dakin. An objection by Dr. Richmind that the meeting was technically bad and infringed a rule governing the summoning of special meetings was over-ruled by the chairman ho held that the rule had been complied with by the publication of 11 days' notice of the meeting. _

At this stage Sir Gilbert Greenall arrived and took charge of the meeting. Mr. RYLANDS moved the adoption of a new rule giving the Board of Management power to call for the resignation of any honorary officer or member of any Board or Committee, whenever in their opinion - the interests of the institution make it desirable. He pointed out that a similar rule had bean adopted in other institutions, and it was conceivable that in certain circumstances it might be of considerala!e value to the Board of Management. Should nuy CRS3 arise, however improbable, where one of those in an honorary position at the Infirmary did something which was not, in the opinion of the Board, consonant with the best interests of the institution the only course open at the present time was to report the matter publicly to the governors, and produce possibly a scandal. That would he a course of action much more serious than the Board of Management would like to adopt, and con- squently they wculd hesitate very much before they did anything of the kind. Under the new rule there would be no washing of dirty linen in public. Mr. 11. ROBERTS seconded and the resolution was ca7ried with one dissentient.

Dr. IVIANsoN wrote resigning the position of honorary assistant surgeon on his appointment as visiting surgeon to home patients of the institution. • On the motion of the Rev. JOHN YONGE, seconded by the Rev. H. V. PIGOT, Dr. Binns was appointed honorary assistant surgeon in Dr. Manson's place. A vote of thinks to Sir Gilbert Greenell for presiding concluded the meeting.

div.head: WOMEN'S TARIFF REFORM LEAGUE
div.p: WOMEN'S TARIFF REFORM LEAGUE
Mr. Pierpoint and the Budget.

The newly-formed Warrington Women's Unionist and Tariff Reform League held a meeting in the Con- servative Club Assembly Room, On Thursday evening. Mr 3. Pierpoint (president) presided over a good attend- ance and was accompanied on the platform by Lady Greenall, Mrs. Rylands, Mrs. Ralph Johnson, Mrs. Fulton Smith, Mrs. Pierson (Tariff Reform League, London), Mr. R. Pierpoint and Mr. W. Peter Rylands. Amongst others present were : Alderman Bennett, Councillors Fulton Smith and Broadhurst,Mr. and Mrs. W. E. Atkin, Messrs. E. J. Hall, J. Harding, and H. Hayes.

Mrs.-.ToFra'soN announced that they had already g3t hundreds of members "and heaps wishing to join." Mrs. PIERPOINT urged the association to support tariff reform which she contended would be for the betterment of our people. We ought to give our own people a chance in preference to the foreigner. (Applause.) Mrs. PIERSON' delivered a long address, in which she stated that the Association stood for" religion, truth, the highest good of the people and the unity of the Empire." Having dealt with the existing food taxes, she asked: If they must tax the poor woman's cup of tea, why should they not equally tax the rich woman's silk frock ?—and there were plenty of silk frocks coming into this country free of tax to-day. If Free Traders must tax the workingman's tobacco, his little drop of whisky that he wanted when he g3t a bad cold —(laughter)—and his glass of beer, why did they not tax the rich man's imported motor car ?(Applause).Free Traders insisted that we in this country would have to pay the tax imposed on imported goods.lf we putit on the luxuries the rich purchased, it would be the rich people who would be paying the tax, not the working people as they were at the present time. She contended that tariff reform, looked at how they would, decidkdly promised to benefit the workers. (Applause). Lady. GREENALL moved a vote of thanks to Mrs. Pierson, and Mrs. RYLANDS seconded. Mr. R. PIERPOINT, in supporting, said the Govern- ment had at last conceded that they were going to build four extra Dreadnoughts. "I hope to Heaven," he continued," that they are in time. But for tlae first time in the history of our country almost since the last century began, we are now striving and wondering whether our naval power is sufficient or not." Continu- ing, he said they would agree that the present House of Commons was a peculiar one—such, he hoped, as the country would not see again, and, if ever, not for many years. The other night the Government had to be supported by the legitimate Opposition in oppo- sition to their own friends as to the navy, because there were many men who, in the words of one of the supporters of the Government, stated that we ought to be "frankly unprepared." The wayin which a country like ours was to continue to be great and powerful was not to be what that foolish man called"frankly unprepared,"but to be always ready and by being prepared for war, so invariably to get peace. With regard to the Budget, it Might be that it would pass through the House of Commons. He did not know what would become of it afterwards. But it was a flagrant example of "tacking "—that was they wanted a Bill for an avowed certain purpose and instead of sticking solely to that purpose they "tacked" on other things to the Bill. There could be no doubt whatever that the present Budget aimed heavily at the land owners—and when be spoke of land owners they must not think that he was referring to the great land owners entirely, because there were small landowners as well. The Budget also went for the brewers and the licensed victuallers, and was an act of revenge on the part of the Government for the injury which it thought/it had received from the House of Lards and from th 6 Conservative rarty. With regard to land tax Aloe, in the Budget it was pro- posed that a man's land should be valued, at his own expense, assessed for taxation, and that he should have no right of appeal to the Courts of Law. This, he thought, would be the first time in the history of this country that an En?lishman had not the right of appeal to a Court of Law in the matter of taxation. Having had some experience of Government offices and officials, he for one should have the greatest fear of trusting himself and things that belonged to him entirely to the judgment of any man who had to be at the same time taxer and judge. (Applause). Mr. W. P. RYLANDS slid he could not see why tariff , reform should ever have become a party question. Every important nation except England was what was called Protectionist. He should be rather disposed to think that if they took the total number of Protectionist individuals in the world and compared them with the number of Free Trade individuals, the proportion would be very much the same as the proposition of sane persons to lunatics in this country. If they had q. district peopled by nobody but lunatics, no doubt those lunatics would regard the rest of the world as insane, and he was very mach disposed to think that was the Case with the people of this country. Dealing with the question of who would pay the duties imposed, Mr. Rylands said that supposing a commodity was imported which was not produced in this country at all, and a duty was imposed, the consumer was bound to pay the whole of the duty. Supposing that a commodity was produced i in this country n such enormous quantities that there was so much competition at home that the price was driven down to the lowest possible point and we exported large quantities abroad, the foreigner would pay the whole of the duty which might be imposed. They had therefore two extreme cases—the one where we produced none, the consumer paid the whole of the tax; and the other, where we produced to excess, the foreigner paid the whole of it. They got every gradation between these two and the proportion of the duty which the foreigner would pay depended upon the proportion of the home manufacture of thslarticle. A vote of thanks was also passed to the President on the proposition of Mrs. ATKIN, seconded by Miss BASKERVILLE.

div.head: LOCAL WEDDINGS.
div.p: LOCAL WEDDINGS.
Kernick —Dupre.

The wedding took place on Thursday, at Holly Park Wesleyan Church, Hornsey Rise, London, of the Rev. F. Widwyn Kernick, M.A., Wesleyan minister, Penketh, and Miss Maud. Alice Dupr6 of Val Plaisant, St. Heliers, Jer,,ey. The bride was given away by her father, and was charmingly gowned in cream satin de luxe, with a wreath of orange blossom and veil of Brussels net. She carried a lovely bouquet of carnations, roses and white heather. Her two bridesmaids were Miss Kernick and Miss Kerry, who wore dresses of ' white lingerie with pale blue hats and sashes, and carried bouquets of delicate pink sweet peas. The .church had been beautifully decorated, and the .service was conducted by the Rev. F. Kernick (father of the bride- groom) and the Rev. J. Grange Bennett. There was a large gathering of relativres and friends, from Jersey and England. The service was characterised by a quiet simplicity and elegance in harmony with the solemnity of the occasion. Afterwards, a reception was held at St. Heliers, Hornsey Rise, the, residence of the Rev. Grange Bennett and Mrs. Bennett. Subsequently the newly-married pair left- for Bristol, en route for , North Devon and Cornwhll, where the honeythoon is to be spent. Mr. and Mrs. Kernick hope to return to Penketh in about three weeks' time, when their many friends in the district will, no doubt, extend to them a very warm welcome.
Jones— Pierpoint.
MR. AND MRS. E. REDMAYNE JONES.

A pretty wedding of considerable local interest took place at *St. Thomas' Church, St. Ahnes-on-Sea, on Saturday, when Mr. Edward Redmayne Jones, son of Mr. William Jones, " Hendre," Waterloo, Liverpool, was married to Miss Margaret Pierpoint, second daughter of Alderman William Pierpoint, J.P., " Newholme," St. \ Annes-on-Sea, and Latchford, Warrington. Owing to the recent illness of the bride's father, thje wedding was a very quiet one. The Rev. C. H. Ellison, M.A., vicar of the pariah, officiated. Mr. E. Richardson was at the organ and played suit- able selections including Mendelssohn's Wedding March." The bride, who was given away by her father, was charmingly attired in white silk crepe-de-chene over soft white satin, trimmed with Brussels lace. She wore a tulle veil, surmounted with a coronet of orange blossom and myrtle, and carried a lovely bouquet of roses, lilies of the valley, jasniine and orange blossom. Her ornaments were a pearl pendant and gold strap bracelet, the gifts of the bridegroom. She was attended by one bridesmaid, Miss Ruth Earl Griffiths (niece of the bride), who was attired in a white embroidered lingerie dress, trimmed with Valenciennes lace, with hat to match. She carried a basket of marguerite daisies and wore a gold curb bracelet, preBent3 from the bridegroom. Mr. R. Gerrard Pierpoint (brother of the bride) discharged the duties of best man. , 'she church was prettily decorated with palm's and marguerites, beautiful altar flowers being provided by a member of the congregation. Later in the day the happy couple left for London and the Channel Islands, the bride's travelling dress being a silk Tussore coat and skirt, with burnt straw hat trimmed black glace silk and one large pink rose. Many handsome presents were received, including :—To the bridegroom, a silver breakfast dish and case of fish knives and forks and servers from the office staff; to the bride, -silver entrée dish from members of Warrington Dramatig Society, and art metal coal scuttle from nursing staff of the Hahnemann Hospital, Liverpool.

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE. --- " The Great Awakening "
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE. --- " The Great Awakening "

Those who like a play of thrills and sensations will find something to their taste in "The, Great Awakening." It is a clever melodrame, powerfully acted, and has roused large audiences to a high pitch of interest and enthusiasm. The scenes range from the Coast of Africa to London and Monte Carlo, and the many enthralling incidents are realistically pre seated. Mr. Arthur Hales' strong company is headed by Miss Kate Sydney, who, as the unscrupu- lous Lola Selby has a difficult part which she plays with skill. She is convincing, with- out over-doing the emotional side, and works upon the feelings of the audience to a remarkable degree. Mr. Charles Whitlock gives a vigorous and really clever portrayal of James Selby, alias "Pierce," an escaped convict, and Mr. John Davidson shows high talent in the dual role of Sir Henry Merton, Bart., and Jack Merton. Mr. St. John Stuart as Guy Logan, an adventurer, makes the most of an unpopular part, and Mr. C. W. Spencer is admirable as Richard Wilson, Lola's father. The inuch-wronged lovers, Captain Harry Lambert and Molly Merton, are well impersonated by Mr. H. Wallace Curnock and Miss Georgina V. France, while Miss Nana Flensburg and Mr. Willie Scott provide plenty of comic relief. The scenic effects are excellent. As usual there are some pleasing orchestral selections, under the conductorship of Mr. Norman Latham, who has now Undertaken the additional duties of acting manager.

div.head: NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME;
div.p: NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME;

Next Monday at the Royal Court Theatre, the clever young actress-manageress, Miss Ellen Snow, supported by an excellent company, will. present !‘ Why Men Love Women," a charming romantic Anglo-Indian love story, written by Walter Howard, the brilliant author, whose romantic plays, " Her Love against the World," " The Midnight Wedding "and "The Prince and the Beggar Maid, recently delighted crowded houses at the late Sir Henry Irving 's Theatre, The Lyceum, London. " Why Men Love Women" should prove a strong holiday attraction to Warrington play .goers, as it is a fine drama full of stirring incidents, pathos and comedy. The characters include a young English artist, a beautiful heiress who sacrifices her fortune for love, a Russian army captain, a young English 'officer, and some members of comic-opera . company which' has come to grief financially in India, where the action of the play takes place. Each scene is an exquisite picture of that country of gorgeous colour and wonderful atmosphere of mystery and romance. The piece has drawn large audiences in the provinces, and in one large theatre in Manchester, alone over 19,000 people paid for admission in one week.

div.head: Ladies' Bowling Main.
div.p: Ladies' Bowling Main.

A plelsant little function took place last Saturday afternoon at the Rectory, Church-street, namely, the third annual ladies' bowling main. The green which had been 'kindly provided by the Rector, was in excel- lent condition, and some very exciting play was witnessed. An a/ fresco tea was partaken of, after which the party were photographed before returning to the green, to watch the finishing stage of the Main. The Rector and Mrs. Willis also came on the green, and took a „lively interest in the proceedings. At the close the Rector very kindly distributed the prizes to the successful trundlers as follows :-1, Miss M. Hankinson ; 2, Mrs. Carman; 3, Miss L. Lawrence; 4, Mrs, Hughes; 5, Miss G. Lawrence; 6, Mrs. Squire.

TRICKS OF THE CATTLE,: DEALER. "I was foreman, and Lad charge of all the cows, and when any customer who had treated me well wanted a good cow, I let him 'ave it, for the griv'ner didn't Know 'ow much milk they gave—l had to tell 'im. There was one customer that always used to give me ten bob whenever we sold him any cows, and I saw he 'ad the best, though the gitv'nor would try to poke 'irn off with the wrong 'uns. But once," and here George chuckled to himself, " I fairly 'ad a mean swine that gave me thruppence for two 5-gallon cows I picked 'im out. I chucked it gown the gutter, and he come again he asked me to pick 'im out two more. I did. I had 'em ready for him, all bagged up—the two worst cows we got in the whole lot. He comes back in a week, and says to me: I say those two were fair rotters you sent me.' Yes,' I answers, • and so was your money.' " "Farm and Home."
